stories.Headline: Researchers find Chinese agricultural livestreamers ignore AI disclosure mandates
stories.Summary:
Researchers Tianxing Tang and Zhihua Hu conducted an external audit of the Douyin livestreaming platform between June 9 and June 13, 2026. They investigated whether agricultural producers selling their own harvests complied with national mandates requiring labels on synthetic media. The study found that statutory artificial intelligence labeling requirements were entirely invisible among these agricultural producers. Every detected announcement of synthetic media came from software vendors, commercial intermediaries, or commentary channels. No produce growers openly disclosed using artificial intelligence tools across hundreds of evaluated videos and profiles.

The regulatory framework began with the Provisions on the Administration of Deep Synthesis in Internet Information Services in January 2023. It expanded through interim generative artificial intelligence management measures later that year before culminating on September 1, 2025. This final stage included the Measures for the Labeling of AI-Generated Synthetic Content and national standard GB 45438, 2025. These rules require technical providers to embed implicit metadata and explicit notices into synthetic files for platforms to verify. Uploaders must also declare synthetic workflows through platform interfaces and follow national advertising laws for commercial broadcasts.

The researchers stated that public transparency mechanisms fail to show if genuine farmers or automated representations operate digital storefronts. They explained that external observers cannot determine if smallholders reject artificial intelligence or deploy synthetic avatars without mandatory disclosures. The authors advanced the concept of the authenticity penalty to explain why growers might avoid these disclosures. They argued that labeling content as synthetic damages the primary economic asset of farmers who rely on perceived authenticity. Consequently, voluntary compliance is incentive-incompatible for growers because it imposes severe reputational and pricing penalties.

The audit affected the analysis of 10 product categories including navel oranges, apples, peaches, honey, mountain goods, tea, sweet potatoes, rice, and mangoes. These searches returned 67 response files covering 575 videos and 455 unique deduplicated authors. The researchers found that 68.4 percent of accounts retrieved via technical keywords were commercial intermediaries offering software or tutorials. Only 3.2 percent of 189 evaluated policy snippets named authenticity as a farmer asset. No platform-side artificial intelligence labels appeared in the metadata of any of the 575 video records.

Agricultural produce is classified by economists as credence goods because true qualities cannot be verified through pre-purchase inspection. Buyers rely on indexical cues like weathered faces and regional dialects to evaluate the authenticity of the grower. Generative tools and synthetic voices can now fabricate these exact visual and vocal cues associated with rural authenticity. Prior research viewed blockchain as a tool for verification, but generative tools allow third parties to manufacture simulated identities. This dynamic reinforces commercial reliance on specialized third-party marketing firms rather than empowering rural smallholders.

The researchers concluded that effective platform governance cannot depend on public label-reading alone to ensure synthetic transparency. They noted that their audit identifies limitations in public surface monitoring rather than providing definitive proof of illicit non-compliance. It remains open whether smallholders avoid artificial intelligence tools entirely or utilize synthetic scripts and avatars without public declaration. Disentangling these two explanations would require access to internal platform data and private sales metrics. The study highlights a policy tension between promoting rural artificial intelligence adoption and enforcing synthetic transparency.

stories.Headline: China's first fully AI-generated feature film flops at the box office
stories.Summary:
China recently released its first fully AI-generated feature film titled Sanxingdui: Future Past, but the project flopped at the box office. The production was created without any human actors or a traditional camera crew to film the scenes. According to data from the tracker Beacon Pro, the movie earned only about 1.8 million yuan, which is roughly 270,000 US dollars. This meager return occurred after the film had spent three weeks playing in theaters across the country. The 100-minute science fiction story requires viewers to imagine a world decades in the future where rogue algorithms cause catastrophe.

To prevent this disaster, the characters must decipher warnings hidden inside bronze artifacts from the ancient Shu kingdom. The film's reported budget was tens of millions of yuan, meaning the final earnings were well below the initial costs. Audiences rejected the movie because of its disjointed plot and visuals that appeared far too stiff. Viewers described the movie as being obviously AI, which contributed to the lack of ticket sales in cinemas.

This failure happened even as short AI dramas continue to boom on smartphones throughout China. The contrast suggests that while small AI clips are popular, full length AI features may struggle. The production attempted to merge ancient history with futuristic technology, but the execution failed to attract a wide audience. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Colette Kress becomes interim Nvidia CEO to manage legal crises and aggressive AI investments
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang stepped down as the chief executive of Nvidia during a dizzying week in November 2026 after thirty three years of leadership. He left the company following an alleged spy scandal and reports that he had multiple extramarital affairs with various women. Longtime finance chief Colette Kress has now stepped in as the interim chief executive to lead the company through this crisis. This abrupt departure leaves many questions about the future of an artificial intelligence industry that relied on the company's financial backing. The transition occurs just weeks after Huang delivered a keynote at the GTC event in Berlin on October 21, 2026.

Kress must now manage a situation where Huang committed 120 billion dollars in equity investments and sought 250 billion in guarantees for OpenAI. She previously renegotiated the Ohio data center project to cut that financial commitment in half and checked Vice President Nico Caprez. The company planned to acquire Hugging Face for 12.9 billion dollars in September and invest 10 billion dollars into the firm Anthropic. Kress also faces potential federal and congressional investigations into the dealings of Nvidia involving China and the actions of Alice Huang. These changes may shift the company away from circular financing used by firms like CoreWeave, OpenAI, and also the company Anthropic.

Cognitive scientist Gary Marcus stated that Nvidia acted like a bank by backstopping the industry through a process of circular financing. He described Jensen Huang as a swashbuckler who made bets of arbitrary size while many AI businesses struggle to turn profits. Marcus noted that Kress must clean up the legal mess and answer why Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick did not intervene earlier. He believes lawmakers need to know exactly what information Huang shared with Alice Huang during their relationship and the suspected spy scandal. Kress is expected to focus on managing risk and stability rather than opening new lines of business for the company.

Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue expressed his dismay on X, calling the current situation deeply regrettable and a truly sad day. Many AI companies are affected because they relied on the aggressive financial backing and the large bets made by Huang. Some Nvidia engineers are unhappy, with over 1,600 comments on an internal post urging the board to bring Huang back. Analysts suggest that a CFO is the best choice for interim leader to send a message of confidence to markets. The board aims to secure steady leadership while the company deals with extreme instability and the fallout from the scandal.

The company previously operated under an arrangement where Huang made business decisions quickly and intuitively while taking reports directly from executives. This aggressive spending strategy allowed Nvidia to bankroll the AI boom but created risks of overextension that Kress internally opposed. The board chair position has remained vacant since the company was founded, which allowed Huang to operate with very little oversight. Kress has spent thirteen years at Nvidia and is known for avoiding the public spotlight and choosing her words very carefully. This background in finance contrasts with the engineering background of Huang, who led the company for over three decades.

Harvey Jones, a mentor to Huang for twenty five years, has been appointed as the new chairman of the Nvidia board. The board will now supervise and check the strategy of the CEO to reduce the financial risk of the company. It remains open whether the long careers of Jones and Kress will prevent them from fully breaking with the past. The planned acquisitions of Hugging Face and the investment in Anthropic may now be subject to revision or total cancellation. It is not yet clear if the board will eventually heed the employee sentiment and find a way to return Huang.

stories.Headline: Ninepoint files prospectus for Anthropic HighShares ETF with covered call strategy
stories.Summary:
Ninepoint Partners LP filed and obtained a receipt for a final prospectus qualifying units of the Ninepoint Anthropic HighShares ETF, the company announced on November 13, 2026. The ETF is expected to begin trading on the Toronto Stock Exchange under the ticker ANHI, subject to satisfying the TSX's original listing requirements. Trading is expected to start the business day following the completion of an initial public offering by Anthropic, PBC, currently anticipated on or about November 19, 2026. The ETF combines leveraged exposure to Anthropic, the company behind Claude, with a professionally managed covered call strategy designed to generate income. Ninepoint is based in Toronto and oversees approximately $8 billion in assets under management and institutional contracts.

ANHI will offer a management fee of 0.29% and intends to pay twice-monthly cash distributions, like other ETFs in the Ninepoint HighShares suite. The ETF seeks long-term capital appreciation through purchasing and holding, on a levered basis, Class A common stock of Anthropic, and regular cash distributions. ANHI will hold up to 100% of its total assets, including assets acquired with borrowings, in Anthropic Class A common stock and write covered call options on up to 50% of those holdings. The covered call strategy will be reviewed monthly for cash flow sustainability, and the risk rating is High. The ETF is considered an alternative mutual fund under applicable securities legislation, permitting strategies generally prohibited for conventional mutual funds, such as investing up to 20% of net asset value in a single issuer, borrowing cash, short selling beyond conventional limits and employing leverage.

Karl Cheong, CFA, Executive Vice President and Head of ETFs at Ninepoint Partners, said Anthropic's upcoming public listing is an opportunity to invest directly in the company, and he anticipates strong interest from Canadians seeking TSX-listed exposure. Cheong said Ninepoint designed ANHI to provide Canadian investors a way to participate in Anthropic's growth potential while seeking regular income through a covered call strategy. Ninepoint is the investment manager of the ETF. The ETF does not have a fixed distribution amount, and the amount of ordinary cash distributions may fluctuate, based on the Manager's assessment of prevailing market conditions.

The amount and date of any cash distributions will be announced in advance by press release. The ETF intends to pay cash distributions based on its ability to generate monthly cash flows from writing covered call options and any dividends received on portfolio securities, as applicable. The Manager will review the level of distributions quarterly to consider sustainability, and may change the frequency of distributions at its complete discretion, with any change announced by press release. The ETF is generally exposed to risks including absence of an active market for ETF Units risk, ADR risk, artificial intelligence industry and regulatory risk, borrowing risk, collateral risk, concentration risk, covered call strategy risk, currency risk, cybersecurity risk, derivatives risk, equity investment risk, exchange risk, foreign investment risk, foreign withholding tax risk, halted trading of ETF Units risk, inflation risk, interest rate risk, large capitalization issuer risk, leverage risk, market risk, no ownership risk, options availability and liquidity risk, Passive Launch Public Issuer Investment Risk, performance risk, regulatory risk, risk associated with an investment in the Launch Public Issuer, specific issuer risk, tax risk and trading price of ETF Units risk.

Commissions, trailing commissions, management fees, performance fees if any, and other expenses may all be associated with investing in the ETF. The ETF is not guaranteed, its values change frequently and past performance may not be repeated. stories.Headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO and leaves open source AI without its most influential advocate
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as the chief executive officer of Nvidia on November 14, 2026, according to a report by Nathan Lambert. This sudden departure is described as a decapitation that creates a major setback for the American open model ecosystem. Lambert notes that the timing of the announcement followed a midterm political swing in the United States. The resignation removes a powerful champion who had supported open source AI for about two years. This event leaves the open model movement without its most influential advocate and protector.

Nvidia must now stabilize its operations and deliver to customers over the next 24 months to prevent a total implosion. The company faces challenges including potential chip smuggling investigations and the loss of talent to poaching sharks. The open model economy is currently in its nascency and requires established revenue flows and clear use cases. Some Western models like Inkling 2 Small from Thinking Machines are far behind Kimi K3.1 Pro. Meanwhile, Mira is reportedly seeking a new funding round at a valuation of 40 billion dollars.

Nathan Lambert says that Jensen Huang was more than a cheerleader because he used his power to prevent crises. He argues that the open model economy has correctly focused on enterprise post training and the ownership of intelligence. Lambert believes that the movement is regressing in operational capability just as attacks and stakes are destined to rise. He suggests that open model believers must now engage in soul searching and build a new coalition. The author claims that the shoes Huang emptied will never be fully refilled.

Dylan Patel, the CEO of SemiAnalysis, says that talent is a bigger problem than money for the open model ecosystem. He notes that the most talented people work at OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepMind, and Meta, leaving others split across startups. Inference startups are struggling to get chips because OpenAI and Anthropic are buying up most of the available capacity. Chris Hughes warns that blunt federal and state regulations could create a costly moat for the largest players. These regulatory changes would only benefit the biggest companies that can afford to navigate the complex rules.

The articles state that Nvidia's business operations are extremely dependent on Jensen Huang as an operator and a founder. Huang had flooded the open model zone with funding, but this financial support is very likely to dry up. The open model ecosystem has faced pressure from the AI safety community and Democratic government funding for regulation. There is a recurring concern that a popular Chinese open weight model could trigger a cybersecurity crisis. The media often drives narratives based on harm and risk rather than the availability of exact information.

The open model movement may now turn to hyperscalers like Satya Nadella, Andy Jassy, or Mark Zuckerberg for support. The industry must determine if a truly frontier open model player can be incubated within the United States. It remains unclear if Thinking Machines or other small labs can overcome their deficits in compute and deployment. The articles leave open whether the open model economy can become a meaningful engine without Huang's protection. Future success depends on whether the ecosystem can survive sloppy state level and national regulations.

stories.Headline: Majority of Indians prefer instant AI health answers over waiting for doctors in BCG survey
stories.Summary:
A Boston Consulting Group global survey found that 61 percent of Indians prefer instant AI health answers over waiting for doctors. This study was conducted during July and August 2026 and included 9,914 consumers across 10 different countries. The findings were published on November 15, 2026, by Sumit Jha in a report about the consumerisation of health care. This shift shows that more people in India are using digital technology to seek medical information instead of professionals. The report indicates that patients are increasingly seeking greater control over their treatment decisions, convenience, and their healthcare expenditure.

India scored 66 out of 100 on the Healthcare Consumerization Index, ranking second behind China, which scored 72. The United Arab Emirates ranked third at 63, while Brazil followed in fourth place with a score of 62. In India, 60 percent trust digital health information as much as professional advice, which is 19 percentage points above average. Additionally, 78 percent of Indian respondents want more control over treatment choices, and 73 percent want control over costs. Around 68 percent expect retail level convenience, and 58 percent view medicines as common consumer goods.

Chris Meier of BCG stated that consumer patients are reshaping rules to expect more intuitive, responsive, and personalized health care experiences. He is a managing director and senior partner who co authored the report on the consumerisation of the health industry. Sabrina Kristic, also a managing director and senior partner, noted that health care decisions are more complex than cosmetics. She warned that these decisions have potentially serious consequences, even if products blur the line between health and lifestyle categories. Both authors believe that providers must now balance patient choice and convenience with clinical quality and patient outcomes.

Millennials were most likely to prefer instant AI answers at 52 percent, followed by Generation Z at 47 percent. Baby boomers showed the lowest preference for these digital tools, with only 25 percent choosing AI over a doctor. Doctors from Harvard and Johns Hopkins warn that AI mass surveillance can cause chronic anticipatory stress and physical sickness. Vulnerable groups, including undocumented immigrants, may avoid clinics or pharmacies due to a fear of persecution from surveillance tools. These experts argue that AI surveillance is a structural determinant of health that can create avoidable health inequities.

The BCG report explains that digital platforms can improve information access but may also expose users to fragmented services and misinformation. People with limited digital literacy or confidence may be excluded from these new digital first models of health care. Meanwhile, the New England Journal of Medicine highlights how private companies now control the data ecosystems used for surveillance. Traditional surveillance required human oversight, but AI can continuously comb through social media, financial transactions, and geolocation records. This allows private actors to analyze vast amounts of personal data and share it with government agencies.

Next, healthcare providers must find ways to balance transparency and convenience with equity and the overall quality of patient outcomes. Clinicians can help by documenting patient fears about data usage to provide evidence for policymakers and various legal litigators. Some states, including Washington, Nevada, and Connecticut, have passed laws to extend privacy protections to certain consumer health data. More than 20 state attorneys general have sued the federal government for sharing Medicaid data with Palantir and ICE. The articles leave open whether AI will serve population health or become a driver of structural harm.
Orgs: johns hopkins university school of medicine

stories.Headline: Bank of America survey finds 72% of Americans plan to avoid AI for holiday shopping
stories.Summary:
A Bank of America survey released in November 2026 found that 72% of Americans do not plan to use AI tools for holiday shopping this year, up from 49% in 2025. The 23-percentage-point jump was reported by Fortune on November 14, 2026, in a story by Tatiana Sataua. Tech companies have spent the past year teaching AI how to shop, and Adobe expects traffic from AI tools to U.S. retail sites to jump 130% this holiday season. Google has introduced an AI-powered shopping cart, Meta's Muse can search for products and prepare purchases for approval, and OpenAI's new ChatGPT Wallet lets eligible users pay for purchases through an AI agent. The survey suggests a gap between the industry's ambitions for AI shopping and what consumers say they want from it.

Among those who do not plan to use the technology, 42% cited personal or ethical reasons, 37% said it takes away the personal aspect of gift giving, and 26% said they do not trust AI recommendations. The survey found that 87% of Americans expect to spend the same amount or less on holiday shopping this year. It also found that 63% said they base their spending strictly on their own budgets rather than what friends or family spend. The survey found that 17% plan to use AI to compare prices or deals, 14% for gift ideas or inspiration, and 7% to write messages or cards, and respondents could select more than one use. Bank of America said it asked the AI shopping question the same way in both years, though the survey only measures intentions, and the bank does not have data showing whether shoppers are actually using AI less.

Lora Monfared, head of consumer credit card products at Bank of America, said shoppers may be growing more selective about when AI is worth using, especially as they keep a closer eye on holiday spending. She told Fortune that some of last year's curiosity about AI may also have worn off, and that we could be seeing a bit of AI fatigue. She said gift shopping is personal, and people want to feel good about what they are giving. She said that same budget-focused approach may be shaping how consumers use AI and social media to shop. Monfared's comments were reported by Fortune in its November 14, 2026 story.

Colleen Kirk, a professor of marketing and management at New York Institute of Technology, told Fortune that the hesitation may have less to do with what AI can do than what shoppers feel they lose by using it. She said gift giving is a very personal act, and gifts, especially to close family and friends, are given from the heart. In her research studying consumer psychology, she has found that consumers can feel guilty when they use AI to write heartfelt messages because the words no longer feel entirely their own. She said that effort creates what researchers call psychological ownership, or the feeling of having a personal stake in something, and that using AI can take away this sense of ownership. Kirk said AI may have a more natural place in the less personal parts of shopping, such as finding coupons, comparing prices, or buying groceries and household supplies, and she suggested consumers come up with their own ideas first, then turn to AI to help narrow their options.

Amazon.com Inc. is considering building a global product database to minimize buyers' use of Google and other websites, according to a Reuters-reviewed internal document reported by GuruFocus on November 13, 2026. The initiative, called World Product Graph, gathers data on internet-sold products, including items Amazon does not sell, so shoppers can compare goods, find newer models, and buy without leaving Amazon. The project would merge manufacturer and retail website data, Coke and Bayer are sharing product information, and Amazon is considering a Procter & Gamble experiment. Amazon's Alexa for Shopping, formerly Rufus, may benefit from the project, though the assistant's replies were wrong or partial and the service was pricey, according to an internal paper. Amazon refuted the paper, stating that its shopping assistant is 97% accurate worldwide, and the concept included an October 2027 start date that Amazon has not verified.

Amazon said the paper is preliminary and may not reflect its current goals, and retail sales and advertising income depend on Amazon's shopping traffic. The Reuters-reviewed document reflects competition from AI shopping bots that can compare and buy across sites. Fortune reported that it is an awkward moment for tech companies betting that shoppers will eventually trust AI to do more than recommend products, including making purchases on their behalf. Kirk said research has found that people feel more ownership over an outcome when they generate their own ideas before using AI. She said some consumers may decide that letting AI handle the less personal tasks is a worthwhile trade-off, and that consumers might just decide it is worth it to give up a little bit of ownership of the process in exchange for getting more time for those special emotional connections with the humans they love.

stories.Headline: Cisco raises AI infrastructure sales forecast to $9 billion as Cerebras and CoreWeave beat estimates
stories.Summary:
Cisco reported quarterly results that beat estimates on both revenue and profit, and it raised its forecast for AI infrastructure sales to hyperscalers to $9 billion for the fiscal year, more than double the prior year, according to an article by Brian Sozzi published on Yahoo Finance on November 13, 2026. Cerebras, an AI infrastructure company, also beat on sales and earnings, and it guided to a core gross margin of 47% to 49% and sales of $310 million to $330 million for the current quarter, against analyst estimates of a 42.1% margin and $271 million in sales. CoreWeave beat on the top and bottom lines earlier in the week and pushed back on the view that it would need high-yield debt to fund growth, and its shares rose 22% over the week. The article tied the moves to an AI trade that may be back after an early fall slumber, in a week dominated by coverage of scandals involving Jensen Huang, whom the article described as having lost the CEO role at Nvidia. Cisco CEO Chuck Robbins said the company was executing against its strategy and seeing growing demand as customers invest in infrastructure for what he called the AI or SI era, and KeyBanc analyst Brandon Nispel said the stock looks attractively valued after earnings.

Barclays analyst Tom O'Malley said key customers remain intact and Cerebras is adding new hyperscalers, but the industry is seeing delays across many providers that are slowing the OAI ramp and could push the timing of revenue. O'Malley added that the stock had fallen 33% over the past month against a 14% drop in the SOX index, and he said clearing the bear case and adding customers should more than offset industry-wide concerns about those delays in the near term. Cerebras shares rose 13% in premarket trading on Friday, and the article said the new focus should be on execution of OAI and the new customer set. CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator said the company already has a robust pipeline of customers competing for capacity, and at current pricing levels the 2027 renewals would generate approaching $4 billion of incremental annualized revenue with no additional capex required. Intrator said that figure grows to nearly $10 billion of annualized incremental revenue when 2028 renewals are included, and he said that if data center construction across the sector were to slow, installed compute would become scarcer and GPU pricing might stay higher for longer.

The article listed related headlines, including one saying Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang addressed a CoreWeave stock plunge and said he was optimistic, and another saying CoreWeave stock sank as the resignation of Jensen Huang rippled through the AI trade. The article gave no further detail on the Huang resignation beyond those references and the mention of scandals. The article's market data showed Nvidia shares at $160.90, down 3.19%, and CoreWeave at $52.04, down 8.06%, while Cerebras stood at $108.36, up 10.85%, and the Nasdaq Composite was at 25,033.07, down 1.31%. The article did not say what happens next beyond the analysts' near-term views and the company guidance for the current quarter. It did not give a date for the Huang resignation or name a successor at Nvidia, and it did not describe the scandals beyond the word itself.

stories.Headline: Google open-sources AQuA to diagnose production AI agent failures
stories.Summary:
Google open-sourced its Ambient Quality Agent, known as AQuA, a reference implementation that analyzes production AI agent sessions, verifies recurring failure patterns and investigates root causes against deployed source revisions. Google did this, and TechGig published its report on Nov 14, 2026 at 05:00 AM IST, while InfoQ published Leela Kumili's report on Nov 13, 2026. The tool targets silent quality regressions that conventional infrastructure monitoring can miss, such as agents ignoring user preferences or skipping required tool calls while returning successful responses. AQuA runs alongside an agent in Google Cloud, outside its request path, reading telemetry from Cloud Trace, Cloud Logging or BigQuery. It samples up to 1,000 recent sessions per run and processes them through five stages: sampling, reviewing, clustering findings, verifying candidate clusters and tracking issues.

Developers can configure domain-specific quality criteria through a goal.md file and add deterministic custom metrics, and AQuA can run on a schedule, after a deployment or on demand. For root cause analysis, AQuA compares failing sessions with an immutable source snapshot captured at deployment, and its diagnosis agent identifies relevant code or instructions, cites file and line ranges and proposes changes when the cause lies in the repository. It can also attribute failures to external dependencies, tool handoffs or retrieved data, but AQuA does not apply fixes or open pull requests automatically. Google evaluated 32 sessions from a multi-agent travel application, identifying 42 findings grouped into nine candidate clusters, and the verifier rejected three unsupported clusters after checking up to three full transcripts per candidate cluster, leaving six verified issues. Two involved bypassing seat availability checks and losing a traveler's vegan preference during delegation, and after developers modified prompts and replayed the sessions, seat-selection bypasses fell from 15 sessions to two, dietary-preference omissions dropped from seven to zero and sessions passing all checks increased from five to 13.

The Google blog post states that an insight is its citations, not a self-reported confidence score, and that findings link to supporting traces, with proposed root causes required to reference valid lines in the deployed snapshot. AQuA tracks findings as NEW, RECURRING or automatically RESOLVED after 14 days without being observed, and Google identifies sampling limits and incomplete reproduction of external state as constraints. Google's Agent Platform evaluation service supports regression testing and production quality monitoring, while Arize Phoenix provides open-source tracing and evaluation, and AQuA focuses on grouping production failures and linking verified findings to deployed source code. Google's open-source implementation helps teams integrate production agent diagnosis into development and evaluation workflows, according to the articles. The Google blog post describes the citations as the insight rather than a self-reported confidence score.

Reacting to the announcement on LinkedIn, Dmytro Aprelenko, engineering manager at Redcore, wrote that agent orchestration definitely needs better continuous diagnosis to catch these loops early. AQuA validates source references and links findings to supporting traces, and cluster verification filters false positives, though it cannot confirm every session exhibits the same failure. The articles state that these results came from controlled replay, not production traffic, and that sampling can miss rare failures while replay may not reproduce external state. The tool is affected by these constraints, and teams integrating production agent diagnosis into development and evaluation workflows are the users the open-source implementation serves. The articles do not name further individuals beyond Dmytro Aprelenko of Redcore and author Leela Kumili of InfoQ.

The articles give as background that AQuA is a reference implementation designed to analyze production AI agent sessions, verify recurring failure patterns and investigate root causes against deployed source revisions. They state that the tool targets silent quality regressions conventional infrastructure monitoring can miss, such as agents ignoring user preferences or skipping required tool calls while returning successful responses. They describe AQuA operating alongside an agent in Google Cloud, outside its request path, drawing telemetry from Cloud Trace, Cloud Logging or BigQuery. They note that Google evaluated 32 sessions from a multi-agent travel application, identifying 42 findings grouped into nine candidate clusters, with six issues confirmed after verification. They add that the verifier rejected three unsupported clusters after checking up to three full transcripts per candidate cluster.

The articles state that AQuA can run on a schedule, after a deployment or on demand, and that developers can configure domain-specific quality criteria using a goal.md file and add deterministic custom metrics. They say AQuA tracks findings as NEW, RECURRING or automatically RESOLVED after 14 days without being observed, and that Google identifies sampling limits and incomplete reproduction of external state as constraints. They note that Google's Agent Platform evaluation service supports regression testing and production quality monitoring, while Arize Phoenix provides open-source tracing and evaluation. They state that AQuA does not apply fixes or open pull requests automatically, and that its open-source implementation helps teams integrate production agent diagnosis into development and evaluation workflows. The articles leave open how AQuA performs beyond the controlled replay of 32 sessions and how the sampling limits and incomplete reproduction of external state affect diagnosis in production traffic.

stories.Headline: MeitY seeks data collection details from Pronto, Snabbit and Urban Company's InstaHelp over physical AI training
stories.Summary:
The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology sought details from home services platforms about their collection of first-person video and sensor data from gig workers. The ministry asked Pronto, Snabbit and Urban Company's InstaHelp for information on data used to train physical AI models. A meeting chaired by MeitY secretary S Krishnan brought together senior executives from quick home services platforms and other technology and robotics companies. The meeting discussed concerns around workers' consent, consumer privacy and data sovereignty, according to a report by ET. Officials are concerned that recordings of everyday household activities could infringe workers' rights, compromise consumer privacy and pose risks to national data security.

The ministry sought details on the standard operating procedures companies follow for collecting, processing and storing such data. It also sought information on safeguards for obtaining workers' consent and protecting the privacy of other individuals captured in the recordings. MeitY further sought clarity on whether companies were selling, sharing or transferring the collected data to physical AI developers outside India. It asked Pronto to submit details of its data collection practices and the SOPs it follows, ET reported, citing people familiar with the discussions. Pronto confirmed it was running an opt-in pilot involving first-person video recordings of household chores, initially available only to customers who actively opted in during booking and limited to less than 0.01% of its users.

Pronto said it participated in the meeting as part of a broader industry consultation involving home services platforms, robotics companies and other stakeholders. A spokesperson said the consultation gave the ministry and industry participants an opportunity to exchange perspectives, share existing practices and discuss opportunities and challenges emerging from the evolving AI landscape. The spokesperson said Pronto shared its current practices as part of this exchange and looks forward to continued engagement with MeitY and other industry stakeholders. Pronto stated that raw footage was deleted immediately after work completion, while an anonymised, end-to-end encrypted recording remained accessible only to customers for 48 hours. Pronto said this anonymised footage was subsequently used for AI training, as outlined in its terms.

Snabbit clarified that it had conducted a limited assessment of the technology in a controlled training-centre environment but decided against proceeding with the proposal. Urban Company founder Abhiraj Singh Bhal said the company neither records inside customers' homes nor plans to do so. Inc42 has reached out to Snabbit and Urban Company for their comments on the development, and the story will be updated upon receiving responses. Concerns were also reportedly raised about India becoming a source of cheap training data for foreign AI companies. Executives suggested that the country should focus on developing its own physical AI capabilities rather than merely supplying data to overseas developers.

The development comes shortly after Pronto faced scrutiny over a pilot programme to record household chores using cameras worn by service professionals to generate training data for robotics systems. The controversy also brought Snabbit and Urban Company under scrutiny over their potential involvement in this. In July, Pronto formalised its data collection experiment through Verified, an opt-in premium service in which professionals wear head-mounted or body-mounted cameras during visits. Last month, Pronto founder Anjali Sardana launched Provision Labs, a San Francisco-based physical AI venture that will collect data to train and test AI systems designed to perform real-world tasks using robots and other machines. Provision Labs also announced the acquisition of Mumbai-based Basilisk Industries, a startup focused on perception technologies, and Basilisk founder Shourya Watwani will lead Provision's hardware efforts and work on its in-house post-processing models.

The relationship between Pronto's household data collection and Provision Labs' operations remains unclear. Inc42 said the story will be updated upon receiving responses from Snabbit and Urban Company. The articles do not say what action MeitY will take after reviewing the details submitted by the platforms. The articles do not say whether the ministry set any deadline for the companies to respond. The articles do not say whether other home services platforms beyond Pronto, Snabbit and Urban Company's InstaHelp were asked for details.

stories.Headline: Singapore probes Super Micro over potential false declarations regarding server purchases
stories.Summary:
The Ministry of Home Affairs identified Super Micro Computer as part of a larger probe into potential false declarations regarding server purchases. This investigation began in February 2025 and involves the US-based server supplier, which has known links to the chipmaker Nvidia. Singapore authorities stated on November 12 that the firm has provided limited cooperation during the ongoing inquiry. The government also noted that the US Department of Justice and the Federal Bureau of Investigation provided limited assistance despite repeated requests since September 2025.

The probe involves Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed and alleged Chinese spy, who was barred from re-entering Singapore in February. US authorities are investigating whether entities linked to Huang attempted to smuggle Super Micro products into China. Separately, co-founder Yih-Shyan Wally Liaw and two other men were charged in the US for conspiring to divert 2.5 billion US dollars of AI technology to China starting around October 2023. Additionally, two Super Micro employees were among nine people indicted in Taiwan for illegally exporting 130 B300 servers to Chinese customers.

Super Micro stated on November 13 that it has been responsive to inquiries and fully cooperated with officials in the US, Taiwan, and Singapore. The company denied that Megaspeed was ever a customer and claimed to maintain a robust compliance programme to protect American innovation. Regarding the US charges, Wally Liaw pleaded not guilty, while former contractor Ting-Wei Willy Sun pleaded guilty to four counts including smuggling and defrauding the country. The firm continues to operate a small office in Singapore located at Metropolis Tower 1 in Buona Vista.

stories.Headline: Vertiv launches ecosystem with Dow and Solenis to manage AI liquid cooling
stories.Summary:
Vertiv launched a global ecosystem initiative to help data centre operators manage and optimise liquid cooling infrastructure for artificial intelligence workloads, the company announced on November 12, 2026. The offering combines an expanded collaboration with materials science company Dow and a new partnership with specialty chemicals and water treatment solutions provider Solenis. Together the partnerships will deliver end-to-end thermal and fluid management services, Vertiv said. The announcement comes as rapid growth of AI workloads drives higher computing densities in data centres, increasing the need for advanced liquid cooling systems. Vertiv said the ecosystem brings together its infrastructure, monitoring and global service capabilities with expertise in coolant technologies, fluid chemistry and water treatment.

The ecosystem integrates infrastructure, monitoring and global service capabilities, according to Vertiv. Dipti Singh's sponsored DataCenterDynamics piece, dated November 13, 2026, says the primary facility water system serves as the heat-rejection backbone for the coolant distribution units that protect the racks. A heat exchanger inside the CDU sits between the technology cooling system and the facility water system, so facility water never enters the servers. Singh puts the heat-transfer relation as Q = UAΔT, where heat moved equals how readily heat crosses the exchanger surface times the surface area times the temperature difference. ASHRAE's integrated design guidance, part of its AI Data Center Energy Performance Framework, says rack densities have climbed from roughly 120 kW to several hundred kilowatts, with megawatt-class racks expected in the near term.

Ron Bednar, Senior Vice President of Global and Americas Services at Vertiv, said AI is changing liquid cooling from an equipment decision into a system-management imperative. He added that operators need to manage thermal infrastructure, fluid health, monitoring and lifecycle service as one interconnected discipline. Bednar believes managing these complex interdependencies and fluid chemistry together will help operators improve system efficiency and uptime, reduce risk and extend equipment life. Singh argues that operators should stop treating the system as a building utility inspected on a schedule and should manage it continuously as an engineered thermal system. She writes that primary-side fouling, low flow, unstable temperature, biological growth and corrosion debris each eat into the CDU's thermal margin.

Singh says the facility and technology loops need separate chemistry specifications, and the parameters monitored on the facility side should look much like those on the technology loop. Her list includes pH and conductivity, chloride, hardness, alkalinity and silica, dissolved oxygen where relevant, inhibitor residual and glycol concentration, suspended solids and corrosion metals, and microbial indicators. She tells engineers to drop the assumption that deionized water is safe by default, because without buffering and inhibitors it can aggressively pick up ions from the metals and other materials it touches. Steven Lucente, a business development manager for Xylem's Applied Water business who leads its data center business development, wrote in an October 5, 2026 article in Data Center Knowledge sponsored by Xylem's Bell & Gossett that the power a data center draws can bring a water footprint of its own. Manfreid Chua, ZutaCore's VP of Business Development, AI and Sustainability, cites IEA figures in an Enterprise Viewpoint piece and argues the challenge of supporting much higher computational density while using energy and resources responsibly starts at the chip.

Singh says specifications should spell out capped storage for pipe, clean methods of assembly and the use of temporary strainers, and should set flushing velocity, turnover volume, passivation criteria, acceptance limits for differential pressure across filters, endpoints for particles or turbidity, and rules for preserving branches that stay idle until a later phase. She recommends checking headers, branches and CDU connections against both the initial and the expanded loads, and says design reviews should map which racks lose cooling in each failure. Commissioning should record clean-system performance at representative loads and test how controls respond to failures, she says. She also covers the tradeoff behind every choice of heat rejection: evaporative systems use more water but less power, a closed loop recirculates its coolant and uses little water itself but isn't zero-water, and dry cooling avoids evaporation but runs more compressor and fan power, which pushes power usage effectiveness up. Her rule of thumb is that water-stressed sites with plenty of power may accept that penalty, while power-constrained sites with plenty of water may favor evaporative cooling.

Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's 2025 update says data centers could account for 9.5 to 15.3% of US electricity by 2030, and the IEA estimates data centers worldwide consumed about 415 TWh in 2024 and projects use could reach about 945 TWh by 2030, with AI a major driver. ASHRAE says integrated liquid-cooled facilities can achieve a PUE of about 1.10 versus about 1.4 to 1.6 for traditional designs, and its framework says warm-water, chiller-less cooling enables near-zero water use in many climates. Singh notes that water usage effectiveness counts water per kWh of IT energy and leaves out the water used to generate the electricity. Lucente suggests project teams begin with the full water cycle: the source of the water, the quality it needs, how it is treated and moved, how much can be reused, how heat is rejected and what happens before discharge. ASHRAE says that when integrated design is not applied effectively, facilities risk stranded capacity, operational instability and costly retrofits.

stories.Headline: ReNew plans ₹80,000 crore Andhra Pradesh investment for green data centre and silicon manufacturing
stories.Summary:
ReNew Energy Global announced in November 2026 that it plans to invest about ₹80,000 crore in Andhra Pradesh for data centre infrastructure and clean energy manufacturing. The plan includes a 1 GW green hyperscale data centre in Anakapalli that is designed to run on renewable energy. The company has allocated ₹67,000 crore for the data centre and ₹11,000 crore for polysilicon and metallurgical silicon facilities in Anakapalli and Nellore. It also plans to invest ₹1,500 crore in a permanent magnet manufacturing facility in Rambilli, with commissioning expected by March 2029.

Separately, ReNew will set up the ReNew Centre for Technical Excellence in Visakhapatnam under the PM SETU Scheme. The centre will develop a cluster of five industrial training institutes in Gajuwaka. ReNew already makes solar cells and modules and is developing a 6.5 GW ingot and wafer facility in Anakapalli, expected to be commissioned by March 2028. The new facilities will add polysilicon and metallurgical silicon production to its existing operations.

The investment comes as India expands its data centre capacity to support artificial intelligence and cloud computing. Installed capacity grew from about 375 MW in 2020 to 1.57 GW by August 2026 and is projected to reach nearly 8 GW by 2030. The articles say power availability, water consumption and project approval timelines remain challenges for the sector. Google announced in October 2025 that it would invest about $15 billion, or ₹1.3 lakh crore, in an AI infrastructure hub in Visakhapatnam between 2026 and 2030.

Clean Max Enviro Energy Solutions also signed a preliminary agreement with the Andhra Pradesh Economic Development Board for an investment of about ₹50,000 crore. Its proposal includes 3 GW of combined wind and solar capacity and 1 GW of pumped hydro storage. These would supply a 2 GW green compute factory in Kurnool, developed with Neysa. Neysa, an AI cloud provider, will anchor 1 GW of the facility's IT load.

stories.Headline: Samsung SDI and LG Energy Solution showcase AI data center battery systems at RE+ 2026
stories.Summary:
Samsung SDI and LG Energy Solution will compete at RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas starting November 17. These two companies will showcase energy storage systems and backup power solutions for artificial intelligence data centers. They disclosed their participation plans on November 15 for the three day renewable energy trade show. The event draws about 40,000 visitors and 1,300 companies to the largest renewable energy show in North America. Both firms are targeting North American orders by emphasizing their local production capacity for these battery systems.

LG Energy Solution will use a 279 square meter booth to show the JF3 AC LINK with US-made LFP batteries. This product increases energy density by 26 percent and uses AI and digital twin technologies for grid stabilization. Samsung SDI will exhibit the SBB 2.0 using locally produced LFP prismatic cells in a 20-foot container. Samsung will also show the U8A3 prismatic battery using lithium manganese oxide for uninterruptible power supply applications. LG will display the JP6 Rack for UPS and BBU products based on cylindrical 2170 batteries.

Kang Chang-beom of LG Energy Solution said stable power storage and efficient operations are essential for AI industry growth. He stated the company will become an energy platform by combining battery technology with intelligent operations and North American production. Samsung SDI claims the U8A3 is the first to pass all UL Solutions large-scale indoor fire test criteria. An industry official noted that companies now focus on profitability rather than the cutthroat competition seen in the past. This shift follows a trend where the three major battery firms moved toward making profits this year.

The competition affects Big Tech clients like Amazon, Microsoft, and Google who need cooling and power for AI chips. LG Energy Solution is sitting out a 1,180MW South Korean auction, leaving Samsung SDI and SK On to compete. This auction totals about 7.08GWh in storage capacity, which is larger than the first two rounds combined. Samsung SDI has about 15GWh of production capacity in South Korea with roughly 5GWh of remaining supply. SK On has about 3GWh of LFP capacity converted from an EV line in Seosan for deliveries.

Samsung Electronics previously spent 1.5 billion euros to acquire Germany's Flakt Group for data center climate control technologies. The company is now pursuing US cooling maker Modine to gain North American production facilities and customer networks. Modine recently began mass producing 2 to 3 megawatt chillers at a 63,400 square meter plant in Grand Prairie, Texas. Modine's data center revenue reached 439.7 million dollars in the third quarter, which is up 95 percent from last year. Samsung is also building a 240 billion won production line in Gwangju to start operating in early 2028.

Samsung may acquire Modine for 7.5 billion to 8 billion dollars through a merger agreement or a tender offer. The deal requires approval from two-thirds of voting rights, meaning about 35.41 million votes in favor are needed. LG Electronics is also competing by building a chiller plant in Virginia to begin operating in the first half of 2027. Other competitors like Daikin and Vertiv are expanding through acquisitions to win large projects from North American Big Tech firms. The articles leave open whether Samsung shareholders or Modine's board will ultimately agree to the proposed acquisition.

stories.Headline: Researchers introduce ChemInsight benchmark to evaluate chemistry reasoning in large language models
stories.Summary:
Changyu Hu and nine other authors introduced a benchmark called ChemInsight on November 14, 2026, to evaluate large language models on chemistry tasks. This new tool assesses whether these models can handle multi-step reasoning and structured chemical understanding through a specific set of challenging questions. The researchers designed the system to diagnose the reasoning capabilities of various models by using a two-dimensional scoring method for evaluation. This benchmark consists of 203 chemistry questions organized into 50 bundles to support the scope and depth scoring evaluation scheme. The team evaluated ten representative large language models and found that their performance was consistently low across all the tested metrics.

The ChemInsight system requires scope scores and depth scores, which were below 30 percent and 11 percent for the ten tested models. The research paper spans 16 pages and includes 6 figures, with Changyu Hu, Yiming Zou, and Xin Tang contributing equally to work. Zhenduo Zhang, Wang Ren, and Xiao Li served as the corresponding authors for the study on chemistry understanding and reasoning in models. In Taiwan, the AI Evaluation Center began ranking models in September based on language proficiency, Taiwanese society, and specific Taiwanese values. These rankings include the GSAT university entrance exam, while the startup APMIC rose from 15th to 1st place between September and October.

The authors of the chemistry study asked if statistically driven training methods are effective at modeling symbolic language like the SMILES chemical notation. They also questioned if intensive training on large, domain-specific corpora could improve performance or what factors limit current advancement in chemistry. Ling-Jyh Chen, chief executive of Taiwan AI Academy, stated that proficiency in Chinese does not translate to an awareness of local context. Chen argued that models from U.S. companies like Google and OpenAI often fail to understand the culture and values of Taiwan. The Ministry of Digital Affairs stated that Taiwan must control its own data and perspectives to ensure democratic views are understood.

The AI Evaluation Center says it measures understanding of democratic institutions and historical experiences, though it does not prescribe politically correct answers. Alice Yang, a research fellow, questioned if Taiwanese values can be defined objectively and suggested the government fears Chinese influence. Audrey Tang, an ambassador at large, noted that Taiwan has 20 national languages, 16 recognized Indigenous peoples, and 42 language variations. Tang argued that gathering everyone's data for one national model is misguided and that sovereignty should be implemented at the local level. The Ministry of Digital Affairs believes authoritarian regimes use artificial intelligence to rewrite the past and dominate the future of human society.

The chemistry researchers noted that the performance of the ten large language models was substantially lower than the performance of human experts. Earlier versions of ChatGPT were trained on 190 million Chinese words, most of which were simplified Chinese originating from mainland China. This training caused the chatbot to fail a question about beef soup noodles, which do not contain chunks of meat. APMIC improved its GSAT score by nearly 17 percentage points because it was fine-tuned using data provided by the Taiwanese government. U.S. models perform well on language and society metrics but fall behind Taiwanese models on the specific Taiwanese values metric.

The chemistry study leaves open whether domain-specific training can fix the low depth scores and the failure to model symbolic chemical language. The AI Evaluation Center remains vague about the exact methods used to measure the third metric regarding specific Taiwanese values. It is unclear if a single national model can truly represent the diverse voices of the many different Taiwanese indigenous groups. The researchers continue to investigate what specific factors limit the advancement of current large language models when performing complex chemistry tasks. Future developments may determine if sovereign AI is the key to securing democracy or if it is fundamentally an anti-democratic approach.

stories.Headline: Chinese AI firms use restricted Nvidia Blackwell chips despite US sanctions
stories.Summary:
A Radio Free Asia investigation revealed that sanctioned Chinese entities obtained restricted Nvidia AI chips despite strict United States export controls. This discovery occurred as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang announced his resignation on Thursday following a scandal involving an alleged extramarital affair. The U.S. government is investigating Huang's ties to Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a former Megaspeed executive. She is suspected of collecting intelligence for Beijing and helping Chinese clients acquire restricted chips through her connections. This situation has been described as an AI industry earthquake that has attracted intense attention from outside observers.

The National Supercomputing Center Jinan, also called Shandong Computing Center, won a bid for RTX 5090 and DGX Spark products. On June 17, 2026, the China Government Procurement Network announced Qiyuan Jiasu (Tianjin) Technology Co., Ltd. won the bid. The winning bid price was RMB 148,500, which is approximately 22,000 US dollars, for one batch of AI equipment. The RTX 5090 uses Blackwell architecture with 32GB GDDR7 memory, while the DGX Spark uses the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip. These products were solicited by the Jinan center as of June 2026 despite its status on the entity list.

The U.S. Department of Commerce is responsible for the entity list and stated that Jinan supported Chinese military modernization. Chris Tseng of the Research Institute for Democracy, Society and Emerging Technology said controls rely heavily on corporate self-compliance. He noted that licenses are required to transfer regulated items to controlled entities even through legitimate third-country distributors. Sylvia Chen of DSET stated that third-party enterprises bear legal liability if they illegally transfer controlled products within China. She explained that the Bureau of Industry and Security has only fifteen export control officers worldwide to verify end-users.

DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax, and Ant Group are affected because their models show evidence of using restricted Blackwell GPUs. Unemployment Labs, led by Will Depue, found that these firms used B200, B300, GB200, and GB300 chips for training. The report analyzed six systems released since April, including DeepSeek V4-Flash, V4-Pro, Kimi K3, K3.1-Pro, MiniMax M3, and Ling-3.1-Flash. These companies may have skirted controls by renting compute in Southeast Asia or using smuggled chips via workaround routes. The report estimates that 12,000 Blackwell GPUs were deployed, with costs reaching roughly 500 million US dollars.

The Shandong Computing Center was established in 1976 and is affiliated with the Qilu University of Technology in China. The U.S. Department of Commerce placed the center on the entity list in April 2021 for national security reasons. Broad export restrictions on advanced computing chips to China began in 2022, following the initial listing of the center. Sitonholy (Tianjin) Technology was an Nvidia Elite Partner until it was sanctioned by the U.S. on April 11, 2024. The Trump administration allowed limited exports of H200 chips but did not approve exports of Blackwell or Rubin chips.

Nvidia must now investigate the sales and ultimate flow of products if Qiyuan Jiasu inherited Sitonholy's original business operations. The U.S. government continues to investigate the role of Alice Huang in smuggling advanced AI chips into China. It remains open whether the RTX 5090 cards purchased were the original version or the China special edition. Researchers cautioned that they did not verify the physical location of the chips or prove specific export law violations. The articles leave open whether Qiyuan Jiasu is simply a shell company used to bypass the Entity List.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO following reports of affairs and spy allegations
stories.Summary:
Nvidia's board met on Wednesday to decide whether to remove CEO Jensen Huang, The Wall Street Journal reported, a move that threatened to end 33 years of founder-led management. The meeting followed Huang's admission, according to The New York Times, of an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. officials suspect of being a Chinese spy. The Times also reported a second affair, with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care. Huang then resigned as CEO, in a blow to the AI boom he helped foster, after reports linked his personal relationships to scrutiny over China and chip exports. Colette Kress, the company's veteran chief financial officer, became interim CEO as Nvidia confronted a leadership crisis and investor concerns over its financing deals.

Republican Rep. Jim Banks and Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren issued a bipartisan statement urging immediate action on export controls for AI semiconductors bound for China. Several bills are expected to be folded into an amendment to the National Defense Authorization Act, including an AI monitoring act, a chip security act and the MATCH Act. The AI monitoring act would bar exports of H200-class and more advanced semiconductors to China for a set period. A floor vote is seen as possible in the second week of December, with a presidential signature after mid-December emerging as a realistic scenario. Nvidia's board also faces questions over the investment web Huang built, in which the company has invested in and guaranteed payments for AI companies that in turn buy its chips.

The sources name Nvidia's board as the body that met to decide whether to remove Huang, and Huang himself as the executive at the center of the allegations. Huang admitted the affair with the woman U.S. officials suspect of spying for China, according to The New York Times. A second affair, with Powell, is reported by The Times, and Reuters, citing two people familiar with the matter, reported a relationship with a second employee after Huang resigned. The articles do not quote Huang or the board directly. They record only that Huang admitted the first affair and later stepped down.

Eight experts interviewed by the JoongAng Ilbo said Nvidia's technological lead is unlikely to crumble, though its succession planning, culture and investment network face uncertainty. Shin Jae-yong of Seoul National University said no one has emerged as a potential successor, and that whether a solid Plan B exists is the biggest uncertainty. Yoo Eung-joon, a former head of Nvidia Korea, said the culture will not be shaken because employees have high expertise and autonomy, while Kwon Ki-bum of Korea University called the episode a major crisis for organizational continuity and culture. Kim Joung-ho of KAIST warned that cooperation with Korean companies could slow, and Noh Geun-chang of Semicon Research Lab said vendor financing will shrink for a time if financial companies grow cautious. Morgan Stanley cut its target price for Samsung Electronics by 19% and for SK hynix by 38%, and SK hynix supplies more than 50% of Nvidia's HBM.

Nvidia's chief engineer and its CFO emerged as favored candidates as Huang's leadership came into question. Taiwan barred Alice Huang, who has been linked to Jensen Huang in allegations of an extramarital affair, from returning. Powell is one of about 60 senior executives who report directly to Huang and is considered a key figure at Nvidia. The company prizes intellectual honesty, and Huang is known for a hands-on style, personally reading employees' Top 5 Things emails to track even small changes. Before the scandal, Nvidia held 80% of the AI accelerator market, and Huang had personally made physical AI the company's next growth engine.

The NDAA amendment is expected to reach a floor vote in the second week of December, with a presidential signature after mid-December as a realistic scenario. A former senior U.S. official said some restrictions could appear in economic and technology exchanges between the United States and China. Tighter export rules could disrupt SK hynix's plan to expand its plant in Dalian, China. Anthropic is set to list on the Nasdaq on the 19th or 20th, a supply-and-demand variable for South Korean semiconductor and AI-related shares. Kress is serving as interim CEO, but the articles do not say who will take the permanent post, nor whether Nvidia's board will pursue any further action over the affairs.

stories.Headline: FuelCell Energy joins federal StabilityMax program to test fuel cells for AI data centers
stories.Summary:
FuelCell Energy, a fuel cell company headquartered on Great Pasture Road in Danbury near the Bethel border, will take part in a three-year federally funded program to test whether fuel cells can provide electricity to data centers where there are rapid fluctuations in power consumption. The company announced the project in a release dated Nov 13, 2026, reported by staff writer Rob Ryser. The program is known as StabilityMax. Under the project, FuelCell Energy will develop a fuel cell test facility in Danbury, creating a national laboratory-supported testbed for evaluating integrated power solutions for AI data centers. The federal government wants to know whether fuel cells, which already power commercial and industrial facilities, can handle the heavy demands of artificial intelligence data centers.

The project runs three years and is led by the U.S. Department of Energy's National Laboratories of the Rockies. FuelCell Energy reported 425 employees worldwide last year, most of them at the company's Danbury headquarters and its Torrington manufacturing plant. FuelCell planned to keep its staffing levels the same. Details about the StabilityMax grant program, such as how much federal money is involved, were not disclosed. The pairing of fuel cells with data centers made news in October when a developer proposed to reinvigorate a 1.3-million-square-foot office structure in Danbury by bringing in a data center and using fuel cells to power it.

Mayor Roberto Alves said Thursday that FuelCell Energy's participation in the national research effort is a strong example of the innovation and expertise rooted in Danbury. Alves said he was pleased to see a Danbury company working with leading national labs on the challenge and looked forward to learning what the project demonstrates about performance, cost and the effects on the electric grid. Kathleen Blomquist, the company's director of communications, said the project isn't about testing whether fuel cells can power data centers because they can. Blomquist said the question is how to optimize a fuel cell-based power system for the rapidly changing demands of AI infrastructure, including how fuel cells, batteries, power electronics and advanced controls work together as computing loads fluctuate. Zhiwen Ma, a principal investigator at the National Laboratories of the Rockies, said fuel cells combined with data centers provide unique solutions to meet the power demands of AI infrastructure.

Ma said that through the project, NLR will help demonstrate how integrated fuel cell systems can rapidly respond to data center power needs while limiting impacts to the utility grid and ratepayers. Shankar Achanta, chief product and technology officer at FuelCell, said the insights gained through the work will help optimize system designs, validate performance under real-world conditions, and support future deployment of fuel cell-based solutions for digital infrastructure. The company's release said that as AI adoption accelerates, data centers are driving unprecedented demand for electricity and creating rapid fluctuations in power consumption. A data center is an umbrella term for computer processing plants that support all the ways artificial intelligence is used today. Public concern about energy usage by data centers has made headlines across Connecticut and the region.

A fuel cell makes electricity from fuel and air, eliminating the need to burn fuel. The company's headquarters sits on the city's east end. A FuelCell Energy power plant stands on Triangle Street in Danbury. The three-year project isn't as much about testing whether fuel cells work but about applying the technology to the next level. The federal government also wants the work to limit impacts to the utility grid and ratepayers.

The articles do not say when the three-year project begins or ends. The articles do not disclose how much federal money is involved in the StabilityMax grant program. The articles do not say what results the test facility is expected to produce or when. The articles do not say whether the October proposal for the 1.3-million-square-foot Danbury office structure is connected to the StabilityMax project. The articles do not say what the national laboratory-supported testbed will cost or who beyond FuelCell Energy will run it.

stories.Headline: Adobe and Google integrate AI models into creative and productivity tools
stories.Summary:
Adobe and Google expanded their strategic AI partnership on November 14, 2026, to integrate advanced models into creative tools. This collaboration brings Google AI models into Adobe software and extends Adobe tools across the Google productivity ecosystem. Adobe also unveiled new AI agents and features at the Adobe MAX 2026 conference in Miami. This annual creative event opened on October 10 and showcased the evolution of the Firefly generative app. The updates aim to turn Firefly into a comprehensive AI creative studio for all digital creators.

Google Gemini models will power Acrobat, allowing users to edit PDFs via conversational prompts through Google Workspace, Drive, and Gmail. Adobe Firefly, Photoshop, Premiere, and Express will integrate Google image and video models, including Gemini Omni, Veo, and Nano Banana. Firefly now supports 36 models, including ByteDance's Dreamina and Seedance 2.5, Runway's Gen-4.5, Kuaishou's Kling 4.0, and OpenAI's GPT. Adobe also partnered with Disney for custom Firefly Foundry models and Microsoft for Arm-based Windows PCs and Microsoft Photos. New tools include Firefly Design in beta, Firefly Builder in private beta, and the CX Enterprise Coworker in GenStudio.

Forrest Key, vice president for Firefly and agentic AI, stated the company wants to help everyone create digital content. He described Firefly as the best platform for both new creators and professionals to build their digital work. Deepa Subramaniam, vice president of product marketing for Creative Cloud, said updates provide professionals with precision, control, and flexibility. She noted that these new tools allow professionals to focus on the decisions that shape their own creative work. The companies are also exploring custom Google image models for Photoshop to enable near-real-time editing through text prompts.

Users of Photoshop, Premiere, Illustrator, InDesign, and Lightroom are affected by these updates, including new lighting and color tools. Premiere mobile users gain natural-language editing and licensed music from UMG and WMG for personal, non-commercial video projects. Designers can use Firefly Design to combine illustration, animation, and 3D tools on a single canvas for efficiency. Marketing teams can now use the Ideation Space in Workfront to build campaign strategies and briefs using AI. Business users can coordinate agents and workflows across planning and activation using the new CX Enterprise Coworker interface.

Adobe's multi-model strategy allows users to work with different AI models alongside professional editing tools in the Creative Cloud. Firefly was developed as a generative AI app offering image and video generation, editing, and now agent-based workflow tools. The company introduced a plan mode for reviewing agent plans and a model picker for selecting specific AI models. Always-on agents are being previewed to handle repetitive background tasks like organizing assets and checking content quality. Adobe also developed Firefly Graph in beta for users who want to build repeatable and efficient creative workflows.

Next, Adobe will expand integrations with Gemini and Gemini Enterprise to bring Acrobat and creative tools into those platforms. The company is rolling out beta features like Generative Remove in Premiere and real-time co-editing in InDesign. Local MCP integrations are being previewed to allow third-party agents to edit native project files while keeping layers editable. Adobe continues to test Firefly Builder for turning spoken descriptions into prototypes for websites and mobile apps without coding. The articles leave open how the custom Google models for Photoshop will perform in real-time text-to-image editing.

stories.Headline: Luminal raises $25 million in Series A funding to help AI models run on various chips
stories.Summary:
Luminal, a company that provides an inference cloud and develops inference compiler software to test running AI models on different chips, raised a $25 million Series A round led by Standard Capital, CEO Joe Fioti told Axios Pro exclusively. The funding was reported by Chris Metinko of Axios in a story dated November 12, 2026. The company describes its own product as a search compiler and inference cloud provider. The round is a Series A, the first major venture financing stage after a seed round. The money is meant to improve inference, the stage where a trained AI model answers requests rather than being trained.

Luminal's technology lets customers run their AI models on different chips instead of relying on Nvidia, according to the article. That matters because Nvidia has been the dominant supplier of chips used for AI work. The article gives no further details on how the $25 million will be split or how many employees the company has. Joe Fioti, the chief executive of Luminal, is the person the article names as speaking about the deal. He told Axios Pro exclusively about the raise and the lead investor, Standard Capital.

The article does not include any other direct comment from him beyond that disclosure. No other executives, investors or customers are named or quoted in the piece. The context the article supplies is that Luminal's approach offers customers a way to avoid depending on a single chip vendor, Nvidia. The story does not say what Luminal plans to do next with the funding, when the round closed, or what the company's valuation is. It also does not say whether the company has other investors or existing customers.
