stories.Headline: Google releases Gemini 4 Carbon and opens Artificial Analysis benchmarking to businesses
stories.Summary:
On November 15, 2026, David Wilson reported in Small Business News that Google released the Gemini 4 Carbon model, a system for multimodal knowledge processing. Google announced that starting that day, businesses could explore the benchmark and assess their own models through the platform Artificial Analysis. Artificial Analysis provides an open-source agent harness called Stirrup, which lets businesses test capabilities using standardized tools in a controlled environment. The Gemini model includes an autorater that independently evaluates model outputs against expert metrics. Google said an agentic autorater built on a non-Google model grades each deliverable.

The autorater checks files, renders documents and analyzes spreadsheet formulas, matching expert evaluations 96% of the time. Artificial Analysis runs an evaluation set of 200 tasks with a privacy focus, and the tasks are not disclosed so they cannot be used as training data. Google also made available 10 public tasks for experimentation on platforms like Hugging Face. The Gemini 4 Carbon ranks second in evaluation quality while completing tasks six times cheaper on average than the highest-scoring model. Google's technical report found some models take between 30 and 130 turns to complete tasks.

According to Google, the agentic autorater built on a non-Google model grades each deliverable. Google's report states that the findings underscore the importance of strong perception abilities for effective task completion. The article by David Wilson says small business owners may need a certain level of technical expertise to implement these AI models effectively. Wilson writes that owners may want to assess whether they have the resources and workforce capability to fully leverage AI, or consider partnerships with tech firms specialized in AI implementation. Wilson also notes owners must remain vigilant about data security, integration with current systems and the potential need for ongoing training and support.

Wilson states that small businesses often operate with tight budgets and resource constraints, and can benefit from the efficiency by reducing costs of manual processing or competing solutions. He writes that for small businesses, improved accuracy means errors could be identified and rectified faster in internal processes or customer data management. He says the 10 public tasks allow small business owners to test and calibrate their agents in a public setting. Wilson adds that adapting to new technologies can be daunting for many small businesses, particularly when existing operational frameworks may not readily accommodate them. He concludes that Gemini 4 Carbon offers a robust, cost-effective system for improving operations from customer relationship management to streamlined decision-making.

Wilson's article says the Gemini 4 Carbon was recently released by Google and sets a new benchmark for evaluating AI models and their applications in real-world scenarios. He writes that the platform provides an open-source agent harness called Stirrup for testing in a controlled environment. The article states the private nature of the primary tasks is crucial for maintaining the integrity of evaluations. Wilson notes the technical report offers deep insights into performance across varied tasks, revealing significant differences in efficiency and capabilities. He writes that choosing a model with strong performance under varying conditions could impact overall productivity and user satisfaction.

Wilson says businesses can explore the benchmark and assess their own models through Artificial Analysis starting November 15, 2026. He directs readers to visit the original post for additional information. The article leaves open which specific tasks make up the 200-task evaluation set, since they are not disclosed. It does not say how small businesses can access the 10 public tasks beyond mentioning platforms like Hugging Face. It does not specify what technical expertise or training would be required to implement the models. It does not detail how data security or integration with current systems would be handled.

stories.Headline: Kansas education board requires school districts to adopt AI classroom policies
stories.Summary:
The Kansas State Board of Education created an instructional technology policy earlier this week, the Kansas State Department of Education announced in a press release on Nov. 13, 2026, from Topeka. The policy requires Kansas public school districts and accredited nonpublic schools to develop policies outlining how technology is used in classrooms. The policy establishes statewide minimum requirements for instructional technology use while allowing local school boards to decide how those expectations will be implemented. Kansas Education Commissioner Dr. Jake Steel said the policy is intended to ensure technology strengthens teaching and learning rather than replaces meaningful interactions between teachers and students. KSDE officials said the policy was developed following months of input from educators, parents and other education partners.

Every district and accredited nonpublic school must adopt both an instructional technology policy and an implementation plan, and both must be approved by local school boards and reviewed annually. The plans must address the purpose and intended use of classroom technology, student access to school-issued devices, whether students can take school-issued devices home, digital citizenship and student well-being, the use of artificial intelligence by teachers and students, student privacy and cybersecurity protections, and technology expectations and violations. Schools will also be required to establish guidelines for how artificial intelligence tools, including chatbots and generative AI, are used. Districts and accredited nonpublic schools must make their policies and plans publicly available on their websites and submit their adopted plans to the Kansas State Department of Education by July 1, 2027. Beginning in the 2028-29 school year, parents or guardians must receive access to their school's technology-use plan and acknowledge it before students receive access to school-issued devices, and the policy will remain in effect until July 1, 2030 unless it is reauthorized, amended or extended.

Steel said the State Board has sent a clear message that technology only belongs in the classroom when it strengthens teaching and learning. KSDE officials said the policy was developed following months of input from educators, parents and other education partners. KSDE officials said it encourages schools to involve families and caregivers in developing their technology-use plans. It also recognizes that some students may need additional or different access to technology because of disabilities, medical needs, language needs or other educational requirements. The Kansas State Board of Education created the policy earlier this week, according to the KSDE press release.

Princeton University recently decided to offer access to ChatGPT Plus or Pro to its students and faculty through a new one-year pilot program, The Daily Princetonian wrote on Oct. 30. The Daily Princetonian later published an editorial about the program on Nov. 6, questioning how the implementation of AI in an academic environment will affect students' ability to learn and how it reflects on the university's fundamental mission of education. The Daily Princetonian's Editorial Board said it was not convinced that a sweeping ChatGPT pilot will suit the distinct learning methods across disciplines. Students at the College have had the ability to use several different AI tools at their full capacity for about a year now, after Vice President for Operations Sharon Blanton announced in an email to the College on Oct. 2 that students and faculty were granted secure access to Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot and Google NotebookLM, The Signal reported in 2025. Students can find an instructional article on the College's website titled "Getting Started with Gemini: Your AI Assistant for Campus Life."

Artificial intelligence has been developing at an exponential rate since ChatGPT was first introduced to the internet in 2022, and after about four years it has become an integral part of every app, including search engines like Google. The Daily Princetonian wrote that students will be able to request access to ChatGPT Plus before the start of next semester, and faculty and staff could request access beginning Wednesday. The tech giant Google recently announced that if schools ban use of their AI features, students will no longer be able to use Google Search, according to The Guardian. Students at the College were encouraged to use the tools responsibly and to follow course guidelines, which can differ for each instructor. Princeton's implementation of ChatGPT Plus and Pro, which one typically has to pay for, also brings up the question of how much money is being spent to give access to all students and faculty who request it.

The Kansas policy will remain in effect until July 1, 2030 unless it is reauthorized, amended or extended, and districts and accredited nonpublic schools must submit their adopted plans to the Kansas State Department of Education by July 1, 2027. Beginning in the 2028-29 school year, parents or guardians must receive access to their school's technology-use plan and acknowledge it before students receive access to school-issued devices. The Daily Princetonian's Editorial Board questioned how the implementation of AI in an academic environment will affect students' ability to learn and how it reflects on the university's fundamental mission of education. The Signal reported that it is important for colleges to consider whether aligning themselves with AI companies would truly be beneficial for all their students. The articles leave open how much money Princeton is spending on the pilot and how each Kansas district will implement its plan.

stories.Headline: LG CNS hosts robotics forum to advance physical AI deployment in industrial settings
stories.Summary:
The global robotics industry is racing to turn artificial intelligence into physical machines that can perceive, reason, and act in the real world. Experts say these advances are transforming manufacturing and other sectors, while LG CNS hosted a forum in Seoul on November 12, 2026. More than 100 researchers and industry professionals met at the Future Robotics Lab in Magok to discuss deploying physical AI in industrial settings. This movement includes a surge in humanoid robot shipments, with over 22,000 units delivered globally during the first half of 2026. These shipments represent a 300 per cent year-on-year increase, and totals are expected to exceed 50,000 units by the end of the year.

Dubai targets deploying 200,000 robots by 2032 through its Robotics and Automation Program, while GITEX World RobotiX occurs December 8 to 11, 2026. This event at the Dubai Exhibition Centre in Expo City Dubai features Unitree, which holds a 31 per cent share of the global market. Other participants include UBTECH, AiMOGA, DEEP Robotics, Micropolis Robotics, Mangobot, Lumos Robotics, Lootah Robotics, Light Origins, and Raydiculous, which debuts its TP01 and DINOBOT. LG CNS introduced its PhysicalWorks Forge learning platform and PhysicalWorks Baton agentic AI platform, while Lumos Robotics showcased the NIX S3 with 21 degrees. The forum in Seoul included faculty and students from the University of Toronto, Sogang University, Chung-Ang University, and Korea University.

Mazen El-Kurdi of Mangobot said visitors should see what working alongside robots feels like, rather than just looking at the machines themselves. Cecile Wei of Lumos Robotics stated that robots must perform useful tasks reliably in real environments instead of just moving for demonstrations. Hazem Ghazal of Lootah Robotics said they are building an integrated robotics ecosystem so organizations can select different robots for different requirements. Tingxiang Fan of Light Origins believes the bunny-shaped robot is ready to enter consumers' homes for hands-on interaction in household scenarios. Lee Jun-ho of LG CNS said engagement with academia will help turn research results into innovation within actual industrial settings.

Professor Lee Chi-geun discussed combining data from different robots and using flow matching and action chunking to help machines produce smoother, continuous movements. His presentation identified that differences in robot movement, latency, and data availability remain significant challenges for deploying robot foundation models in the world. The technology affects consumer services, education, entertainment, and domestic environments, as well as factories, warehouses, and other industrial settings like car factories. Airbus is testing UBTECH robots, while Dubai Police use autonomous patrol robots from Micropolis Robotics and Mitsubishi Electric uses Lumos MOS robots. Participants also discussed how human roles may evolve as robotics advances and what capabilities companies and universities need to develop.

LG CNS draws on more than two decades of experience and has completed over 1,000 smart factory and smart logistics projects in the past. Lumos Robotics reported that its first-generation MOS robots completed over 1,000 hours of failure-free operation performing material handling, quality inspection, and screwdriving tasks. Raydiculous developed the TP01 humanoid for commercial interaction and public services, which can communicate in both English and Arabic and perform movements. The DINOBOT is described as the world's first intelligent bipedal walking bionic dinosaur and will demonstrate realistic movement and interactive capabilities. Embodied AI integrates AI models into physical bodies or hardware systems, allowing robots to interact more naturally with people in various environments.

The industry will continue showcasing advances in embodied AI and robotic workforces featuring multilingual receptionists and wearable exoskeleton technology at the upcoming GITEX event. Companies will further explore robot foundation models, data, hardware, and simulation to overcome the technical challenges of real-world deployment in industrial operations. The articles leave open how exactly human roles will evolve as these robotics technologies advance and integrate further into the global workforce. It remains to be seen if the bunny-shaped robot and other consumer models will successfully enter homes and domestic environments as planned. Future developments depend on whether research from universities can be successfully turned into industrial innovation through continued engagement with the private sector.

stories.Headline: AWS releases AWS Emulator built entirely by AI agents to run 200+ cloud services locally
stories.Summary:
AWS released AWS Emulator, a free local emulator of its cloud APIs, on November 11, 2026. The tool lets developers run a stand-in for more than 200 AWS services on a laptop, a dev server or in CI, with no AWS account and no service fee. The AWS CLI and SDKs talk to it instead of AWS, and code does not need to change. The unusual part is that autonomous AI agents wrote and reviewed all of its code, and the team has not written or reviewed any code itself.

The emulator is built from 438 AWS API models, with one Rust crate per service. It runs on Linux x86_64 and aarch64 through RPM or Debian packages, or in Docker on macOS and Windows with a 2 GiB memory limit, while source builds need 100 GB of free disk. In release v1.0.322 it passed 24,243 of 42,857 scored fidelity tests, or 56.6%, and 49,810 of 68,007 individual steps, or 73.2%. AWS KMS scored best at 93.9%, Amazon SQS reached 89.8%, and AWS CloudFormation was worst at 15.8%. Cross-service workflows passed 2,752 of 6,569 tests, or 41.9%, and unimplemented operations return HTTP 501 NotImplemented.

The project began with a prompt to Kiro, which returned a passable Amazon SQS emulator in about 15 minutes. AWS then split the work across three teams of agents: test writers derive scenarios from the public Smithy API models and check each against real AWS, issue finders replay those tests and file failures, and fixers take one issue each and submit a patch. Every patch passes a merge gate covering build, code review, security and fidelity, and several security agents run adversarial reviews. Matthew Goldberg reports hundreds of concurrent agents fixing thousands of issues a day, and the release pipeline runs on AWS Developer Tools with CodeCommit as the agents' repository.

The articles compare the tool with LocalStack, Moto and Floci. AWS Emulator is free under CC0 1.0, covers 200+ services, needs no vendor token and serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297 by default. LocalStack has free non-commercial and paid plans, Moto is free under Apache-2.0, and Floci is free under MIT. AWS publishes a scores.json file with each release, and the tests live in aws-emulator-evaluation-suite, including failing ones. The articles do not say what happens next beyond these releases and scores.

stories.Headline: Shufti launches patented on-device AI age verification that keeps facial images on the user's device
stories.Summary:
Shufti launched its Privacy-Preserving Age Verification Solution, incorporating patented on-device AI technology, on Nov. 13, 2026, in London, according to a GlobeNewswire release. The company described itself as a Glocal identity verification, Anti-Money Laundering and fraud prevention platform. The solution lets businesses confirm users' age eligibility without the facial image or any other higher-assurance proof of age leaving the user's device. The technology is protected by US Patent No. 12,749,342 B1, titled AGE VERIFICATION, issued by the United States Patent and Trademark Office. The patent covers an AI-based system combining on-device facial analysis, split inference and encrypted One-Time Age Tokens.

The solution uses patented split-inference technology to divide AI processing between the user's device and a secure verification server. AI models analyse facial characteristics to estimate age and assess liveness locally, helping identify spoofing attempts involving photographs, masks, screen replays and manipulated images. The device generates an encrypted One-Time Age Token containing intermediate AI outputs rather than transmitting the original facial image. The verification server validates the token, completes the remaining AI processing and determines whether the user meets the required threshold, such as 18 or 21. Tokens are time-limited, can be marked as used after verification and may be restricted to a specific merchant to prevent unauthorised reuse or sharing across platforms.

Shufti's wider Age Verification Solution lets businesses select the level of assurance appropriate to their risk exposure, users and regulatory requirements while minimising collection and exposure of personally identifiable information. It offers docless age checks through facial age estimation or eIDV, configurable age thresholds and confidence-based escalation, risk-based verification, document verification or authoritative database checks, and biometric liveness detection supported by iBeta Level 3 PAD conformance. Shahid Hanif, CEO of Shufti, said a business should not have to collect someone's full identity simply to confirm whether they are old enough to access a service. He said the company developed the solution to help businesses prevent underage access without requiring every legitimate user to provide higher-assurance proof of age. He said the patented on-device approach keeps facial information on the user's device while securely confirming age eligibility, and called the US patent an important milestone.

The articles said a self-declared "I am over 18" click offers little assurance, while an ID upload and selfie can provide stronger evidence but many users are reluctant to share such personal information, particularly for sensitive services. Businesses collecting these records must also manage their security, retention and deletion. In the UK, Ofcom does not recognise self-declaration as a highly effective age assurance method under the UK Online Safety Act. The European Commission is advancing privacy-preserving proof-of-age tools that allow users to establish age eligibility without revealing their identity. The solution supports adult entertainment platforms checking age before content access, social media services applying minimum-age policies, gaming and gambling operators verifying eligibility at registration, and e-commerce businesses checking age before restricted purchases.

Shufti said dividing the final AI model between the device and server reduces exposure of the complete model, making it harder to reverse-engineer the verification process or manipulate locally generated results. The articles said an adult entertainment platform may need to confirm a visitor is over 18, while a regulated gambling operator may also require documentary proof of identity. Shufti's Glocal Trust OS unifies KYC, KYB, eIDV, age assurance, AML screening, agentic transaction monitoring, Know Your Agent and fraud prevention. Shufti's biometric liveness technology holds iBeta Level 3 PAD conformance under ISO/IEC 30107-3. Shufti is recognised as a Leading vendor in Liminal's 2026 Age Verification and Age Estimation Indexes, receiving the highest-tier Exceptional rating for Market Presence in both categories.

Shufti invited businesses to book a personalised demo of the patented Age Verification Solution. The articles listed Aroosa Virk, Brand and Communications Manager at Shufti, as media contact at partnership@shuftipro.com. A photo accompanying the announcement was available at a GlobeNewswire attachment link. The articles did not say when the solution would become generally available or how it would be priced. The articles did not name any business that has adopted the solution.

stories.Headline: Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigns as CEO amid national security concerns
stories.Summary:
Nvidia announced on November 12 that co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive and from the board. This sudden leadership change occurred as the KOSPI index faced volatility following U.S. data center regulation concerns. Investors are now worried about the future of the artificial intelligence industry without its primary leader. The departure follows allegations that Huang had an extramarital relationship with a woman named Elise Huang. This person is reported to have links to Chinese intelligence services, raising national security concerns.

The company named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive while searching for a permanent successor. The board reportedly prepared to oust Huang after the Wall Street Journal reported the news on December 12. The KOSPI closed at 5,290.53 on November 13, which was down 52.20 points from the previous session. This index was 4.56% above the November 6 close of 5,059.69, despite sliding to 4,990.66 on November 9. The Kosdaq ended at 699.66 on November 13, which was an increase of 3.13 points.

Nvidia stated it will maintain its customer contracts and its product development schedule despite the leadership change. Hana Securities said the direct impact on AI chip demand would be limited because specialized teams handle development. Mirae Asset Securities judged that a sharp drop in HBM demand is unlikely even if orders shift. President Lee Jae-myung reaffirmed his commitment to normalizing the capital market during a meeting on December 13. He suggested that a deep valley in the market could lead to a high mountain.

Korean chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK hynix could feel effects if customer relationships or investment strategies change. SK hynix may be more sensitive because a large share of its high-bandwidth memory goes to Nvidia. Foreign investors bought a net 1.23 trillion won of Samsung Electronics but sold 1.05 trillion won of SK hynix. Samsung Electronics rose 2.23% over the second week of November, while SK hynix fell 3.80%. Retail investors sold 3.03 trillion won during the first two weeks of November.

The KOSPI had previously plunged 11.71% due to concerns over data center construction rules after U.S. midterm elections. The index jumped 4.39% on November 10 as international oil prices fell amid Middle East diplomatic hopes. Sentiment was supported by AI cloud provider CoreWeave, which reported higher third-quarter revenue and raised annual guidance. Foreign investors sold 10.41 trillion won in the first week of November before buying 460.8 billion won later. Shinyoung Securities noted the KOSPI forward price-to-earnings ratio is 3.7 times, below the decade average.

Nvidia reports quarterly earnings on November 17 U.S. time, which is early November 18 in Korea. Investors will watch what the interim chief executive says about AI ecosystem investment and next-generation GPU development. The direction of Korean stocks depends on how the leadership vacuum affects actual chip demand and investment. It remains important whether the earnings forecasts for SK hynix and Samsung Electronics can hold their levels. The articles leave open whether the uncertainty will lead to reduced AI investment or tighter China export controls.

stories.Headline: Samsung breaks ground on HBM packaging plant in Asan and moves opening to June 2028
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics broke ground on a high-bandwidth memory packaging plant on November 12, 2026, to expand the artificial intelligence server supply chain. This new facility is located at the Onyang campus in Asan, South Korea, and focuses on advanced packaging for HBM memory. The company is accelerating the project to meet the rising demand for server memory used in various modern artificial intelligence systems. Construction of the plant is the first project under a regional industrial mega-project program led by the South Korean government. The facility is now scheduled to begin its operations in June 2028, which is one year earlier than previously planned.

The project requires 6 trillion won, or 4.48 billion dollars, for construction and 40 trillion won for advanced equipment installed in stages. Total medium and long term investment for the Onyang expansion is roughly 46 trillion won, including three clean-room floors of 31,000 square meters. Samsung Electro-Mechanics is investing 8 trillion won in package-substrate production for central processing units and graphics processors in the Chungcheong region. Samsung Display is investing 67 trillion won in an 8.6-generation production line for information technology displays within the same South Korean region. Samsung Electro-Mechanics will also spend 4.27 trillion won in South Korea and 2.51 trillion won in Vietnam for flip-chip ball grid array substrates.

The South Korean Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources announced the groundbreaking and said it would coordinate permits for the new projects. The ministry also stated it would help the company secure necessary transport infrastructure along with essential water and electricity for the site. Samsung said during its third-quarter earnings announcement that it had already completed negotiations over HBM supply volumes for the year 2027. The company noted that customers continued to seek additional supply, which prompted the decision to move the plant opening date forward. Samsung Electro-Mechanics disclosed in September that its substrate expansion for high-performance computing applications will start mass production in September 2028.

Customers seeking more high-bandwidth memory are affected by packaging capacity, which is a separate manufacturing step from producing the memory wafers. Advanced packaging connects stacked memory dies with processors and other components, making it a critical constraint on the finished HBM supply. The expansion at the Onyang campus was prompted because the existing Samsung campus in Cheonan has run short of available space. This makes Onyang a major production base for advanced AI memory to support the needs of various global technology customers. The project is part of a broader investment program across the Chungcheong region to bolster the regional industrial economy.

The South Korean government identified 112 materials, components and equipment suppliers with additional investment plans totaling about 23.6 trillion won around the projects. HBM combines stacked memory dies with high-speed connections for AI accelerators, which are essential for the operation of AI servers. The government is supporting these industrial projects by managing the infrastructure and permits required for the massive scale of the investments. Samsung Electro-Mechanics is focusing its substrate investments on AI servers and other high-performance computing applications to meet the growing market demand. These efforts are part of a strategic move to secure the supply chain for artificial intelligence hardware in Asia.

The investment for the Onyang plant will be deployed over several years, with equipment spending following the initial construction in phases. Samsung has not disclosed the planned output capacity of the new plant or the specific customer commitments for the facility. The company has also kept the expected financial returns from the 46 trillion won investment private at this current stage. It remains open whether the increased capacity will fully satisfy the rising demand for AI server memory by June 2028. The articles do not state the specific names of the customers who are seeking additional high-bandwidth memory supply.

stories.Headline: Meta uses AI to identify teenagers on Instagram and apply account protections
stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms announced in a statement dated November 9 that it is expanding its AI-powered age-estimation technology to find Instagram users it suspects are teenagers, even when they signed up with an adult birthdate. Accounts flagged this way are automatically moved into Teen Account protections, which Meta says will reach millions more teenagers across the world. The Epoch Times reported the move on November 10, 2026, and Biometric Update covered it the same day. Meta describes the protections as built-in safeguards that limit the content teens see, the time they spend on the app, and who can contact them. The company says some teens misrepresent their age online to reach experiences they are not old enough to use.

Starting this month, parents in the United States on Instagram will receive a notification explaining how Meta applies the age-appropriate protections and how they can help make sure their teen is logged in with the correct age. Teens aged 13 to 15 need parental permission to make some account protections less restrictive. Those aged 16 and 17 have more freedom to change certain settings, but still face restrictions, such as content limits, that cannot be altered without a parent's approval. Meta says it is continuing to roll out the technology on Facebook, and later this year it will begin launching similar measures globally on Threads. The company has also started using Apple's age-range signal in Australia as an additional way to help determine users' ages.

Meta is the company behind the expansion, and it says it uses AI and other signals to estimate a user's age. Larry Magid, CEO of the nonprofit ConnectSafely, explained the method in a November 6 post on Meta's website. He said the signals include profile information, comments, posts, captions and bios, such as references to school grades or birthdays, and that Meta can also analyze visual patterns in photos and videos. Magid stressed that this visual analysis is not facial recognition, because it looks for general characteristics suggesting an underage person in order to estimate an age range, not to identify anyone. He added that Meta deactivates suspected under-13 accounts and requires proof of age to prevent their deletion.

Meta also said it has long supported legislation requiring age verification and parental consent at the app store level. It argues that one verified signal from a person's device, shared consistently with all apps, is far more effective and privacy-preserving than asking every platform to verify age separately. Meta says it uses Apple's signal voluntarily, but that teens will get inconsistent protections across apps while sharing and using the signal stays optional for app stores and developers. It describes its own AI system as a backstop that can correct mistakes and feed them back to the app store for correction across all the apps a teen uses. Meta also says it has set a strong standard for age assurance and is investing in stronger technology to catch accounts that may belong to children under 13.

Biometric Update's Joel R. McConvey criticized the approach, writing that Meta responds to calls for platform accountability by hitting the problem sideways, in a game of misdirectional tennis. He argued that the age inference system is a form of profiling whose methods, accuracy and privacy implications are not subject to the public scrutiny applied to independently evaluated third-party tools. He also said it removes user choice, applying a model that recalls U2 pushing its album onto everyone's iPod. He noted that effective age assurance tools exist and that Meta already works with vendors, notably Yoti for facial age estimation on Instagram, and he said data from Australia shows how unserious the company has been about following laws it dislikes. Teens are the people directly affected, and the Electronic Privacy Information Center, through Megan Iorio, voiced support for California's AB 1709, saying design features that manipulate kids are the problem.

The expansion follows a roughly $18.1 billion settlement Meta reached in August with multiple U.S. jurisdictions over allegations of endangering children. Those lawsuits accused the company of deliberately designing its platforms to be addictive, knowingly exposing children to mental harms, and misleading people about the safety of its products. Meta agreed to pay $17.1 billion to settle suits from 47 states, territories and the District of Columbia, and $1 billion to settle a Texas suit. As part of the deal, Meta agreed to institute age-verification protocols, content controls and time limits for children. Biometric Update reports that the agreement involves 52 bipartisan attorneys general and makes about 30 percent of the payments conditional on TikTok and YouTube adopting comparable measures and making matching payments.

Meta, Google and TikTok filed separate lawsuits on November 4 seeking to stop California from enforcing Assembly Bill 1709, a new state law meant to protect children under 16 from the effects of social media. The law bars platforms from offering underage children features judged psychologically exploitative that could cause compulsive use, including autoplay videos and personal recommendations. Platforms are obligated to delete the accounts of children with such features. The companies allege that the measure violates First Amendment free speech protections. The Epoch Times also notes that Meta recently settled with a teen during a trial over social media addiction claims, which the articles cite without giving details.

In the weeks ahead, U.S. parents on Instagram will begin receiving the notifications, while the technology keeps rolling out on Facebook and reaches Threads later this year. The articles do not say how accurate Meta's age estimation is, how many teens it has identified, or whether the system will face independent evaluation. They also leave open whether Apple's age-range signal will spread beyond Australia, and whether app stores or developers will be required to share and use it. The outcome of the lawsuits from Meta, Google and TikTok against California's AB 1709 is likewise undecided. Biometric Update adds that the company's statements about online safety rest on credibility it may not have.

stories.Headline: Nebius plans $40B to $45B infrastructure spend for 2027
stories.Summary:
Nebius Group announced on November 12, 2026 a capital expenditure roadmap projecting between $40 billion and $45 billion in infrastructure spending for 2027. The plan covers expansion of global graphics processing unit clusters and data centre operations. The announcement followed a revision of the full-year 2026 capital expenditure target to approximately $27 billion. Nebius aims to surpass one gigawatt of operational power capacity across its facilities. The company serves hyperscale clients and enterprise foundation model developers.

Roughly 75% to 85% of the projected 2027 capital outlay will be covered by customer prepayments on qualifying long-term contracts and asset-backed credit facilities secured against investment-grade commercial commitments. Nebius disclosed delays at third-party co-location sites affecting short-term deployment schedules. A primary bottleneck occurred at a 300-megawatt data centre facility in Vineland, New Jersey, operated by partner DataOne. That facility was to fulfill portions of a contracted capacity deployment for Microsoft valued up to $19.4 billion. The New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection scrutinised site commissioning regarding temporary natural gas generation units, prompting an accelerated transition to permanent Bloom Energy fuel cells.

Timeline revisions pushed commercial activation for certain capacity blocks from late 2026 into the first half of 2027. Nebius is shifting future capacity additions toward owned-and-operated sites to mitigate counterparty and operational risks. The expansion roadmap focuses on scaling proprietary sites, including a second facility in Mäntsälä and new development in Lappeenranta, Finland. It also includes domestic US campus developments in Missouri and Alabama. Management indicated the financing approach relies on prepayments and loans rather than traditional equity or bond sales.

Nebius shares tumbled 10% after the company delivered disappointing 2026 guidance alongside news of a massive capital expenditure surge. Meta recently announced plans for a $25 billion bond sale to fund its AI infrastructure blitz. SoftBank is reportedly eyeing a $50 billion investment in Malaysia for AI and data centers. S&P Global Ratings recently revised Meta's outlook to negative, citing worries about AI infrastructure spending outpacing free cash flow generation. Elon Musk warned of "guppy-level death" for hundreds of GPU providers, triggering a selloff across neocloud stocks.

Nebius is the former Yandex cloud unit and spun out of Yandex less than two years ago. The customer prepayment model is not entirely new, as hyperscalers have long used capacity reservation agreements to lock in revenue. CoreWeave has tested a similar model with mixed results, and its debt-fueled buildout has raised concerns about leverage ratios. Nebius takes customer cash, secures additional loans against the guaranteed revenue stream, and orders Nvidia H100s and builds facilities. The company's pitch to investors is that customer prepayments provide a more sustainable funding source than debt markets, which can freeze up during downturns.

The $40 billion figure puts Nebius in rarefied air, as it attempts to match the capital deployment of companies 50 times its size. Delays at the Microsoft data center project have exposed the fragility of the model when construction timelines slip or power delivery gets pushed back. As facilities expand to multi-hundred-megawatt scales, environmental footprint and power grid interactions become critical operational factors. Very few academic institutions possess the balance sheet flexibility or procurement authority to enter into multi-year capacity prepayment arrangements. Research computing administrators must ensure external cloud compute deployments comply with institutional research data management policies and data sovereignty requirements.

stories.Headline: Malaysia probes Megaspeed unit over possible illegal re-export of AI chips
stories.Summary:
Malaysia's trade ministry announced on 13 November 2026 that it is probing a company called Speedmatrix regarding the movement of AI chips. This company is the Malaysian unit of Megaspeed, which is based in Singapore, and is currently under official investigation. The ministry is checking if advanced AI chips imported by the unit were later re-exported to other countries illegally. This probe is being conducted together with the customs department to see if the shipments complied with Malaysian law. The investigation follows reports that high performance chips linked to an Nvidia case may have been diverted from Malaysia.

Speedmatrix is a tenant at data centres in Malaysia and can bring AI chips into the country without a permit. However, since July 2025, any entity that wants to export, re-export, transship, or transit US AI chips must obtain permits. Giving customs false information about these items is a serious offence, and the ministry is checking for such violations. The ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry, known as MITI, is working closely with authorities in Singapore and the US. MITI is also considering stronger controls where necessary to prevent the illegal movement of these high performance semiconductor chips.

MITI stated that Speedmatrix has never been cleared of wrongdoing and that official visits to its facilities were regular monitoring. The ministry said it is working with the customs department to establish if any chips were re-exported to other countries. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said there is no indication that AI chips linked to Megaspeed were shipped out of Malaysia. He added that Malaysia has received no request for assistance from Singapore or the US but will collaborate on probes. Ibrahim stated that the government wants to make sure the rules are being followed regarding the movement of these chips.

Singapore is also investigating Megaspeed because servers containing chips were exported through Singapore to Malaysia but suspected of going elsewhere. Singaporean authorities barred Alice Huang from re-entering the country in February for giving investigators inaccurate information about her Megaspeed role. A US senator alleged that the firm may have been used to get around US controls on advanced semiconductor chips. The US alleges that Alice Huang spied for China, although China denies this and Singapore says she was not investigated. The Nvidia scandal has reportedly wiped almost half a trillion dollars off the market capitalization of the American chip giant.

Megaspeed is under scrutiny over ties between former executive Alice Huang and Jensen Huang, who was the chief executive of Nvidia. Jensen Huang resigned over an affair with Alice Huang, who is a Chinese national and a suspected spy for China. Megaspeed is accused of steering Nvidia AI chips to China despite US export rules designed to slow Beijing's AI development. The reports describe the chips generally as advanced or high performance, but they do not identify the specific chip model. None of the reports states that a re-export from Malaysia has been established, as the checking is still underway.

Megaspeed stated on its website that it takes its US compliance obligations extremely seriously but did not comment on the MITI statement. The next confirmable developments include the outcome of the customs check and any official assistance requests from Singapore or the US. It remains open whether the US Commerce Department will release official text regarding remote access through third country data centres. The articles leave open whether Malaysia will actually announce a change to its permit regime to strengthen its current controls. No statement has been provided by Nvidia regarding the probe into the re-export of chips through the Speedmatrix unit.

stories.Headline: CIQ struggles to hire experienced engineers despite AI writing over 90% of its code
stories.Summary:
At a recent event called The Great Coding Reset in Salt Lake City, executives discussed the evolving nature of software engineering. Bjorn Hovland, the president of a company called CIQ, revealed that artificial intelligence now writes more than 90% of the code for his business. This shift occurred over the last few years, changing the way the company approaches its technical development and staffing needs. Despite the massive amount of automated output, the firm is currently struggling to find and hire enough qualified engineers.

The current hiring strategy at CIQ requires experienced programmers rather than beginners to manage the AI generated output. Hovland stated that the company hires almost no junior developers and generally seeks candidates with five to 10 years of professional experience. This requirement exists because senior engineers must verify if the mountains of automated code actually work for government and corporate clients. Founder Gregory Kurtzer demonstrated this power by using AI to build a Linux compatible operating system kernel in only 11 days.

Bjorn Hovland admitted that he previously expected the company might never need to hire another engineer due to automation. He now believes that experienced engineers using AI tools can become vastly more productive than those who work alone. Gregory Kurtzer warned that programmers who resist using these tools because they enjoy writing code manually risk falling behind their peers. He suggested that the ability to judge results is becoming more valuable than the act of performing every manual step.

The industry faces a troubling dilemma because the lack of junior roles may destroy the traditional career ladder for new programmers. Hovland advised young people to build their own software projects to learn how complex systems work under the hood. This shift suggests that knowing what to create is now more important than the mechanical process of writing the code. The demand for deep software understanding is increasing even as basic programming tasks are eliminated by artificial intelligence.

stories.Headline: Five nonprofits sue Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI and SpaceX to halt all AI development
stories.Summary:
A coalition of five nonprofit online safety and advocacy groups filed suit in the San Francisco Superior Court on Thursday, alleging that artificial intelligence systems are already autonomously breaking the law and causing harm. The suit demands an immediate injunction to halt all further development of AI, particularly ChatGPT, Grok, Muse, Gemini, and Claude. The plaintiffs allege that several Big Tech companies violated the Business and Professions Code of California's Unfair Competition Law, specifically the section prohibiting unlawful business practices. The plaintiffs allege that under the code AI is a public nuisance, defined as anything injurious to health or an obstruction to the free use of property that interferes with the comfortable enjoyment of life or property by an entire community or neighborhood. The suit was filed by Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen, Heat Initiative, and Future Tech Insights, doing business as The Alliance For Secure AI, and names Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI, and SpaceX.

The complaint quotes Elon Musk, who controls SpaceX and has invested heavily in AI, as saying AI has the potential of civilization destruction. The complaint also quotes Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, as saying AI developers do not understand how their own AI creations work. Amodei also said AI could enable a group to carry out a large-scale biological attack, which he called a grave threat to U.S. national security in a hearing before a subcommittee of the Senate Judiciary Committee. In June, the mother of a Canadian child who died by suicide filed a suit against OpenAI, alleging ChatGPT encouraged the girl's suicide. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier sued OpenAI in the same month, alleging ChatGPT harmed children by providing information to school shooters, advising children on self-harm, and intentionally addicting children.

Attorney Matthew Platkin, who filed the complaint on behalf of the plaintiffs, said in a press release from Public Citizen that it is patently illegal for companies to develop and release products they know are unsafe in any respect, let alone have the potential to exterminate the human race. Platkin said they are asking the court to intervene before the risks AI executives have warned us about cause devastating and irreversible harm. The plaintiffs wrote that no other industry is allowed to treat its own development of unsafe products, much less ones that could kill us all, as inevitable. A group of state attorneys general filed a similar suit in October. In July, Illinois passed legislation holding AI developers responsible for safety risks, including a requirement for audits of safety issues by independent third parties, with publication of the results.

The University of Missouri's Career Center directs students looking for work to Handshake, which describes itself as the career network for the AI economy and which Mizzou partnered with in 2017, guaranteeing students an account and access to the platform's job network. Handshake AI pays around $60 million monthly to students from over 1,600 institutions and connects other AI companies to Mizzou students for remote projects usually lasting between two weeks and six months. Handshake AI's entry-level positions offer hourly rates of $17 to $30, while positions requiring years of extensive experience can offer over $100 hourly, and last academic year Handshake AI paid out $117,174 to Mizzou students. According to Cynthia Singleton-Diaz, student coordinator I at the Career Center, 1,623 Mizzou students have submitted 2,710 applications to jobs posted by Handshake AI. Mizzou junior Prajit Rayaprolu was an AI trainer for seven months last school year, attracted by the work's simplicity, flexible hours and a friend's recommendation, and while he felt fairly compensated he eventually stopped seeing the job as sustainable for his well-being.

Amanda Nell, senior student services coordinator at the Career Center, said there are lots of networking opportunities and skill-building opportunities and that they invest and innovate the platform on a pretty regular basis. During his time as an AI trainer, Rayaprolu sorted online photos and evaluated AI-created images and videos for realism, and he was also tasked with writing lengthy prompts and having conversations with AI assistants to complete tasks. Researchers investigating this digital labor use the term human computation to describe human labor in tasks AI struggles with, including sorting data, labeling pictures and letting AI know when it makes a faulty or unfair association, and this labor was extensively used in the early development of AI models such as ChatGPT, Llama, Claude and Gemini. In the early development of AI models much of this training was done by workers paid below their local minimum wages, often contracted through middlemen who assigned digital labor as gig work, and the most popular subcontracting platform for human computation, Amazon Mechanical Turk, was discontinued Sept. 30, 2026, with workers paid per task as independent contractors at rates as low as 1 cent. Peter Mueser, an emeritus professor and specialist in labor markets, said this work was valuable to outsourced workers, as in any growing industry workers are attracted only when jobs pay higher wages than their alternatives.

Elizabeth Lucas, an AI fellow at the Missouri School of Journalism, said these are all things that are part of bigger systems that have really broad impacts and that it is incumbent upon us as humans to think about that and recognize that and see ourselves as one small piece of a very large system. Hayden Hawkins, an undergraduate student representative on the AI standing committee, said in an email that it is imperative that artificial intelligence companies ensure their workers receive fair pay, maintain worker safety and consider data privacy when sourcing their labor. The median wage on MTurk was significantly above the World Bank's $3-per-day international poverty line, though The Journal of Collaborative Computing and Work Practices reported that other crowdsourcing platforms pay around or below this line. Companies hoping to employ students at Mizzou for human computation are vetted by the Career Center before they can be connected with students, and the Career Center works with Mizzou's standing AI committee and UM System Associate Director of AI Justin Palozola to ensure operations on Handshake align with system policy. MU Career Services notifies potential users of Handshake that users are responsible for evaluating the safety, wages, working conditions and other aspects of job listings.

Rayaprolu said he stopped working for Handshake AI after it created a large Slack channel where it frequently posted new guidelines, limited the hours employees could work per day and started to require employees to complete quizzes before they could start working for the day. On Oct. 1, AI trainers working on Project Hedgehog, the project Rayaprolu had spent the majority of his time working on, were required to pass an assessment, and if they did not pass they risked being removed from the project. Rayaprolu also mentioned a four-level rating system for every output he submitted, with scores matching bad, acceptable, good or excellent outputs, and he said that if your scores dropped below two you weren't allowed to access any assessments. The process some social scientists call human computation was first used on a large scale by a Stanford professor, Fei-Fei Li, and as generative AI development progressed companies used this process to test their models and create training data, often sharing methodologies and employees. The extent to which human computation is currently being used in the training of AI systems is unclear, as many tech companies view pre-training strategy as a trade secret that provides them with a competitive advantage, and the future of human computation is unpredictable as AI is increasingly used to evaluate and learn from its own inputs.

stories.Headline: OpenAI supports bipartisan congressional efforts to block China from accessing AI chips and tools
stories.Summary:
OpenAI recently backed a bipartisan congressional effort to block China from accessing artificial intelligence chips and sophisticated chipmaking equipment. This move follows the ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday after a scandal involving an extramarital affair. Howard Lutnick is expected to travel to China this week on Air Force One with President Donald Trump. Trump will meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping during the APEC summit. The trip occurs as Lutnick faces criticism for his handling of export controls on advanced AI chips.

Congress is weighing three proposals to be attached to annual defense legislation that must pass by the end of 2026. The AI Overwatch Act, pushed by Jim Banks and Elizabeth Warren, seeks to freeze Nvidia chip rules for 18 months. The Match Act aims to restrict chip tools, while the Chip Security Act requires mechanisms to prevent smuggling. These measures target high-end chips and machinery from ASML Holding NV to reduce the diversion of Nvidia processors. The US is also investigating Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company, for improper chip smuggling into China.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is responsible for export restrictions, but Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says Commerce has the pen. Bessent has pushed for months to blacklist Megaspeed, while Lutnick is accused of allowing loopholes for advanced chips. The White House stated it maintains complete confidence in Lutnick despite reports that his job could be on the line. A senior US official said the Nvidia scandal should not have any bearing on the upcoming China trip. This official noted that national security matters are developed through the administration's interagency process.

Nvidia allies and trade groups argue that these new provisions would harm the ecosystem of companies tied to the chipmaker. Lawmakers like Mike Johnson, Hakeem Jeffries, and Chuck Schumer have voiced support for the proposed export control measures. Senator Jim Banks stated that Congress has a generational opportunity to address how China accesses US chips. Representative John Moolenaar said Nvidia must appoint leadership that makes national security a top priority. The Justice Department is conducting an espionage probe into Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive suspected of spying.

Jensen Huang previously used his influence to kill the Gain AI Act, which required checking for US customers first. Democratic lawmakers claim the administration has failed to enforce existing export restrictions since Trump returned to office last year. China's Ministry of Commerce previously vowed to take necessary measures to safeguard its interests against such export controls. China has used its own controls on rare earth minerals to retaliate against US restrictions on semiconductor chips. The Ministry warned that these bills would disrupt the stability of global semiconductor industrial and supply chains.

The administration is wary of policies that might imperil a trade truce with China expiring on January 10. The three bills could still be scrapped if President Donald Trump decides to threaten a veto. It remains unclear if Senate Majority Leader John Thune will join the other leaders in supporting the measures. The articles leave open whether Lutnick will regain his footing after clashing with other Trump administration officials. The outcome of the Justice Department's espionage probe into Alice Huang and Jensen Huang is also unknown.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO following a board investigation
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as the chief executive officer of Nvidia on Thursday, November 12, 2026, following a board investigation. This sudden departure occurred after reports surfaced regarding two extramarital affairs involving the co-founder of the company. One of these relationships was with a Chinese businesswoman whom United States authorities suspect of spying for the government in Beijing. The news of the resignation caused immediate volatility for the company's stock as investors reacted to the scandal.

The company announced that Colette Kress, the veteran chief financial officer, will now serve as the interim chief executive officer. Nvidia shares experienced a sharp decline, dropping roughly 14 percent from the previous Wednesday closing price to an intraday low of 148.80 dollars per share. By the early afternoon, the stock had recovered some ground but remained down by 4.3 percent at 166.19 dollars. This leadership change comes at a time when the Nasdaq has seen gains or losses greater than 1 percent in seven of the last 10 trading days.

Investment analysts expressed mixed views, though many believe the company remains the clear leader in the artificial intelligence chip market. Bret Kenwell of eToro U.S. stated that Huang was the crown jewel of the AI trade and his exit will increase scrutiny of next week's earnings report. Dan Ives from Yorkville Ives noted that the board can now move into a new chapter despite this dark moment for the organization. He argued that the company is still two to three years ahead of its nearest competitors in GPU technology.

The company continues to follow a strategic roadmap for its next family of chips to power the ongoing artificial intelligence boom. James McCann of Edward Jones warned that the lack of a clear succession plan risks adding to the current market price volatility. He suggested that investors should avoid over-concentration in tech companies and instead maintain a well-diversified portfolio of large and midcap stocks. The firm's future now depends on whether the shift in leadership will materially affect its long-term strategy and execution.

stories.Headline: Japan weighs binding safety orders and penalties for AI firms
stories.Summary:
The Japanese government is considering a plan that would require businesses involved in artificial intelligence to take measures to ensure safety, with penalties for those that violate the rules. A source familiar with the matter said on Wednesday that the proposal was presented at a closed-door working group meeting on AI-related legal systems. The move comes as concerns grow about advanced AI models behaving unpredictably and after a series of recent high-profile data leaks and unauthorized access incidents that are suspected to involve misuse of AI. Under the approach being considered, the government would be able to issue legally binding orders to businesses that do not cooperate with authorities after an AI-related incident. Failure to comply would carry penalties, which are expected to be limited to incidents involving advanced AI.

Because AI-related businesses range from research firms and developers of foundation models to providers of services for end users, the government will examine which types of firms should fall under the regulations. The working group aims to present an overall outline of its review of the law, including possible revisions, by the end of the year. The current framework is Japan's AI law, enacted in May 2025, which lets the government investigate businesses and issue guidance in cases of malicious conduct. That law has no penalty provisions, and its measures are nonbinding. The proposal would therefore add enforcement power that the existing law lacks.

The source's account of the meeting is the basis for the reporting, and the articles do not identify specific officials who made the proposal. The articles place the proposal alongside other recent security developments in Japan, including a government emergency cybersecurity package and reports of a cyberattack suspected to have involved a North Korea-linked hacking group. The working group's outline is due by year-end, and the articles do not say when any legislation would be submitted or take effect. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Kukoon Rugs and Seating Matters adopt AI to scale operations and boost staff productivity
stories.Summary:
Traditional industries in Northern Ireland began adopting artificial intelligence to become more competitive, as reported by Darran Mashall on November 15, 2026. Two specific companies, Kukoon Rugs and Seating Matters, have integrated this modern technology into their daily business operations. These firms use the software to scale their operations and improve the overall productivity of their various staff members. The adoption of these tools allows these traditional businesses to modernize their processes while maintaining their historical roots. This shift is happening across different sectors, including carpet making and the manufacturing of specialist clinical seating.

Kukoon Rugs, a family firm in Newry, County Down, uses AI daily in finance, commercial, marketing, supply chain, and product departments. Seating Matters, located in the Sperrin Mountains outside Limavady, exports clinical seating to healthcare facilities in the US and Australia. The products from Seating Matters have also appeared in television dramas such as Coronation Street and Emmerdale. These companies sell their goods online and through some of the biggest retail chains found across the UK and Ireland. The technology is used to sift through data, such as finding a relevant email from six years ago.

Chief Executive Paul Vallely says AI allows his team to perform more accurate, efficient, faster, and more thoughtful work. He believes the technology removes the most boring tasks from office roles and increases the excitement and engagement of his team. Managing director Martin Tierney states that AI has revolutionised back office functions like accounting, finance, and pulling data from 20 sources. Tierney claims that while AI will not replace jobs, a person who knows how to use AI could replace a worker. He compares the power of artificial intelligence to a calculator on steroids that makes accountants more productive.

Staff members at Seating Matters are affected by the technology, which Tierney says has actually led to new jobs being created. He notes that the technology is poor at customer service but excellent for managing laborious tasks and avoiding filing cabinets. Vallely argues against claims that AI negatively impacts creative industries, stating it releases time for more research and analysis. The employees are encouraged to use the software to solve problems and speed up mundane tasks within specific guardrails. These guardrails ensure that no patient information or financial information is ever put into the AI software.

Northern Ireland has a long manufacturing tradition, becoming world famous for shipbuilding and linen after the Industrial Revolution in the 19th century. Rug making is also an ancient skill that has existed in the Newry area for a very long time. The articles explain that the basic products may not change, but the design, creation, and marketing processes are changing. Tierney mentions that in the 1800s, people feared calculators would replace accountants, but the technology only increased their productivity. This historical context shows a pattern of traditional roles evolving through the introduction of new tools like Excel.

The companies will continue to use AI to handle mundane tasks while ensuring a human always checks the final work. Seating Matters will keep using the software to flesh out ideas through a chat interface without needing an IT degree. The articles leave open whether other traditional industries in Northern Ireland will follow this path to remain competitive. It remains unclear if the cautious approach to patient and financial data will change as the technology evolves further. The long term impact on the creative nature of rug making and clinical seating design is not fully detailed.

On Thursday's Ramsey Show, Dave Ramsey told him he "was very conservative and very smart to get started." Ramsey projected the money would double about every six or seven years and reach $8 million at 69. Three days earlier, Steve Eisman, the investor made famous by The Big Short, said "65% of the S&P is basically AI. So you own an index, it's basically AI."

Eisman said investors who think the index protects them "are not okay" if something bad happens. Ramsey's projection works on paper, since turning $500,000 into $8 million over 28 years requires about 10% a year, roughly the index's long-run pace. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (SPY) was up 13% year to date, against Ramsey's 12.5% on-air figure. The Vanguard 500 Index Fund ETF (VOO) held 38% of net assets in information technology at midyear. Eisman's 65% adds the utilities supplying data centers, the industrials building them and the banks financing them, leaving only staples and healthcare, "which add up to only 14% of the S&P," outside the trade.

Roughly $325,000 of Jamal's index money rides on continued AI spending. NVIDIA's market value stands near $4.53 trillion, and the stock fell 22% over the past month during what Fortune called tech's biggest selloff in years. Every S&P 500 owner took in part of that drop, whether they knew it or not. In a hypothetical 40% decline, Jamal's $500,000 becomes $300,000, and getting back to even takes a 67% gain, or about 5.4 years at 10% a year.

Ramsey's projection assumes Jamal lives on his VA disability and leaves the money alone, so the loss exists only on paper if he never sells. Taking $30,000 a year is a 6% withdrawal rate before a crash and uses up 10% of the portfolio after it, which is sequence-of-returns risk. Jamal's $100,000 money market is his shock buffer, and at the current one-year Treasury yield of 4.3% that much cash makes about $4,280 a year without any AI exposure. Eisman's advice for money he wants protected was "I would just buy short-term Treasuries.

The yield is decent and they are safe." In the same episode, Ramsey mentioned having no bonds and no gold, only paid-for real estate and growth stock mutual funds. The article concludes the advice works for this caller but "conservative" is the wrong word, since an S&P 500 fund is a reasonable long-term holding for a debt-free man with lifetime government income and also a pure stock position with a heavy tilt toward one theme. The article says an S&P 500 fund is safe only for money you will never need to sell during a crash.

It suggests measuring your cash runway by dividing cash and Treasury holdings by yearly expenses your guaranteed income does not cover, and a result under three years means a long bear market could force selling stocks at a loss. It suggests checking your fund's real AI share by adding technology, communication services and utilities weights and comparing the total to Eisman's 65%. It suggests running the 40% test by multiplying your stock balance by 0.6, and a number that would push you to sell signals a review of whether cash and short-term Treasuries would cover withdrawals until a recovery. Americans who work with a financial advisor have saved more than twice as much for retirement, on average, and Americans say they need $1.46 million to retire comfortably.

stories.Headline: JPCERT/CC finds about 1,000 servers likely used for AI-driven cyberattacks
stories.Summary:
Around 1,000 servers suspected of serving as bases for advanced artificial intelligence-driven cyberattacks have been online since October, a Japanese-led international investigation showed on Nov 14, according to Kyodo News. The probe was carried out by the Japan Computer Emergency Response Team Coordination Centre, known as JPCERT/CC, in cooperation with overseas cybersecurity firms. The investigation found that the servers may have used AI to search for vulnerabilities and to target websites worldwide. Hacking, which previously required time even for those with specialised knowledge, has become easier with the emergence of high-level AI, the reports said.

JPCERT/CC began its investigation in early October and identified AI tools in the discovered servers, and it is tracking 600 to 700 of them. According to the centre, most of the servers hosted AI-powered platforms such as the penetration-testing tool Artex, and they appeared to be searching for system vulnerabilities and attempting to steal configuration files. One server contained traces of a programming support tool created by AI from the US company Anthropic, which suggested that attackers weaponised AI to enhance their hacking capabilities. Some publicly accessible servers contained tools for analysing the internal structure of smartphone applications and programmes for testing system vulnerabilities, and attackers are believed to have analysed apps and attempted unauthorised access through interfaces that exchange information with external systems. Servers hosting the tools can be set up in physical facilities or operated through virtual frameworks, the articles said.

Ken Sajo, an analyst at JPCERT/CC, warned that AI is still in the early stages of being used for cyberattacks and that more sophisticated attacks will increase in the future. The articles did not name any other officials or give further statements from the organisations involved. The reports, published by The Straits Times and The Mainichi on Nov 15, 2026, both credited Kyodo News and carried the same account of the investigation. The articles did not say what happens next beyond the centre's continuing tracking of the servers.

stories.Summary:
Grok AI forecast on November 14, 2026, that XRP may fall to $0.80 before the end of 2026, a 17% drop from its current price of $0.96. The forecast was reported by Sam Daodu in articles published by 24/7 Wall St. and finance.yahoo.com. Grok's projected downside target of $0.80 is based on insights from crypto analyst Ali Martinez. The AI assigns a 35% chance that XRP will reach this price before December 31. In the past week, XRP has already decreased by 17.4%, down from roughly $1.16.

XRP is currently trading below its 20-day average of $1.20 and its 50-day average of $1.33. XRP is also 73.7% lower than its all-time high of $3.65. Grok identifies three support levels below the current price, each derived from different analytical tools. The $0.90 level is about 6% beneath the current price and marks the lower edge of a weekly descending channel, intersecting with a rising trendline from the 2020 to 2021 lows. The $0.87 level is approximately 9% below and is tied to the 0.786 Fibonacci retracement level derived from the previous surge from around $0.10 to $3.69.

The $0.84 level is about 12% lower and is the 100-month simple moving average, which Grok considers the lower boundary of a supportive range between $0.84 and $0.90. For Grok's prediction to materialize by year-end, XRP will need to breach all three support levels within approximately six weeks. Grok lays out three possible scenarios for XRP's year-end price, with two suggesting it will finish above $1. The bear scenario gives a December 31 price of $0.82, a 14.5% change from $0.96, with a 30% probability. The base scenario gives $1.05, a 9.5% change, with a 50% probability.

The bull scenario gives $1.40, a 46% change, with a 20% probability. The combined probabilities of the base and bull scenarios indicate a 70% chance that XRP will end 2026 above $1. The bear scenario would require a significant Federal Reserve shock, such as a half-point rate hike on December 9, or a hawkish outlook that would push Bitcoin below $60,000. When Grok made its forecast, Bitcoin was trading around $65,300, meaning an 8% drop to $60,000 is plausible. XRP typically follows Bitcoin's movements.

The model identifies two events that could help avoid the bear scenario: Bitcoin reclaiming and maintaining a price above $75,000 heading into year's end, and a return to net inflows into U.S. spot XRP funds. If XRP reaches $0.80, Grok anticipates it would take about eight weeks to rebound above $1. Grok's most probable year-end price for XRP is $1.05, about 9.5% higher than the current price but still below the 50-day average of $1.33. The model accounts for the oversold RSI near 19, which could signal a bounce, while also considering extreme market fear and ongoing fund outflows that might limit further upward movement. stories.Headline: Wealth advisers pitch charitable giving help to new AI millionaires
stories.Summary:
Wealth advisers courting newly minted AI millionaires are pitching a service beyond the usual portfolio management, namely help in giving money away, according to advisers and clients described in a Wall Street Journal report published by Mint on 15 November 2026. Anthropic is planning to go ahead with its stock-market debut the following week, a listing expected to create another wave of fortunes only months after SpaceX produced a similarly large bonanza. Many of these new clients are in their 20s and 30s and have had little time to think about managing wealth that appeared effectively overnight. Some prospective clients want to give away 25% of their wealth or more, so advisers must show they can structure charitable giving, align investments with values and measure the impact of the money.

Advisers often suggest donor-advised funds, known as DAFs, because they give the donor an immediate tax deduction while allowing grants to charity at a time of the donor's choosing. A common strategy is to fund a DAF with shares of highly appreciated stock, which lets the donor avoid the capital-gains taxes that selling the shares would trigger. DAFgiving360, formerly Schwab Charitable, said it received more nontraded pre-IPO shares and private-business interests in the fiscal year ended 30 June than in any previous year, and it has seen unprecedented numbers of new DAFs opened and funded this year. The seven co-founders of Anthropic have pledged to donate 80% of their equity to charity, and the company's IPO prospectus outlines a donation-matching program letting employees give equity awards to charity. OpenAI offers to match employee contributions to DAFs through a partnership with the provider Daffy.

Akash Magoon, chief executive of the AI startup Adonis, said that at 30 and unmarried the idea of parking money in a trust for a child he does not have is hard to fathom. A prominent bank invited him and other prospective clients to a New York Knicks game at Madison Square Garden during the NBA semifinals last spring, and although he enjoyed it, a follow-up meeting left him feeling the advisers had not tailored the pitch to his circumstances, including his philanthropic goals. Julia Reed, national director of charitable consulting at DAFgiving360, said the ability to advise on charitable giving is front and center and nonnegotiable, adding that these wealth creators tend to focus on giving back to their communities and seeing results in their lifetime. Shirl Penney, chief executive of Dynasty Financial Partners, said these clients buy into the idea that AI is powerful and can do a lot of good but can also eliminate jobs, and feel an obligation to give back. Dynasty is on an internal list of wealth-management firms provided to Anthropic employees, according to people familiar with the matter.

Magoon, raised in Baltimore by Indian immigrants, aims to give away at least 10% of his wealth in line with the Sikh religion, and after selling his interest in the AI-enabled insurance benefits tool Nayya in 2022 he worked with advisers at Merrill Lynch who helped him set up a DAF. He contributed nearly $200,000 to the fund and used it to pay for a scholarship for five students a year to attend his alma mater, the University of Maryland, and study computer science or economics, with recipients required to be born and raised in Baltimore. He recently renewed the scholarship for another five years and said he wants his adviser to educate him on the different mechanisms for being charitable. Amir Memon, managing partner of OneWell, said advisers there helped three clients pool tens of millions of dollars to create a joint foundation earlier this year, and Haley Schaffer, who founded Waypoint West about a year ago, said old-school private banks pursuing newly wealthy young clients face a disconnect. Charitable consultants say only a handful of major philanthropic gifts have come from AI founders so far, so a flood of donations is not necessarily imminent.
