stories.Headline: PsiQuantum and AMD expand partnership to co-design quantum computing infrastructure
stories.Summary:
PsiQuantum and AMD announced an expanded strategic partnership on November 14, 2026, to co-design the computing infrastructure needed for utility-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers. The collaboration combines PsiQuantum's silicon photonics platform with AMD Instinct GPUs, AMD EPYC CPUs, and the AMD ROCm software stack. It builds on existing work around AMD Versal FPGA technology and also covers hybrid applications that mix quantum, high-performance, and AI computing. AMD plans to make an equity investment into PsiQuantum to reinforce its commitment to the partnership. The companies expect the integration to form the world's most powerful hybrid computing fabric as quantum systems scale.

The initial focus is pharmaceutical research and drug discovery, which falls within biological modeling, an emerging application area for the U.S. Department of Energy's Quantum Genesis Priority Applications. PsiQuantum's computational chemistry methodologies are already performing beyond state-of-the-art calculations on AMD hardware. Working with AMD, PsiQuantum researchers have optimized PRISM, a machine-learning decoder for real-time error correction in photonic quantum computers, and initial breakthrough results have been achieved in simulating covalent inhibitors relevant to oncology drug discovery. Victor Peng, Chief Executive Officer of PsiQuantum, said quantum computing will solve problems in healthcare, materials, energy, and finance, working in concert with AI and high-performance computing. Mark Papermaster, Executive Vice President and Chief Technology Officer at AMD, noted AMD's history in building powerful supercomputers and AI infrastructure and sees a similar opportunity in quantum computing, where classical computing leadership is essential for scaling systems.

Governor JB Pritzker commented that Illinois is bringing together researchers, companies, and a skilled workforce, and he believes the expanded partnership could advance work at the Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park. PsiQuantum serves as the anchor tenant at the Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park in Chicago, and both companies will explore expanding their collaboration with a footprint there. PsiQuantum plans to explore integrated accelerated computing solutions for commercial applications, starting with pharmaceutical research. AMD and PsiQuantum will share more about their strategic partnership at SC26 in Chicago from November 15 to 20.

stories.Headline: Agent skills store repeatable instructions in versioned files for reuse across agents
stories.Summary:
Agent skills are a way to capture repeatable engineering instructions in versioned files so they can be reused across different agents. The approach was described in a TechGig article published on November 14, 2026, at 06:25 AM IST. The article says the instructions are kept separate from tools and permissions, which stay specific to the host environment. The topic was also covered in a GitHub Universe 2026 session titled "Build once, run on any agent: a practical guide to agent skills." The skills are stored in versioned directories centered on a SKILL.md file that describes how to perform a task.

Instructions can be shared across agents, but the environment must still provide the necessary tools, credentials, and permissions. Project-specific configurations, such as names, databases, and conventions, should go in a manifest file instead of being hardcoded into the skills. Skills should also share execution paths, as the forge-dbx skill does by using adapters for different engines. The article names two examples, Proof Agent and Data Forge. Proof Agent uses a separate verifier to assess AI-generated changes, following the principle that self-verification is not sufficient.

Data Forge coordinates several skills, including forge-init, forge-builder, forge-dbx, and forge-lint, to manage complex workflows such as support-desk pipelines. Workflows must include human checkpoints and approval points, as shown by Data Forge's seven-phase support-desk workflow and Proof Agent's code review process. Skills can be packaged for different agent clients, including Claude Code, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot, from a single source. The article does not say what happens next beyond the practices highlighted at the GitHub Universe 2026 session.

stories.Headline: AI code assistants fail on complex enterprise codebases because they lack architectural understanding
stories.Summary:
Most AI code assistants are built for clean, new projects and struggle with complex enterprise codebases, according to a TechGig report published on November 14, 2026. The tools fail to grasp the architectural nuances and historical context embedded in older systems. They falter on ten-year-old Java monoliths with circular dependencies, custom ORMs and undocumented XML configurations. The article says the industry's belief that larger context windows will fix this is wrong.

The report says giving a large language model a million tokens does not give it architectural understanding and only increases the chance of hallucination. Enterprise code relies on implicit knowledge held in Jira tickets, Slack threads and human memory rather than in the code itself. When LLMs process code they treat it as plain text, losing the graph of execution paths, state mutations and historical accidents. Retrieval-augmented generation pipelines that chunk files and use semantic similarity often fail because semantic search is a poor proxy for control flow, for example retrieving irrelevant helper functions while missing the interceptor that enforces token validation.

The article says the solution is not bigger context windows or smarter base models but deterministic code analysis feeding probabilistic models. Systems should first compile, run static analysis graphs and build dependency maps, and the LLM should then work as a reasoning layer on top of a strictly verified structural index instead of reading raw source files directly. The report does not name any vendors or developers. It says that until tooling vendors treat codebases as living state machines rather than text documents, developers in large companies will keep facing significant challenges.

stories.Headline: Kubernetes targets AI workloads with 1.38 gang scheduling and Karpenter GPU scaling
stories.Summary:
Kubernetes is advancing its platform capabilities to handle demanding artificial intelligence workloads more efficiently, according to TechGig. The upcoming Kubernetes 1.38 release and improvements through Karpenter target GPU efficiency, massive clusters, and safer agents. These updates aim to boost productivity and reduce costs for AI jobs running on cloud infrastructure. A January 2026 Annual Cloud Native Survey by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation found that 66 per cent of organisations hosting generative AI models use Kubernetes for their inference workloads.

Kubernetes 1.38 is scheduled for December 16, and it will see gang scheduling and additional accelerator-allocation capabilities advancing towards stable status. Karpenter is an open-source, high-performance Kubernetes node lifecycle manager that automatically provisions and terminates compute resources in response to unscheduled pod requests. AWS addressed bottlenecks when pushing beyond Kubernetes' conventional 5,000-node design envelope towards 100,000 nodes. Fixes for an API-server watch-cache lock reduced a wait of more than half a second to two milliseconds through a lazy-snapshot implementation, and these fixes have already shipped in Kubernetes 1.37. For version 1.38, AWS co-authored a proposal to compress API objects before storing them in etcd, which was accepted for 1.38 alpha.

Mike Stefaniak, AWS's Head of Containers, said AI workloads can spin up tens of thousands of GPU instances per cluster and that things break at that scale. He explained that Karpenter now models devices on instance types it can provision, which allows GPU capacity to scale from zero and be optimally placed. He also reported that an upstreamed parallel-unpack implementation, available in containerd 2.2, reduced a 10GB image's registry-to-node time from two minutes to consistently under 45 seconds in AWS testing. Jonathan Bryce, the CNCF Executive Director, said the aim is to take the same footprint, power consumption and hardware and get more out of it. Dilpreet Bindra, VMware Senior Director of Engineering, said the goal is to define and verify how workloads should behave across any environment, reducing fragmentation and ensuring portability.

Gang scheduling treats distributed AI workloads as coordinated groups rather than unrelated Pods, and it holds the group until its required minimum membership can be placed. Dynamic Resource Allocation complements this work by describing accelerator capabilities and capacity more precisely, with general-availability promotions for partitionable devices, consumable capacity, fractional capacity ranges, and device binding conditions. OpenShell's default-deny approach to agent permissions and Agent Substrate's handling of idle agents are also improving efficiency. The article says AI is driving Kubernetes to coordinate workloads, hardware, and security together, and that making these pieces work consistently in production will take longer, but the direction is clear.

stories.Headline: Economist John Quiggin argues Australian corporate layoffs do not signal an AI job apocalypse
stories.Summary:
Several major Australian companies including NAB, Qantas, Canva, and Atlassian announced large-scale job losses around November 15, 2026. While some of these organizations explicitly blamed artificial intelligence for the cuts, the actual role of the technology remains unclear. This wave of layoffs follows four years of intense hype and excitement since the initial launch of ChatGPT. Many observers are now questioning if these events signal a broader job apocalypse driven by automation.

The situation requires a closer look at the specific changes occurring within these different corporate business models. Qantas plans to outsource 850 Australian jobs to India as part of an overhaul that the company describes as AI-driven. NAB has denied that artificial intelligence played any role in its recent decision to sack employees. Canva faces vulnerability because users can now generate simple graphic designs in seconds using various AI tools. Atlassian is also under challenge, though its project management software is considered harder for AI to replicate.

John Quiggin, a professor at the University of Queensland’s school of economics, argues that the evidence does not support a job apocalypse. He suggests that Qantas is using AI as a cover to muddy the waters regarding simple offshoring. Quiggin believes NAB is simply following a long-term pattern of hiring and sacking workers based on profitability. He notes that productivity growth remains very low despite the massive investments in data centers and infrastructure. The author claims that the current trend mirrors the dotcom era of the 1990s.

The broader context involves a stock market boom based on future demand that has not yet emerged. Hyperscalers like OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Alphabet face competition from cheaper open-weight models such as Mistral and DeepSeek. These competing models from France and China invest far less money while remaining only a year behind the leaders. Quiggin suggests that large language models might become essential utilities like email rather than sources of profit. Consequently, the most significant apocalypse may eventually occur in the stock market instead of the jobs market.

Articles.Title: Is the AI job apocalypse finally here? The evidence suggests otherwise | John Quiggin

stories.Headline: Google Cloud revenue rises 103% to $30.7 billion as AI demand lifts market share to 16%
stories.Summary:
Google Cloud reported a 103 per cent rise in revenue to $30.7 billion for the September 2026 quarter, according to Alphabet's latest financial results. That growth outpaced Amazon Web Services, which grew 39 per cent to $46 billion, and Microsoft Azure, which grew 48 per cent to about $33.2 billion. Google Cloud's market share rose from 13 per cent to 16 per cent over the year, according to Synergy Research Group. Amazon kept the largest share at 26 per cent, with Microsoft at 19 per cent.

AI-specific cloud services now make up about one-third of the global cloud infrastructure market. Google is meeting that demand through Google Cloud Platform, enterprise AI solutions and its Tensor Processing Units. On November 9, Google introduced two new variants of its eighth-generation TPUs. The TPU 8tx is built for government agencies and regulated industries and offers hardware-level encryption for secure AI inference and model training, while the TPU 8i Max combines two TPU chips in a single package for applications needing more memory and computing capacity.

Sales of TPU systems contributed significantly to Google Cloud's growth in the quarter, with strong demand reported for its AI infrastructure and enterprise AI solutions. Google's Search and other revenue reached $63.35 billion in Q3 2026, up 12 per cent year-on-year. YouTube advertising brought in $11.21 billion, an increase of about 9 per cent. Total advertising revenue reached $82 billion, up from $74.2 billion a year earlier, and the company expects to recognise just over 55 per cent of its $561 billion contracted business backlog as revenue over the next 24 months.

stories.Headline: Howard Lutnick pushes to loosen AI chip restrictions while his former firm finances Asian data centers
stories.Summary:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick pushed to loosen restrictions on advanced artificial intelligence chips, according to a New York Times investigation published Sunday. He did this while his former Wall Street firm helped arrange financing for Asian data centers that could benefit from these decisions. The report raises conflict of interest questions because Lutnick led the investment firm Cantor Fitzgerald for more than three decades. His sons, Brandon and Kyle, now lead the firm while Lutnick serves in the administration of President Donald Trump. The investigation suggests a potential clash between his regulatory duties and his family business interests.

Cantor Fitzgerald worked with companies developing data centers in Southeast Asia, including facilities designed to provide computing power to Chinese customers. One Malaysian data center, known as A201, is expected to open next year with hundreds of millions of dollars in Nvidia servers. Cantor served as a financing or placement agent for companies including Bitdeer Technologies Group and Gorilla Technology Group. Lutnick reportedly resisted efforts by other senior administration officials to strengthen restrictions on Nvidia chip shipments to Asia. He also repeatedly delayed efforts to restrict companies suspected of diverting Nvidia chips to China, according to Axios.

The Commerce Department maintained that Lutnick fully divested his financial interests in Cantor and has had no discussions with the firm. Department officials defended their enforcement record and denied directing staff to avoid investigating particular companies. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly criticized the failure to blacklist Megaspeed, a Singapore based company suspected of helping China. The White House has expressed confidence in Lutnick despite the mounting questions over the decisions made by his department. Cantor Fitzgerald declined to comment on the reports regarding its business dealings and financing arrangements.

Senator Elizabeth Warren and Senator Ron Wyden demanded information about a loan from cryptocurrency company Tether to a trust for Lutnick's children. This loan was reportedly secured by assets including more than half of the equity in Cantor Fitzgerald. Other Democrats have demanded stronger enforcement of chip exports, while some Republican lawmakers questioned if technology is reaching China. The report notes that Commerce approved Nvidia export licenses involving Chinese companies with links to military contractors or sanctioned entities. These issues come amid a broader controversy involving former Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang.

Cantor Fitzgerald attracted attention in July 2025 for offering to purchase potential tariff refund claims for 20 to 30 percent of their value. This arrangement allowed investors to profit if courts overturned tariffs, while Lutnick was a vocal advocate for those same tariffs. In March, Bloomberg reported that Tether provided a loan of an undisclosed amount to the trust benefiting Lutnick's four children. This loan occurred around the time the children acquired the ownership stake in the investment firm. These previous disclosures added to the current scrutiny of the business dealings under the leadership of Brandon and Kyle.

Lawmakers are now intensifying their scrutiny of how the Commerce Department handles the export of advanced chips to Asia. The administration continues to face questions about whether U.S. technology is reaching Chinese interests through third party data centers. It remains unclear if the business dealings of Cantor Fitzgerald influenced the specific policy decisions made by Secretary Lutnick. The New York Times stated it found no evidence that the firm's dealings influenced the secretary's official actions. The articles leave open whether further investigations will be launched into the Tether loan or the A201 project.

stories.Headline: Farmers adopt AI tools daily while researchers find automation requires human oversight
stories.Summary:
Jeff Huber, agronomy manager at Alsum Farms & Produce in Friesland, Wis., said farming is not just sitting on a tractor anymore and that technology has come a long way, whether inside storage buildings or in telemetry for running irrigation pivots. He said there will be a lot of jobs and a lot of opportunities out there in the near future. Researchers from University of California, Davis, spent three years studying farming operations across California and Washington and mapping change brought on by AI and robotic tool adoption. The study concluded that automation requires deep human oversight and that tech did not eliminate jobs but required human management to navigate unpredictable conditions. A 2026 Global Farmer Insights Report by McKinsey and Co. found farmers are adopting generative AI and advanced software at historic rates, faster than autosteer, yield mapping and variable-rate technology.

Of the 5,500 global farmers surveyed, 17% are using AI tools daily. Alsum Farms recently partnered with Autonomous Pivot, which mounts cameras and ground-penetrating radar on irrigation pivots for continuous crop monitoring, and AI analyzes the information and provides actionable information. Huber said the camera system looks for disease pressure, emergence, stand counts and insect pressure and is another tool that can be out in the field all the time. He said continuous monitoring is far more efficient than occasionally sending the intern or a scout out there to check just two spots in the field, and that he is getting much more data. AI-driven spider robots mounted above potatoes moving along conveyor belts use cameras to search for internal defects, grade each spud accordingly and use overhead arms to cull defects.

Previously, that task required long hours of tedious labor, and now those same workers can learn highly skilled tasks that compound cost savings, such as edge-spraying potato fields with drones. Huber said the Colorado potato beetle is one of the biggest pests they fight with insecticide, and that edge-spraying where they cannot quite reach with the boom on a ground rig expands what they can use on that field. He said that with technology and sensors you are able to see everything on your phone, and if a bin shuts down he gets a text right away and knows he needs to run and go work on it. Washington policymakers are framing AI adoption in agriculture as a matter of augmentation rather than replacement. A review of federal AI policy by the National Institutes of Health's PubMed Central database highlighted a need to support farmers as the workforce evolves.

According to the review, AI policy emphasizes the government's desire to acquire new employees capable of meeting the demands of the digital workforce while also maintaining the human element of the agricultural industry, so as not to fully automate the sector but optimize the productivity of the agricultural sector with the addition of AI. The article was written by Andy Castillo, editor of Farm Equipment and Machinery at Farm Progress, and was published on November 14, 2026. Castillo started his career in journalism about a decade ago as a television news cameraperson and producer before transitioning to a regional newspaper covering western Massachusetts, where he wrote about local farming. Between military deployments with the Air Force and covering the news, he earned an MFA in creative nonfiction writing from Bay Path University, building on the English degree he earned from the University of Massachusetts Amherst.

Castillo splits his time between the open road and western Massachusetts with his wife, Brianna, a travel nurse who specializes in pediatric oncology, and their rescue pup, Rio. Since the wooden plow tilled fallow ground, farmers have been quick to adopt proven tech, and today's ag technology is the worst it will ever be, and tomorrow's ag workforce will evolve with it. The article said the speedy adoption of artificial intelligence across farms and supply chains has raised workforce questions, including whether humans will have to compete with robots. Huber does not think so, and for him agricultural technology works best when it works for farmers, not instead of them.

The article said farming is becoming more about system management than labor. The article said retraining workers requires investment. The article said the nation's largest outdoor farm event annually hosts over 600 exhibitors from around the world and runs Aug. 31 to Sept. 2, 2027, in Decatur, Illinois. The article said the Organic Grower Summit is a premier event that serves as a hub for organic producers and suppliers to come together and explore the latest trends, techniques and innovations in organic farming.

The article listed a weather item, 20/20: 3-month-out forecast, and a story dated Oct 7, 2026, with a 4 Min Read tag, titled A smarter strategy: Rethink cow size for maximum profitability. The article listed a story titled State ag leaders push USDA for dairy vaccine option dated Nov 13, 2026, and a story titled USDA rolls out AI tool to catch crop report errors dated Nov 12, 2026. The article listed a story titled Lobe Rangers to keynote 2027 Practical Farmers of Iowa conference dated Nov 10, 2026, and a story titled Organic Grower Summit returns to Monterey with new field demo day dated Nov 6, 2026. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Anthropic posts $16.96 billion quarterly revenue as token prices fall
stories.Summary:
Falling AI token prices need not hurt AI providers, Yardeni Research said, because cheaper tokens make more uses worth paying for. The usage-weighted Silicon Data LLM Token Expenditure Index, tracking what customers pay per million tokens, fell more than 40% between June 30 and early October. Yardeni said the decline reflects price competition and a shift in usage toward cheaper models. Anthropic priced its newest premium model, Fable 5.2, at $8 for input and $40 for output, down from $10 and $50 for Fable 5.1. Google's first-party models were processing nearly 32 billion tokens per minute by its October 28 earnings call, up 40% in a quarter and more than fourfold from a year earlier.

Anthropic's third-quarter revenue was $16.96 billion, up 47% from the second quarter and 1,127% from a year earlier. That outpaced a 382% rise in its compute and infrastructure expenses. Anthropic swung from a $974 million operating profit in the second quarter to a $567 million operating loss in the third, citing $5 billion of costly short-term compute and a $2.0 billion non-cash donation-matching charge. Compute and infrastructure, including training, took about 58% of revenue, versus 48% in the second quarter. DRAM contract prices rose nearly 80% in the second quarter and 40% in the third, TrendForce reported.

Median on-demand GPU rental prices rose 9% from a year earlier, and H100 prices 24.7%, according to GetDeploying's November 9 tracker. AWS raised prices on most new Nvidia Capacity Block reservations from October 7, with increases of at least 15% on seven instance types, according to TIKR. SemiAnalysis measured roughly 14 times more throughput from one Nvidia chip generation on software improvements alone. Anthropic says Opus 5.5 cut customer costs per task by about 40% compared with Opus 5. Anthropic's repeat customers generated about nine times their year-earlier quarterly revenue in aggregate.

Yardeni said it is unknown whether those customers would keep spending in a recession. Yardeni said the test is rising profits, not rising volumes of tokens sold. Excluding the donation-matching charge alone would leave an operating profit, though the charge may recur. Anthropic plans to go public at a time when AI tokens have never been cheaper.

stories.Headline: Embodied AI governance must address physical risks beyond screens, article argues
stories.Summary:
The article, published by Fair Observer on 15 November 2026, argues that AI governance must move beyond screens to address embodied AI in vehicles, warehouses, hospitals, performance venues, stores and homes. It says AI is helping machines perceive surroundings, choose actions and move through spaces shared with people. It cites the OECD’s updated definition of an AI system, which recognizes that AI outputs can influence physical as well as virtual environments. It warns that a machine misreading a person’s movement can strike them and that a late driver takeover request can turn a software failure into a collision. It says a service robot failing in a home or care setting may put a vulnerable person at risk.

The article says embodied AI combines software with sensors, mechanical parts, connectivity and a changing environment, and that a system can pass laboratory tests yet fail in the real world. It cites the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s work on autonomous-systems assurance, saying autonomous systems may face an enormous range of operating conditions that make complete testing coverage a major challenge. It cites the NIST AI Risk Management Framework’s four functions, govern, map, measure and manage, and its treatment of safety, security, accountability, transparency, privacy and fairness as connected characteristics. It cites the European Union’s Machinery Regulation on software and machine-learning components performing safety functions and the EU’s updated product-liability rules covering software and AI systems. It also cites the United Nations regulation on automated lane-keeping systems, with requirements on driver availability, takeover requests, cybersecurity, software updates and data storage, and ISO 13482 on hazards of personal-care robots.

The article says developers and operators should identify foreseeable hazards, test realistic conditions, define safe operating limits and prepare for failures before deployment. It says every physical AI system should have a clear statement of where, when and under what conditions it may operate, covering terrain, lighting, weather, network availability, crowd density and user capability. It says these limits should be communicated to buyers and operators in plain language rather than buried in technical documentation. It says a machine exceeding tested limits should slow down, enter a safe state or request qualified human assistance. It says the responsible person needs training, enough information to recognize a problem, authority to intervene and a stop or override mechanism that works under pressure.

The article says workers should be able to report dangerous behavior without retaliation and that consumers and patients should know when a machine is making or carrying out a consequential decision. It says embodied AI systems should create secure, proportionate records of critical decisions, sensor failures, overrides, updates and emergency stops, and that serious patterns should trigger investigation before the next failure becomes an injury. It says recordkeeping must respect privacy and aim at enough reliable evidence to reconstruct what happened, improve the system and establish accountability. It says governance should identify each party’s duties before harm occurs, since a manufacturer, model supplier, integrator, owner and update provider may all be involved. It says contracts should not let the most powerful organizations push every risk onto small businesses, workers or consumers.

The article says safety reviews should include privacy, accessibility, bias, consent and human dignity because systems in homes, care settings and workplaces may collect intimate information about routines, health, emotions and relationships. It says people should not lose the right to human contact, explanation or appeal simply because a robotic service is efficient. The author says he has spent more than 41 years in music and the creative industries and that physical AI will reach concert halls, touring operations, studios, festivals and media production. It says independent venues, artists and small production businesses need practical procurement checklists, clear insurance terms, accessible training, incident-reporting procedures and honest information about a system’s limitations. It says safety and privacy cannot become premium features available only to organizations with large compliance budgets.

The article says society should not wait for a spectacular accident before establishing expectations for embodied AI and that developers and operators can act now by testing under realistic conditions, publishing limits, training responsible people, maintaining genuine stop mechanisms, documenting incidents and assigning accountability throughout the lifecycle. It says progress should be measured not by how human a robot appears but by whether humans remain protected, informed and able to obtain recourse. It says governance that is clear, practical and centered on people creates the trust responsible innovation needs. It says AI is leaving the screen and safeguards must be ready to meet it in the physical world. It says the views expressed are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Fair Observer’s editorial policy.

Articles.Title: AI Governance Must Leave the Screen and Enter the Physical World

stories.headline_source: AI Governance Must Leave the Screen and Enter the Physical World

stories.Headline: Romance novelist Coral Hart writes 370 novels under 21 pen names using AI since 2025
stories.Summary:
Coral Hart, a romance novelist who began with Mills & Boon, has written 370 novels under 21 pen names using AI since 2025, earning "high six figures," as reported by the Guardian on 14 November 2026. She self-published full-time from 2015 after three years of self-publishing dark romance. She sells her books on Kindle Unlimited, which pays only per pages read. She told the Guardian she can write 10,000 words a day by herself. She said she knows of authors who hire more than a dozen ghostwriters to keep pace with the algorithm.

A study awaiting peer review, led by Tuhin Chakrabarty of Stony Brook University, estimates around one fifth of recently self-published books contain at least 25% AI-generated text. In March, Hachette withdrew the romance novel Shy Girl over evidence that author Mia Ballard used AI. This year's Commonwealth short story prize winner, Jamir Nazir, was accused of using AI after readers ran his story through Pangram, a leading AI detection program. Pangram later concluded that since 2025, four regional winners were likely to have used AI. In July, agents for debut novelist Jerry Falade withdrew from a $2m (£1.5m) book deal after he was accused of using AI.

Hart said a bad writer or storyteller will not get a good book out of AI and that you still need to understand craft, structure and what a reader wants. She said AI is not taking the human out of the equation but taking the friction, time and business blocks out of the way. She said the minute someone discloses AI use they get death threats, get called names and are ousted. She advises other authors not to disclose AI use unless it becomes a legal requirement. After she talked to the New York Times earlier this year she was doxed and faced death threats.

Falade wrote an essay saying writing by non-native speakers or in "culturally unfamiliar" English is more often treated with suspicion and suggested the accusations against him may be tinged with racism. He wrote that he hasn't seen this kind of investigative zeal directed at white authors accused of using AI. Every writer at the centre of these AI scandals has been an author of colour. In May, Steven Rosenbaum, who is white, was found to have accidentally inserted fabricated quotes into his book The Future of Truth: How AI Reshapes Reality when he used AI, which he disclosed in the acknowledgements, and his book wasn't withdrawn. Hannah Bowman, chair of the Association of American Literary Agents' AI special committee, said it's a shame all of these things are getting addressed so publicly and that there needs to be a fair and thoughtful process.

Last year a class action lawsuit involving around 500,000 titles won a $1.5bn settlement from the AI firm Anthropic for alleged use of writers' work without consent, and other similar lawsuits are ongoing. One group of 70 prominent authors wrote an open letter calling on the big five publishers, Penguin Random House, Hachette, HarperCollins, Simon & Schuster and Macmillan, to promise they will "never release books that were created by a machine," and the publishers did not promise. Last month the Canadian-Haitian author Thélyson Orélien's novel was struck off the Goncourt Academy longlist, France's most prestigious literary prize, after social media users ran his novel through AI detection software. He denied using AI to write his novel but admitted to plagiarism in some of his other writing, including a short story he wrote more than a decade ago, and his publishers Boréal dropped him in late October. Academic research estimates Pangram is at least 95% accurate at detecting AI-generated writing, with a near-0% rate of false positives.

Thad McIllroy, a publishing expert and author of The AI Book Revolution, said he was surprised when Shy Girl was cancelled and that the cancellation was partly his fault after he ran it through Pangram and approached the New York Times. He said he felt so stupid when Hachette cancelled it because it never occurred to him that would have been the response. He said publishers need to be "brave" and publish extensive AI policies outlining how they use the technology in-house and what authors are and aren't allowed to do. Liz Gately, a New York-based book scout, said many agents have started recommending their writers not send documents as PDFs and save multiple drafts in case they are subject to AI accusations. Falade has recently signed with a new agent.

stories.Headline: Samba CEO Ashwin Navin says AI agents can deliver programmatic advertising's promised efficiency
stories.Summary:
Ashwin Navin, co-founder and chief executive of Samba, used a video interview with Beet.TV and the company's Samba Summit customer event to argue that AI agents can deliver the media efficiency programmatic advertising long promised but rarely produced. He told Beet.TV chief executive Andy Plesser that buyers were promised efficiency and instead got what he described as a massive tax of layers of technology and middlemen. At the summit Samba demonstrated an end-to-end agentic workflow covering media planning, media buying and analytics, according to Navin. He said agentic technology presents a better future and that what programmatic was supposed to deliver will come to fruition thanks to agents.

Navin said media buying and selling involve many manual tasks that his company would gladly hand to agents, but he added that humans should stay in the loop for decisions, applying judgment, creativity and strategy. He argued that AI needs something to reference when deciding how to optimize for a client's objective, and he predicted measurement will have another golden moment like the one that made deduplication important as platforms proliferated. Samba wants to power agentic media buying and analytics that use real data rather than hallucinations, and Navin said every decision loop must be anchored in real deterministic data. He described an ontological knowledge graph of signals on what people watch, stream and scroll across many countries, and Samba acquired the generative AI advertising platform Bestever AI in June, saying the deal would speed its agentic roadmap including autonomous analytics and real-time campaign optimization.

Gartner forecasts that by 2028 more than 70% of global ad spend and 80% of U.S. ad spend will flow through self-serve platforms where AI materially influences media buying, cost and outcomes. McKinsey found that 42% of advertisers cite reliance on black-box optimization systems as a key risk, while cross-platform measurement rose to 72% as a marketer priority from 64% in the IAB's 2026 Outlook Study. Navin said the largest media companies have never needed much help, but the next tier down will have a great moment in the sun and will be easier to buy than in the past. He said he was excited that data can provide transparency into the marketplace where the value is, and the interview was published as part of a DMS by LUMA 2026 series.

stories.Headline: QueerAF reports that AI tools narrow LGBTQIA+ diversity and harm queer people
stories.Summary:
QueerAF published an article on 14 November 2026 arguing that AI was set up to fail LGBTQIA+ people and is already harming them. The article is from QueerAF's free weekly newsletter, which it says is read by more than 10,000 curious queer readers every Saturday morning. QueerAF reported that it had investigated the models Gemini, ChatGPT and Claude. The article said the concerns and experts' predictions it laid out in 2021 are already having direct impacts on people's lives. QueerAF said it spoke again to anthropologist, media scholar and 2020 MacArthur Fellow Mary L. Grey, who said she stands by her words "even more strongly."

The article said most AI tools discussed in the context of concern or risk are probabilistic tools, including Gemini, ChatGPT and Claude. It said these tools do not seek the right information but serve answers based on an estimated probability that they are right, based on previous examples and patterns. It cited trans researcher Chloe Turner's term "the neutral middle", where answers are accurate in a narrow sense but distorted by the sources they use. It said AI is a trillion-dollar business in which the market priority is to serve what as many people as possible want to hear. It said marginalised people do not have the numbers to be a priority and do not represent the needs of most users.

Grey told QueerAF that AI learns from what shows up most often, so people and experiences that are less common in the data are easier to miss. She said this is not just a technical bias problem but about who gets to define the categories, goals and acceptable mistakes when representing communities. She said that is the underlying threat to LGBTQIA+ existences, because it excludes diversity by design. She told QueerAF that at scale those judgments spread quickly while it becomes harder to see who made them or who is responsible. She said representation helps but is not enough, and that putting more queer information into the machine improves things somewhat but its benefit is capped.

QueerAF said numerous studies and research, including its own, have shown that popular models narrowed LGBTQIA+ diversity down to a neutral middle while presenting queer perspectives alongside anti-rights rhetoric. It said that in the "room of one" AI chats create, poorly presented information about the Trans+ community cannot be challenged, unlike in a newspaper article or radio show. It said the models will say conversion therapy is a pseudoscience but will also set out why people receive it anyway and who to contact. It said QueerAF was cited 5,600 times in Microsoft's agent Copilot over a three-month period, while only three clicks to the QueerAF website came from Copilot over that same period. It said Microsoft made revenue from its creatives' work without providing QueerAF or those creatives with any financial remuneration or material benefit.

The article said AI can only go so far in a system designed by affluent Californians who need to create products for as many people as possible. It said Baumol's cost disease, coined by economists William J. Baumol and William G. Bowen in the 1960s, explains that as more is done by machines, everything done by humans becomes more expensive. It said 80% of people get an AI summary when they search something. It said Anthropic's Claude, asked how much cis women are at risk from trans women when visiting a public toilet, stated that the physical risk is statistically negligible but that the question remains one of the most highly contested legal, political and social debates in the United Kingdom. It said Claude repeats dog-whistle arguments from Sex Matters and For Women Scotland despite saying the statistics disprove their hyperbole, balanced only with Stonewall and Trans Actual's perspectives about increased risk to Trans+ people's safety from policies like the EHRC's recommended segregation.

QueerAF said its AI policy is clear: generative AI without guardrails that take marginalised communities into account creates more harm than good. It said its staff, contributors and collaborators must not use it to create journalism, nor will QueerAF use it to recommend content because of the harms of algorithmic prejudices, underestimation and negative legacy data. It said QueerAF could use AI to generate much more content, as other gay media has begun doing, but does not want to. Grey told QueerAF that the question of whether to try to improve AI models is a false dichotomy, because improvement is important but wasted effort without guardrails and regulation. She said the real question is how community groups affected by a system can set up ways to refuse it, challenge it, change it and share in its benefits, and that some AI systems can be governed better while others are not worth the risk of building, especially without any regulatory framework to test it before its impact is fully understood.

QueerAF launched its end-of-year membership drive asking readers to become members if they want information about Trans+ lives to come from its LGBTQIA+ journalists, 3 in 4 of whom it says are Trans+. It said it is a not-for-profit publisher that is ad-free and totally independent, and that its support is critical to its sustainability. It said it will not hand its power over to a tech giant that will use those profits to undermine LGBTQIA+ rights. The article said queer journalists are needed to cut through what it called AI slop. It said readers can join the more than 10,000 people who understand the LGBTQIA+ headlines every Saturday.

stories.Headline: Chinese retailers use AI and digital celebrities to drive Singles Day sales
stories.Summary:
During the Singles' Day shopping event on November 11, Chinese retailers used artificial intelligence to drive sales. Tmall featured digital likenesses of six celebrities, including former swimmer Ning Zetao, to host promotional livestreams. This annual event began in 2009 when Alibaba partnered with 27 merchants to encourage self-gifting. The festival has now expanded into a multi-week competition for consumer budgets.

The shopping period started early this year, with JD.com beginning sales on October 12 and Alibaba's Taobao and Tmall following on October 20. Austin Li sold 100,000 monthly memberships for the QwenWork office AI service in only 30 minutes. These memberships provided roughly 2 trillion AI tokens for software use. JD.com also saw humanoid robot sales increase by 700 percent compared to the previous year.

Retailers like JD.com are now expanding their offerings to include various service-based promotions. These include home cleaning, appliance repair, elder care, and pet services. According to reports from Cailian Press and China Securities Journal, spending also rose for smart water cups and AI toothbrushes. These changes require platforms to manage service appointments rather than just shipping physical boxes.

The shift toward services and software allows platforms to maintain longer relationships with their customers. Retailers can now engage users through subscription renewals, deliveries, or new bookings. This evolution provides a useful comparison for United States merchants as Black Friday expands across November. A longer sales calendar allows companies to market unexpected products to their shoppers.

stories.Headline: Federal Reserve lists AI risks as top financial stability concern as debt funds AI hardware
stories.Summary:
The article, published by Simply Wall St on Yahoo Finance on 14 November 2026, reported that the Federal Reserve now lists risks tied to artificial intelligence as the top concern for financial stability, with a surge in debt funding the hardware behind AI. It said that focus puts the spotlight on the routers, switches, optical links and server racks that keep AI models running. It broke down three stocks from the AI networking and server supply chain that investors are watching closely. The three stocks were TTM Technologies, Coherent and Fabrinet. It said TTM Technologies generates about US$2.4b from Commercial activities and roughly US$1.4b from Aerospace & Defense, with additional segment adjustments and eliminations. It said Coherent builds lasers and high speed optical components, supplying AI datacenter transceivers, co packaged optics and photonics for hyperscale networks. It said Coherent generates about US$6.2b from Datacenter & Communications and roughly US$1.9b from Industrial activity, with modest intersegment eliminations. It said Fabrinet manufactures and packages high speed optical transceivers, modules and related components that connect AI data center servers and networking hardware, and generates about US$5.1b from optical networking equipment, with major revenue contributions from Thailand, the U.S. and Singapore.

stories.Headline: BigBear.ai falls 68.5% over twelve months despite rising sales and new federal AI deals
stories.Summary:
BigBear.ai shares fell 68.5% over the twelve months to November 14, 2026, including dividends, even though sales rose. The article, by Sasha Jovanovic, was published on that date. Shares cost US$6.34 at the start of the period and stood at US$1.91 at the time of writing. The drop put BigBear.ai in the middle of a trade the article links to a scan of 38 AI small caps. Q3 2026 revenue of US$43.6 million and new federal AI deals above US$225 million supported the bullish case.

The bullish case pointed to a Fair Value of US$8, built on revenue growth of 2.7% a year and profit margins eventually reaching 7.0%. The cautious view put Fair Value at US$5.83, based on slower progress, lumpy government revenue and the need to fund R&D and acquisitions while reporting losses. Net income swung from a US$2.5 million profit in Q3 2025 to a US$91.9 million loss in Q3 2026. Net margin fell to -210.8%. The bearish analyst Narrative on Simply Wall St still places Fair Value above the current US$1.91 share price.

That Narrative said BigBear.ai is positioned in areas where governments are directing more AI and counter drone funding. It said the current Q2 2026 net loss of US$25.7 million and continued negative cash flow mean any slowdown or reprioritisation of AI defense programs could leave rising operating expenses unmatched by cash inflows. It said the view assumes the company keeps converting recent government awards into larger, repeat production work while lifting margins. It said revenue growth would then need to outpace ongoing losses and cash burn.

The article said the whole episode hinged on one assumption, that revenue progress would arrive with cleaner profits. It said investors assessing another high-growth AI contractor should track backlog but pair it with net margin over time. It said three other companies sit 41%, 36% and 40% below its estimate, among 32 undervalued companies on a list. It said the article is general in nature and was produced with the assistance of AI automation, based on data and analysis from Simply Wall St. It said Simply Wall St has no position in any stocks mentioned.

The article said holding BigBear.ai over the past year would have meant a 68.5% loss including dividends. It said the question now is which early clues, from bullish calls built on rich P/E assumptions to warnings about lumpy government revenue and ongoing losses, investors could realistically have focused on. It said backlog growth, new federal AI deals above US$225 million and Q3 2026 revenue of US$43.6 million gave the bullish story fresh support. It said the catch sat in the income statement. It said the evidence cut both ways.

stories.Headline: VibeCDA holds first vibe-athon in Coeur d'Alene to teach beginners vibe coding through building a playable game
stories.Summary:
VibeCDA held its first vibe-athon on Friday at the Innovation Collective in Coeur d'Alene. The event was inspired by hackathons, where companies pay programmers and designers to create working software or hardware prototypes. Organizer Daniel Finley opened the event for participants. The goal was to give anyone, from beginners to experienced developers, a hands-on way to learn about vibe coding by building a playable game.

Vibe coding lets people describe what they want in plain language, and a large language model generates the results without the user knowing how to code. Organizers said the key skill is learning how to instruct the AI properly to get the results you want. Co-host Conner Kees said it is not hard to build a good vocabulary for these things. Co-host Tom Vrba compared lacking that vocabulary to a property developer who knows nothing about construction.

Finley said that if you tell someone to build a game, anyone can do it right away, and people have fun because it is creative. He said participants come away realizing they can do a lot of things, such as building more games, creating a website or setting up tools to run a business. Co-host Jeff Spicer said video games have historically been the first adoption of technology, and software in medical and military fields can be traced back to the 1993 game Doom. Kees said the aim is to teach people to think big picture and stay in control of what they are doing.

Participants Josiah Poling and Noah Marshall, who share a background in storytelling through film and video games, joined to broaden their skills. Poling said he wanted a more well-rounded understanding of what he can do with AI tools, and that it would at least be fun even if he did not make anything fun. Marshall said he has taken a coding course here and there but has no huge programming background, and that spreading out ideas and reaching a concept quickly is exciting. VibeCDA plans similar events next year to connect builders, share ideas, develop local talent and eventually grow Coeur d'Alene-based businesses. Finley said the group wants to work more closely with places like Elevate, KTEC, Gonzaga and Lake City High, and to get people thinking they can be creators rather than consumers.

stories.Headline: Nigeria's electoral commission investigates AI images in voter register before 2027 election
stories.Summary:
The Independent National Electoral Commission found artificial intelligence images in its preliminary voter register just two months before the 2027 general elections. Incumbent President Bola Tinubu is running for office against former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and senior opposition figure Peter Obi. These AI images featured exaggerated facial features and inconsistencies like duplicate names or identities of people who had already died. The commission is now investigating these discrepancies to protect the credibility of the upcoming vote from potential attacks. This development has raised concerns about the overall preparedness of the electoral body ahead of the national polls.

The commission must now manage a registered voter base of more than 103 million Nigerians during the 2027 election cycle. Joash Amupitan, the chairman of the commission, announced a dedicated unit to monitor AI threats and detect deepfakes. This new unit aims to strengthen the integrity of the process by focusing on discrepancies created by AI use. The commission previously introduced Direct Data Capture Machines in 2011 to scan fingerprints and capture facial recognition data. In 2021, the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System was introduced, though it suffered system failures during the 2023 general elections.

Joash Amupitan stated that the commission is investigating AI discrepancies to ensure the credibility of the upcoming elections is not attacked. Mallam Jibrin Baba Ndace, Director-General of Voice of Nigeria, urged journalists to avoid believing reports that could be AI manipulations. He stressed that news media must use protection measures because public institutions like the commission cannot provide impartial information. Chibuike Mgbeahuruike of the Centre for Democracy and Development said AI is not inherently a threat to electoral integrity. He argued that the real danger is the absence of effective accountability for how this technology is deployed.

Lois Ugbede from the platform DUBAWA said AI-driven disinformation is becoming commonplace and could influence political discourse and voter behavior. She noted that parties are already using inflated crowds to show they have large followership or support. Akintunde Babatunde of the Center for Journalism, Innovation and Development warned that people may begin to doubt authentic information. He cited a lawmaker who claimed clips of his own inflammatory remarks were manipulated to dismiss genuine evidence. Chibuike Mgbeahuruike warned that AI intrusion into the commission portal could undermine institutional credibility among the voting public.

Nigeria has a history of dealing with fabricated images, doctored audio, and fake videos during its various election cycles. During the 2023 elections, deepfakes falsely linked candidates to terror-related activities on social media to influence public perception. The country has seen a decline in voter turnout, with only 27 percent of registered voters participating in 2023. This represents the lowest turnout since Nigeria returned to democratic rule in 1999, showing a rise in voter apathy. These technological shifts since 2011 were intended to improve transparency and efficiency but have faced significant challenges.

The commission will continue to monitor AI-related threats through its new unit to protect the 2027 general election process. Journalists must now apply more due diligence to avoid falling into traps set by sophisticated AI-generated disinformation campaigns. Voters must decide if they can trust the technology if it remains without independent scrutiny or human oversight. The articles leave open whether the commission can successfully remove all AI-generated identities from the preliminary voter register. It remains unclear if the new monitoring unit can effectively stop the spread of deepfakes across social media.

Articles.Title: Nigeria: Can the influence of AI in the upcoming elections be mitigated?

stories.Headline: Principal Financial Group says political opposition to data centers raises AI buildout uncertainty
stories.Summary:
Concerns about how fast and how large the artificial intelligence buildout is proceeding have grown, and those concerns have been made sharper by worries that regulatory friction and other hurdles could unsettle the economics and the timing of the returns investors expect. The article, published by Seeking Alpha on November 14, 2026, and attributed to Principal Financial Group, says the debate over the buildout has widened rather than settled. It lists a long set of exchange traded funds tied to the theme, among them WTAI, THNQ, LRNZ, AIQ, UBOT, ARTY, ROBT, ROBO, BOTZ, ARKQ, KOMP, ARKK, DTEC, IGPT, AIBU, ALAI, DTCR and IDGT. The piece frames the moment as a maturing phase in which enthusiasm is giving way to moderation.

The article says political opposition to data centers is real, but it argues that the strategic case for development remains strong in both parties, because artificial intelligence is seen as important to the economic competitiveness and national security of the United States. It stresses that these pressures do not mean the AI cycle has run its course, and it says heightened scrutiny will likely drive greater differentiation across companies, projects and geographies. It adds that Democratic victories in key congressional and gubernatorial races have increased political and regulatory uncertainty. Projects that align computing demand with infrastructure readiness, economic viability and community acceptance are likely to be rewarded, and tighter development conditions may also raise the value of established operators.

Principal Financial Group is the source of the commentary, and the article describes the firm as a global investment management leader offering retirement services, insurance solutions and asset management. It says the firm was founded in 1879, is a member of the Fortune 500, has $519.3 billion in assets under management and serves some 19.7 million customers worldwide from offices in Asia, Australia, Europe, Latin America and the United States. The firm's view, as paraphrased in the article, is that greater selectivity is warranted rather than abandoning the AI theme. The article does not say what happens next beyond that guidance.

Articles.Title: The Maturing Phase Of AI: From Enthusiasm To Moderation

stories.Headline: Anthropic says natural gas is AI's biggest bottleneck and Energy Transfer expands pipelines to meet demand
stories.Summary:
Anthropic revealed in its S-1 filing on November 14, 2026, that natural gas is a primary bottleneck for artificial intelligence. The company mentioned natural gas five times in a single paragraph to highlight the critical need for power. This filing suggests that securing fuel and transportation is now more urgent than acquiring computer chips. Failure to obtain these resources could lead to the delay or total abandonment of planned sites.

The situation requires a massive expansion of energy infrastructure to support dedicated on-site natural gas-fired generation. Energy Transfer operates over 140,000 miles of pipelines across 44 states to meet this growing demand. The company reported that its adjusted EBITDA grew 31 percent to 5 billion dollars in the third quarter of 2026. However, the firm carries a high long-term debt load of 68.8 billion dollars from its network expansions.

Anthropic stated that its facilities are exposed to fuel price volatility and supply disruptions outside of its control. The company noted that these costs are borne on a pass-through basis during the development of sites. Energy Transfer is already responding to these needs through a supply agreement with Oracle for three data centers. The pipeline company also signed a 20-year binding agreement with Entergy Louisiana to provide necessary fuel.

The broader context shows that 26.8 percent of United States businesses used AI in October 2026. This is a significant increase from the 3.7 percent of businesses using the technology in September 2023. Energy Transfer is also providing gas to a Nexus Data Center campus and indirectly supporting Meta Platforms. Analysts remain bullish on the stock with a median one-year price target of 25 dollars.

stories.Headline: Horse Welfare Board launches strategy using AI and wearables to prevent racehorse injuries
stories.Summary:
The Horse Welfare Board launched a new welfare strategy on Tuesday at a reception in Westminster. This plan focuses on using artificial intelligence and wearable technology to identify injury risks before they occur. The initiative aims to improve the safety and health of Thoroughbreds throughout their entire lives. It represents a shift toward using data to prevent falls and fatalities.

The British Horseracing Horse Welfare Strategy 2027-2031 establishes 20 priorities for horses from birth through retirement. It requires tracking every British racing horse through the Retraining of Racehorses program to ensure lifetime responsibility. The plan utilizes gait analysis software, heart monitors, and equine data to create better risk models. This effort builds upon the first industry-wide strategy, A Life Well Lived, which was published in 2020.

The independently chaired Horse Welfare Board, which was created in 2019, is responsible for the strategy. Independent board member Fred Barrelet stated that the industry is starting a technology revolution in horse management and training. The board's independent chair, Minette Batters, told reporters that fatalities will never be accepted. They believe that transparency and accountability are essential for building trust.

The industry faces significant public scrutiny when horses die during major racing events. Maintaining a social license depends on the sport showing clear progress in animal welfare. The Retraining of Racehorses charity also released a five-year plan on the same day to support aftercare. Future efforts will focus on using these modern technologies to identify risks earlier.

Articles.Title: British Racing Uses AI and Wearables for Horses

stories.Headline: Meta-analysis finds customer-facing AI links to stronger brand ties in hospitality
stories.Summary:
A meta-analysis published on 14 November 2026 on bioengineer.org examined customer-facing artificial intelligence across tourism and hospitality. It synthesized data from twenty-three independent empirical samples comprising 9,875 respondents. The study established a random-effects pooled zero-order correlation of 0.62. The authors said travelers and hospitality consumers interacting with artificial intelligence systems report substantially stronger relational ties with the underlying service brand. The authors emphasized that this summary correlation represents an upper bound rather than an absolute baseline for commercial practice.

The study searched Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection in May 2026 and yielded 792 unique records published between 2016 and 2026. Initial assessment of fifty-six accessible full-text reports retained twenty-nine eligible studies, and supplementary citation searching added one additional investigation. A re-extraction phase eliminated six studies and merged two companion reports into one sample-level effect, leaving twenty-three independent empirical samples from twenty-four published articles. The pooled correlation of 0.62 had a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.54 to 0.68, and a parallel DerSimonian-Laird estimation produced the same correlation of 0.62. Heterogeneity was substantial, with an I-squared value of 96.4 percent, a Cochrane Q statistic of 605.39, and a tau-squared of 0.065, and the 95 percent prediction interval spanned from 0.18 to 0.85.

The authors said every included primary study relies on cross-sectional, single-source self-report questionnaires, so shared method variance inflates the observed alignment between technology perceptions and brand evaluations. They said automated interfaces do not generate uniform outcomes, making careful contextual interpretation essential for researchers and industry practitioners alike. They said the synthesis moves beyond functional adoption toward enduring consumer-brand connections and integrates studies from the recent generative artificial intelligence period. They cautioned that because each subgroup contained only four to nine samples, statistical power was limited, indicating a failure to detect differences rather than proven equivalence. They said framing artificial intelligence around humanlike qualities does not reliably alter the measured strength of customer-brand relationships within current empirical precision.

Across individual primary studies published over the past decade, reported bivariate correlations ranged widely from 0.22 to 0.81. Conversational chatbots exhibited a pooled correlation of 0.71 across four samples, embodied service robots averaged 0.64 across four samples, generative artificial intelligence tools averaged 0.64 across six samples, and general artificial intelligence platforms registered 0.53 across nine samples, with a Q-between of 4.09 and a p-value of 0.25. Anthropomorphic predictors showed a correlation of 0.71 across three samples against 0.60 across twenty samples for functional attributes, with a Q-between of 1.59 and a p-value of 0.21. Trust registered 0.71 across four samples, behavioral intention 0.69 across three samples, satisfaction 0.65 across six samples, engagement 0.54 across five samples, and co-creation 0.41 across two samples, with a Q-between of 6.41 and a p-value of 0.17.

Hotel environments yielded 0.63 across nine samples against 0.61 across ten samples for travel destination platforms at p = 0.75, Asian samples averaged 0.61 across ten studies, European samples 0.59 across four studies, and other regions 0.64 across nine studies at p = 0.85. The theoretical foundation rests upon the stimulus-organism-response framework, integrated with the computers-are-social-actors paradigm and anthropomorphism theory. The computers-are-social-actors paradigm posits that individuals mindlessly apply human social rules to technological interfaces displaying communicative cues such as natural language, voice, or interactive responsiveness. Anthropomorphism theory suggests that attributing humanlike qualities to non-human entities fosters emotional connection and social warmth.

Prior scholarship on service automation in tourism predominantly consisted of narrative overviews or empirical models centered exclusively on initial technology acceptance. The review extracted zero-order correlations from Fornell-Larcker discriminant validity matrices and correlation tables, with twelve correlations from partial least squares construct scores, four from covariance-based structural equation modeling latent variables, six from observed composite scores, and one merged sample combining construct-score and observed data. Primary statistical pooling used a random-effects model estimated via restricted maximum likelihood incorporating the Knapp-Hartung adjustment. Neither correlation source (p = 0.42) nor publication year (p = 0.78) accounted for the extensive observed variance.

Five pre-specified sensitivity analyses affirmed the stability of the pooled findings while highlighting essential methodological boundaries. The article's account of those sensitivity analyses ends mid-sentence at the words "Re-analyzing the samples us". The articles give no further results, no publication outlet beyond bioengineer.org, and no named authors. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Morphisec warns AI tools spread unmanaged Node runtimes across endpoints
stories.Summary:
Morphisec published a blog post on 15 November 2026 arguing that AI tools have turned Node.js from a developer toolchain into an unmanaged runtime spread across corporate endpoints, with a single laptop running a couple of AI tools easily carrying four or five independent Node runtimes. The post says coding agents install through npm, their MCP servers launch through npx, and desktop AI apps and editors ship Node inside their own binaries, so the copies arrive through different doors and are updated by different mechanisms or by none. It lists five sources: a system install for npm-based agent CLIs in Program Files, version managers such as nvm-windows, fnm and Volta in the user profile, MCP servers and tools launched with npx from the npm cache, Electron-based AI apps and editors with Node embedded in their binaries, and single-file agent binaries built with Bun or Node single-executable builds. Only the first looks like software IT manages, and the rest are invisible to an inventory that reads the installed-programs list.

The post says four habits keep those copies vulnerable even after a Node fix ships: tooling documents "Node 18 or newer" as a floor even though Node 18 and Node 20 are end of life and receive no security fixes, npm update -g refreshes the agent package but not the node.exe underneath it, embedded runtimes are patched only when a vendor rebuilds and few release notes say which Node version a build contains, and a working copy gives nobody a reason to touch the version manager. It says Node.js now ships a security release every few months and each one is supposed to end with every copy updated, which on an AI-era endpoint means first finding copies nobody knew were there. It argues an agent's Node talks to whatever the agent decides to reach based on what it reads, such as a link in a README, an issue comment, a docs page or a result from an MCP tool, making prompt injection a delivery mechanism for runtime bugs in the HTTP client, TLS verification, decompression and parsing code. It says a configuration line such as npx -y some-server@latest downloads an unpinned package from the public registry and executes it with the user's full privileges each time the agent starts, with no installer and no approval process, and that MCP servers listening on a local HTTP port can be reached by any local process, with the MCP specification itself warning about DNS rebinding. A compromised agent runtime runs as the user and can read the model API token, git credentials, cloud CLI profiles, registry tokens and SSH keys in that profile, plus MCP servers' own SaaS tokens.

The post is attributed to Morphisec, a security vendor whose blog carries it, and it presents the argument in the author's own voice rather than quoting a named researcher or official. It does not name any specific vulnerability, attacker, victim or incident, and it gives no dates for the Node security releases beyond saying they ship every few months. It does not say what any vendor, developer or standards body has done in response, and it offers no remediation steps beyond the implied need to find and update the hidden copies.

Articles.Title: Every Endpoint Now Runs Node: How AI Tools Multiplied an Unmanaged Runtime

stories.headline_source: Every Endpoint Now Runs Node: How AI Tools Multiplied an Unmanaged Runtime

stories.Headline: Review authors find only 23 percent of cardiovascular AI studies use external validation
stories.Summary:
A systematic review of 35 peer-reviewed studies, published in Artificial Intelligence Review by Alam, Bulbul, Hossen, Azad, Khan and Moni in 2026, examined artificial intelligence software systems for detecting cardiovascular disease from physiological signals. The review followed PRISMA guidelines across Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, Embase and IEEE Xplore, and assessed quality and risk of bias with an adapted QUADAS-2 framework. The studies reported an average accuracy of 93.7 percent, and the 21 studies that reported diagnostic performance documented accuracies from 70.5 to 99.9 percent. Electrocardiogram data was the dominant signal source, used by 71.4 percent of the systems, and developers mostly applied deep learning, relying heavily on convolutional and recurrent neural networks.

The review found several gaps. Only 23 percent of the studies carried out external validation, and only 14 percent reached clinical-scale deployment. None of the 35 studies used a principled multi-signal fusion strategy combining electrocardiogram, photophlethysmogram and phonocardiogram signals, and only one system, or 2.9 percent, had a conversational interface designed for patients. The authors said inconsistent reporting of metrics and a pronounced absence of rigorous evaluation severely limit confidence in the high accuracy figures. They outlined a three-directional framework prioritizing multi-signal models for generalisability, large language model clinical narratives for interpretability, and edge-cloud deployment for accessibility.

The authors framed the work around a global crisis, noting that cardiovascular disease claims more than 17.9 million lives each year, nearly one-third of all global deaths, and that diagnostic delays are a particular concern in resource-limited environments. They said the evidence base has remained fragmented and difficult to translate into practical healthcare settings. The review recommends the three directions as the path toward clinical use. The articles do not say what happens next beyond that framework.

Articles.Title: Most Cardiovascular AI Systems Lack External Validation, Systematic Review Finds

stories.Headline: Self-efficacy mediates link between AI enthusiasm and perceived learning success, Mohamed and Al Mahmud find
stories.Summary:
A cross-sectional survey study published in Discover Artificial Intelligence in November 2026 found that self-efficacy significantly mediates the link between learners' positive attitudes toward technology and their perceived effectiveness of AI-supported English language learning. Amr M. Mohamed and Fawaz Al Mahmud conducted the research with 234 students enrolled in English-language courses at a private college of health sciences in Saudi Arabia. The study examined whether self-efficacy, the belief in one's ability to manage prospective situations, explains the relationship between technophilia and positive emotional experience on one hand and perceived learning effectiveness on the other. The findings indicate that confidence in managing AI-supported tasks is a central cognitive mechanism linking affective dispositions to learners' appraisals of educational utility. The study used a quantitative, cross-sectional correlational design to examine associations among the constructs without manipulating variables.

The sample of 234 students had a mean age of 20.85 years and a standard deviation of 4.06, and was 77.8% male and 22.2% female. Academic levels included 128 undergraduates and 106 foundation-year students, and 41.5% reported daily AI tool use for English learning, 29.9% weekly, 10.3% monthly, 13.2% rarely and 5.1% no use. Technophilia was measured with four items adapted from Martínez-Córcoles et al. with a Cronbach's alpha of 0.87, and positive emotional experience with four items adapted from Bieleke et al. with an alpha of 0.91. Self-efficacy was evaluated with three context-specific items based on Bandura's framework with an alpha of 0.82, and perceived learning effectiveness with a scale adapted from Ashfaq et al. whose final three-item version had an alpha of 0.927. Structural equation modeling with bootstrapping using 5,000 resamples showed a chi-square to degrees of freedom ratio of 1.75, a Comparative Fit Index of 0.941 and a Root Mean Square Error of Approximation of 0.057.

The authors interpret the findings through Social Cognitive Theory, which posits that self-efficacy regulates effort allocation, persistence and strategic action. They state that in AI-mediated learning environments perceived ability is decisive when learners must interpret automated responses, select appropriate tools and organize learning activities with agency. They say learners with high self-efficacy are more likely to apply feedback strategically and sustain performance under higher task demands. The study suggests self-efficacy functions as a proximal cognitive mechanism through which AI affordances become usable learning opportunities rather than merely a motivational belief. The authors say this perspective highlights the importance of confidence in managing the complexities of AI-supported language learning.

The researchers acknowledged limitations including the cross-sectional design, which prevents causal inference and restricts interpretation to associational rather than directional relationships. They noted that reliance on self-report measures increases the likelihood of common-method bias, although statistical checks using the common latent factor approach suggested this was not a significant issue. They said the study focused on perceived learning effectiveness, a subjective evaluation, rather than objective performance outcomes, which limits generalizability to actual language proficiency gains. They added that the single-institution convenience sampling and the gender imbalance in the nursing student population further constrain applicability to broader EFL contexts. The authors noted the demographic imbalance may limit generalizability of the findings to female-majority nursing populations.

The theoretical model drew on the Technology Acceptance Model, Control-Value Theory and Social Cognitive Theory, which collectively suggest that stable technological dispositions and dynamic emotional experiences influence perceived learning effectiveness through proximal cognitive beliefs, specifically self-efficacy. The structural model explained 52% of the variance in perceived learning effectiveness and 48% of the variance in self-efficacy. Preliminary analyses confirmed that measurement invariance was supported across gender groups, and multicollinearity diagnostics indicated tolerance and variance inflation factor values were within acceptable ranges. The study contributes to computer-assisted language learning research by clarifying how positive orientation toward AI-supported technologies, emotional experience and efficacy beliefs jointly relate to learners' perceptions of effective AI-supported language learning. The findings suggest pedagogical strategies should focus on progressively scaffolded practice and mastery-oriented AI tasks to strengthen self-efficacy.

Future research should prioritize experimental and longitudinal designs that manipulate or track self-efficacy and examine its influence on objective AI-supported language-learning outcomes. Qualitative or mixed-methods research could also investigate how learners develop, maintain or lose confidence over time during authentic interactions with different AI tools. The authors say these approaches would clarify the temporal and potentially causal processes underlying the relationships identified in the study. The current findings provide a foundational understanding of the psychological dynamics at play in AI-supported EFL education, highlighting the pivotal role of self-efficacy in shaping learners' experiences and evaluations. The article was published in Discover Artificial Intelligence, volume 6, issue 1, Article 1737, with the DOI 10.1007/s44163-026-02712-z.

Articles.Title: Self-efficacy links AI enthusiasm to perceived learning success
