stories.Headline: Java service logs AI prompts in plain text, exposing customer names, card numbers and phone numbers
stories.Summary:
A customer message containing a name, a card ending 4111 and a phone number was wrapped in a prompt, sent to a model and logged in plain text by a Java service, in an article by TechPanda published on sitepoint.com on November 14, 2026. The article said this happens more often than people admit and that prompts and responses are some of the most personal text an application touches. It said AI calls are messier to log than regular web requests because output changes from run to run. It said prompts are built from a template, retrieved document chunks, chat history and the user's message stitched together. It said cost is paid by the token, so without per-call records you cannot say which feature is burning money.

The article said the first three sensitive groups follow patterns and are easy to catch, while the last two do not. It said metadata includes a request ID, a hashed user or tenant ID, model name, prompt template name and version, token counts, latency, retry count, error type and estimated cost. It said a sensible default is to log metadata for every call and masked content for a small sample, maybe five percent, plus every failed call. It said metadata can be kept for a year and masked content for a couple of weeks, and that the request ID should go into the logging framework's MDC.

The article said one small component should be the chokepoint every AI log call passes through, and nothing else should write raw prompts. It gave regex rules for emails and bearer tokens, with patterns compiled once and a fixed order because a card number can otherwise get half eaten by the phone rule. It said replacement labels such as [EMAIL] keep the sentence readable for whoever debugs it later. It said regex will not catch a name like "Asha Raman" or an address buried mid-sentence.

The article said named-entity recognition can tag people, places and organisations and mask anything above a confidence threshold. It said exact replacement can swap values already known, such as the customer's name from the current session, and that masking at the field level while building the prompt is best of all. It said consistent pseudonyms turn each real value into a short token using a keyed hash, so the same email always becomes something like EMAIL_7f3a. It said an HMAC with a secret from a secrets manager should be used because a plain unkeyed hash of a phone number can be brute-forced in minutes.

The article said one JSON record per AI call should be written with clearly separate fields so dashboards for cost and latency never touch the text fields. It said streaming tokens arrive in tiny pieces and a card number can be split across two chunks, so the full response should be collected in a buffer, masked once the stream ends and logged. It said tool arguments and return values are often the most sensitive thing in the exchange, so the tool name, duration and outcome should be logged by default and arguments only after masking. It said masking lowers risk but never removes it, so content fields should get a short retention period, AI log readers should be limited, log storage and its pipeline should be encrypted, and the hashed user ID should be logged so one person's records can be found and deleted.

The article said a masker that quietly stops working is worse than having none because everyone assumes the logs are clean. It said a small set of messy, realistic samples should be built and run in the CI pipeline, with a new case added every time a leak turns up. It said a scheduled job that scans stored logs for patterns that should never appear makes a good safety net. It said mistakes to watch for include logging raw text at debug level, masking only the user's message while forgetting retrieved documents, system prompts and tool results, letting SDK exceptions carry the full request body into the logs, leaving wire-level HTTP logging on in production, and treating masking as finished once it ships.

Articles.Title: Logging AI Prompts and Responses in Java Without Leaking Sensitive Data

stories.Headline: Changes to Greek life, AI integration, potential city-wide changes, campus support systems and more
stories.Summary:
Washington State University is making several institution-wide changes meant to support students through college, and Greek life is among those subject to change. The Student Belonging and Success Initiative will continue to move forward despite a public protest on Greek row denouncing it. The initiative could delay rush week by a semester for first-year students and is expected to take effect some time next year. It aims to give students more time to explore campus life without the pressure of committing to anything. The initiative is still in development and subject to change, with many aspects modifiable in the future.

As of fall 2023, Greek life housing does not fulfill the first-year on-campus residence requirement. Stronger accountability and recognition standards will also be implemented for fraternities and sororities. Students can also expect changes to the advising system, AI integration, general education reform, bus system changes and the possibility of changes to first-year classes in the coming years. The General Education Reform Committee has been leading many of these revisions. Discussions have involved optional grading in general education courses not related to a student's major and restructuring or removal of U-core, global and late-start classes.

T. Chris Riley-Tillman, WSU provost and executive vice president, said the current welcome week model isn't working. He said the university is very open if chapters want to do it in October or hold events in the first six weeks before a heavier experience. He said Greek chapters are struggling fiscally, citing talk that 11 chapters are about ready to go out of business. He said the university should examine every single thing it is doing. He said next year will be the first year consistency applies to transferring between the six WSU campuses.

Jeremy Watson, Edward R. Murrow College of Communication's director of advising, said the earlier the university can find traction on late-start classes, the better it will be. Late-start classes currently exist in a smaller capacity and are specific to differing colleges on campus. An expansion could bring interchangeable courses, more course options and a stronger support system. How many late-start classes students can take a semester is still under review, and eight-week courses are also available. Seventy percent of WSU students change majors at least once.

WSU uses AI to improve recruitment and recognize when students may need help, and Google Gemini launched as a university-sanctioned resource alongside Microsoft Co-pilot. The Office of the Provost is reconstituting the AI Council. A partnership with The National Institute for Student Success found universities overcommunicate, causing students to overlook most communicative media. Southside Dining Hall's soon-to-be all-you-can-eat meal plan is meant to support food security. $17 million was enacted through the 2025-2027 operating budget for retention and compensation.

Retention has increased 1.1% this year while enrollment has gone down 3.7%, and enrollment across the six campuses has declined steadily since 2019. Riley-Tillman cited rising tuition, economic challenges, after effects of COVID-19, the disbanding of Pac-12 and less of the U.S. population participating in college. Nearly 82% of current WSU students are Washington residents, and changes to out-of-state residency awards are likely as restructuring continues. Fulmer Hall is being rebuilt, and revisions are happening across all six campuses. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Changes to Greek life, AI integration, potential city-wide changes, campus support systems and more

stories.Headline: Al Bentley finds GDS Holdings 59 percent undervalued on AI data center earnings power
stories.Summary:
Al Bentley published an analysis of GDS Holdings on November 14, 2026, to examine if the company is currently undervalued. The report focuses on the relationship between the current share price and the earnings power of the data center business. The company operates DayOne campuses, which are among the largest AI focused data centers in the world. A planned build program for these assets is estimated to cost between RMB 30 billion and 50 billion. The stock trades at a P/E ratio of 7.2x, while the IT sector average is 23.2x and peers average 25.8x.

Analysts from Simply Wall St provided a consensus narrative suggesting the stock is 59 percent undervalued. They stated that the current share price does not fully reflect multi year contracted capacity or the planned build program. The analysis notes that the market may not be fully pricing in earnings that the DayOne assets should support. Investors are affected by a valuation gap that makes the stock look like a laggard despite rising AI compute demand.

The share price of GDS Holdings has gained approximately 71.5 percent over the past three years. This recovery puts pressure on whether the earnings profile can sustain the current value of the company. Future value depends on revenue momentum, margin structure, and key risks that may emerge as new information becomes available. The report leaves open how two major warning signs might change the overall valuation picture.

Articles.Title: Is GDS Holdings (NasdaqGM:GDS) Undervalued Given Its AI Data Center Scale?

stories.headline_source: Is GDS Holdings (NasdaqGM:GDS) Undervalued Given Its AI Data Center Scale?

stories.Headline: ITU’s Jichen Zhu leads a five-year project to study ambiguity in LLM-supported learning and develop the Diffrakt chatbot
stories.Summary:
The IT University of Copenhagen announced on 9 November 2026 that it has received DKK 7.1 million from Independent Research Fund Denmark for a five-year educational AI project. The project is led by Jichen Zhu and is titled Friction by Ambiguity: Improving Engagement and Critical Thinking in LLM-Supported Learning. The research will investigate ambiguity in learning supported by large language models. A planned chatbot called Diffrakt is a research output to be developed.

Diffrakt will use guided questions and deliberately open responses in AI ethics teaching. The team will also research how to calibrate ambiguity to model uncertainty. Christian Hardmeier is co-principal investigator, and Pawel Grabarczyk contributes ethics expertise. Initial testing is planned with ITU students, alongside work with educators.

Zhu's institutional profile identifies Zhu as a professor in Human-Computer Interaction and Design and head of the Human-AI Interaction Lab. The lab's description connects interaction design and critical technical practice with research on how people interpret and live with AI. Independent Research Fund Denmark describes its remit as supporting researcher-initiated, high-risk research within and across disciplines, alongside thematic funding. The announcement does not establish that Diffrakt improves learning.

The article draws a distinction between a funded research question, a planned tool and evidence of educational benefit. It says 9 November marks ITU's announcement and should not be treated as the funder's grant decision date. An institutional assessment can track the proposed technology separately from evidence about students' reasoning and engagement. Funding and a chatbot development plan alone cannot establish that the educational approach works.

stories.Headline: Hong Kong veterinary professionals use AI tools despite a lack of formal training
stories.Summary:
A cross-sectional survey evaluated how veterinary professionals in Hong Kong adopt and perceive artificial intelligence between December 2023 and March 2024. The investigation gathered responses from undergraduate students, doctoral researchers, university faculty, and practicing clinical veterinarians to assess their digital engagement. Researchers published these findings in Frontiers in Veterinary Science to highlight widespread tool usage alongside acute deficits in formal training. The study revealed that seven out of ten respondents used these technologies, yet nearly half felt unfamiliar with fundamental frameworks. Participants across every surveyed tier registered pronounced concerns regarding professional accountability, diagnostic reliability, and systemic rigidity in algorithmic tools.

The research used a thirty-seven-item online questionnaire for Bachelor of Veterinary Medicine students, doctoral students, faculty, and Hong Kong Veterinary Association members. City University of Hong Kong houses the sole veterinary degree program in the territory, which anchors the region's veterinary education. Practicing veterinarians must hold qualifications from the Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons, the Australasian Veterinary Boards Council, or the American Veterinary Medical Association. The final dataset included seventy-nine submissions, with response rates of 26.7 percent for undergraduates, 23.5 percent for doctoral candidates, and 60.7 percent for faculty. Community clinicians had a response rate of at least 1.6 percent from a mailing list of approximately nine hundred and fifty-six registered individuals.

The authors stated that there is an urgent requirement for formalized curricular updates, regulatory frameworks, and context-specific model validation. They noted that academic institutions face growing pressure to embed computational literacy directly into professional syllabi because students show strong interest. The researchers also suggested that continuing education bodies must address the lack of readiness reported by licensed veterinarians through practical modules. They observed that their findings align with international trends of unguided informal uptake and persistent structural apprehension seen in other countries. The authors cautioned that their modest sample size and reliance on self-reporting necessitate a cautious interpretation of the statistical results.

Practicing veterinarians expressed the highest trepidation, with 66.7 percent describing themselves as unprepared for algorithmic integration into clinical care. Only 46.7 percent of these clinicians agreed that algorithmic tools would decrease diagnostic errors or improve overall clinical outcomes. In contrast, 83.5 percent of all respondents believed algorithmic systems could enhance veterinary instruction and clinical practice. Many participants identified practitioner accountability for algorithmic harm as a paramount concern, a sentiment shared by 79.7 percent of the cohort. Other affected stakeholders included 70.9 percent of participants who emphasized the peril of clinical inaccuracies and diagnostic errors.

The study found that 46.8 percent of participants were unfamiliar with artificial intelligence, while 29.1 percent rated their knowledge as very low. Only 17.7 percent of respondents reported receiving formal instruction, yet 78.5 percent expressed an explicit interest in future educational instruction. Approximately 69.6 percent of the population deployed applications for learning or research, with ChatGPT being the most cited tool at 67.9 percent. While 80.0 percent of practitioners had never read a research paper on the topic, 76.5 percent of faculty had. Most users applied these resources to language editing and literature reviews rather than specialized clinical tasks like automated diagnostic imaging.

Future efforts must focus on providing clinically focused continuing education to bridge the gap between exploratory use and safe integration. Institutions need to determine how to best incorporate computational systems into tertiary veterinary schooling to meet professional development needs. The articles leave open how specific regulatory frameworks will be designed to handle professional accountability for algorithmic harm in Hong Kong. It remains unclear how the territory will validate context-specific models to reduce the diagnostic errors feared by many practicing clinicians. The research suggests that while 81.0 percent are likely to use these tools, the path to clinical readiness is undefined.

stories.Headline: Predatory journals publish AI slop papers under academics names without consent
stories.Summary:
On November 13, 2026, investigations reported that a coordinated ring of predatory open-access journals had published low-quality, AI-generated “slop” papers falsely attributed to established academics without their knowledge, submission, or consent. The scheme was discovered when automated indexing alerts flagged bogus manuscripts to senior researchers at institutions including the University of Gothenburg, Stanford University, and the University of California, Berkeley. Alan Said, an associate professor of computer science at the University of Gothenburg, received an automated Google Scholar notification alerting him to a newly indexed paper bearing his name as author. The paper, titled “Intelligence Systems Supporting Sustainable Global Development,” appeared in the American International Journal of Research and Innovation (AIJRI). Said had never written, reviewed, or submitted the work.

Upon examining the text, Said found vacuous, computer-generated prose supported by irrelevant and hallucinated citations, describing the article as having no substantive content and reading “like slop.” Subsequent investigations uncovered dozens of similar papers falsely listing Stanford University professors Fei-Fei Li and Christopher Manning, as well as UC Berkeley faculty Michael I. Jordan and Stuart Russell. None of the listed scholars had any relationship with the publications or the publishing entities. Cross-journal investigations linked the fraudulent papers to a cluster of closely affiliated titles, including AIJRI, the American Journal of Advanced Multidisciplinary Research and Innovation (AJAMRI), and the American Journal For Multidisciplinary Research (AJFMR). All three domains were newly registered in 2026 while hosting fabricated back-archives with dates predating their registration.

The websites shared identical page layouts, graphic templates, a common United States WhatsApp contact number, and overlapping editorial boards featuring faculty primarily from Indian institutions without verifiable affiliations. Multiple titles listed a common editor-in-chief under the name Denish Brown. The network operates on an open-access author-fee model, charging article processing charges (APCs) of approximately $200 for international authors. This operational model mirrors patterns documented in analyses of paper-mill red flags and predatory indexing rings cataloged in Cabells Predatory Reports. When Said contacted the hosting provider and domain registrar to report the impersonation and demand removal, the journal did not retract or delete the paper.

Instead, the site operators merely swapped Said’s name with another author’s name, cycling through several different credited scholars over subsequent days across identical AI-generated text. The case underscores how predatory publishing networks exploit automated discovery infrastructure to bootstrap illicit credibility. Search engines and bibliographic scrapers ingest newly posted web pages rapidly, automatically attaching unvetted articles to researchers’ public bibliographies. Because indexing happens within hours while formal investigation and removal take weeks or months, deceptive journals gain a window of apparent legitimacy. The primary danger extends beyond reputational damage to senior researchers.

By presenting mastheads and author lists populated by renowned scientists, these operations create a deceptive facade of prestige designed to trap early-career researchers, graduate students, and authors under institutional publication mandates. Unsuspecting scholars who submit genuine manuscripts to these venues lose both their publication fees and their work to unindexed, unpreserved repositories that fail minimum standards of scholarly archiving. The emergence of AI-generated identity-theft publishing requires coordinated countermeasures from both individual researchers and institutional research offices. Scholars should review their ORCID record permissions, disabling open third-party write access and configuring trusted-organization controls so that unauthorized entities cannot automatically assert works or affiliations on their persistent records. Researchers should change their Google Scholar profile configuration from automatic article additions to manual review, auditing attributed papers regularly to remove mistakenly linked slop manuscripts.

University research offices, research integrity officers, and scholarly communication librarians should establish rapid-intake channels for faculty reporting unauthorized bylines. Institutions can apply standard COPE flowcharts to structure formal complaints and collaborate across international networks using NISO CREC communication practices. When predatory journals refuse retraction or cycle author names, institutional legal and library teams should issue formal copyright and impersonation complaints directly to domain registrars, hosting infrastructure providers, and indexers to remove fraudulent records at the root. The CASRAI article was published on 14 Nov 2026 and is licensed under CC-BY 4.0. Inside Higher Ed published “AI-Generated Slop Papers Published Under Prominent Academics’ Names” on 2026-11-13, checked 2026-11-14.

Times Higher Education published “Predatory journals publish AI slop under top academics’ names” on 2026-11-13, checked 2026-11-14. The CASRAI article states that everything CASRAI publishes stays free to read, with no account and no card. The article offers an AI assistant that cites the sources behind every answer, labels web answers and says when it can’t answer. Answers draw on CASRAI’s guides and dictionary plus the federal and funder documents CASRAI indexes: Federal Register, Grants.gov, Regulations.gov and UKRI. The assistant works on the CASRAI site and inside Claude, Cursor and the AI tools users already use.

stories.Headline: Teacher-reviewed AI feedback raises piano students performance scores in 16-week study
stories.Summary:
A 16-week quasi-experimental study by researchers Li Lin and Ping’an Zheng found that teacher-mediated artificial intelligence feedback in studio instruction was associated with greater performance score gains than conventional feedback alone. The study ran during the autumn semester of the 2025, 2026 academic year and followed 80 second- and third-year undergraduate piano students in two pre-existing instructional cohorts taught by the same instructor. Over a 12-week intervention period with six biweekly diagnostic cycles, students who received teacher-reviewed performance reports and targeted practice tasks showed a model-based growth advantage of 6.57 points over peers taught with traditional listening-based feedback and demonstrations. The contrast remained evident at a four-week follow-up assessment even after structured task assignments ceased. The findings were published in Discover Artificial Intelligence, volume 6, issue 1, Article 1733.

The evaluation framework relied on ScoreFeedback-Piano v1.2, an assessment pipeline incorporating a locally adapted MT3 encoder, decoder Transformer network for automatic note transcription. The system ran on Python 3.10, PyTorch 2.1, and torchaudio 2.1, sampled audio at 32 kHz, and generated 229-band log-Mel spectrograms with a 10-millisecond hop size. The MT3 checkpoint had been fine-tuned on the GiantMIDI-Piano dataset, with developmental training informed by MAESTRO v3.0.0 and HUPS-Piano-2021 collections, and the frozen checkpoint was fixed in June 2023. The pipeline aligned performed notes to reference events with cost weights of 1.0 per semitone for pitch, 0.5 per second for onset timing, and 0.5 per second for duration, within a local timing slack of plus or minus 15 percent and a 150-millisecond onset matching window. Four skill dimensions were scored on a 0 to 100 scale and weighted 30 percent for technical accuracy, 25 percent each for rhythmic stability and expressive control, and 20 percent for completeness.

The authors, Lin and Zheng, designed the framework on human-centered learning analytics and formative assessment theory, in which diagnostic reports serve as advisory tools for the instructor. They stated that teachers evaluate flagged acoustic passages alongside scores and recordings, translate acoustic deviations into passage-specific practice drills, and verify pedagogical progress in subsequent studio lessons. They noted that automated assessment can identify deviations from a musical score while teachers interpret their musical significance and choose an appropriate response. They warned that accepting automatic recommendations uncritically weakens independent judgment. They concluded that automated acoustic diagnostics offer the greatest educational utility when human teachers actively contextualize algorithmic findings into structured artistic goals.

Three independent external experts with at least 10 years of university piano teaching experience performed blind evaluations at baseline, posttest, and follow-up, achieving absolute-agreement intraclass correlation coefficients of 0.974 at baseline, 0.978 at week 12, and 0.979 at week 16. Across 240 paired evaluation records, the automated platform composite scores achieved a Pearson correlation of 0.972 and an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.971, with a mean absolute error of 1.620 points and Bland, Altman limits from minus 3.976 to positive 4.067 points. Dimension-level scrutiny revealed a positive bias of 1.032 points for technical accuracy but a negative bias of 0.975 points for expressive control. The sample comprised 80 music majors aged 19 to 21 years, 50 female and 30 male, at repertoire difficulty Levels 4 through 6, with the 40 experimental students averaging 5.55 years of prior piano training and the 40 control students 5.71 years. Both groups completed weekly 45-minute individual lessons with the same instructor, totaling 9 hours during the 12-week intervention and 12 hours across the full 16-week study.

At the week 12 posttest, the experimental group achieved a model-based growth difference of 6.5667 points over the control group (95% CI [5.1926, 7.9408], p < 0.001). Observed blinded composite averages rose from 70.0650 to 80.5000 points in the experimental group, compared with 70.4667 to 74.3350 points in the control group, an unadjusted change effect size of Hedges g = 2.1297. Experimental students gained an additional 6.8475 points in technical accuracy, 6.7075 points in rhythmic stability, 5.1100 points in expressive control, and 5.7275 points in completeness, with all contrasts significant after Benjamini, Hochberg corrections. During the maintenance phase from week 13 to week 16, biweekly AI task assignments ceased while weekly private lessons continued and platform access remained available to experimental students. At week 16, blinded expert ratings registered composite scores of 79.2925 in the experimental group and 74.6425 in the control group, a sustained model-based growth difference of 5.0517 points (95% CI [3.6776, 6.4258], p < 0.001).

Practice logs between weeks 1 and 12 showed experimental students completed an average of 219.859 practice minutes per week compared to 192.205 minutes in the control group, an added 27.654 minutes weekly alongside 0.629 additional practice sessions per week. Exploratory parallel mediation modeling showed that bootstrap confidence intervals for practice minutes, error correction, and teacher-estimated feedback uptake all included zero, so these estimates do not establish the mechanisms underlying improvement. The authors emphasized that because the investigation relied on two intact institutional teaching groups assigned to a single instructor without randomized allocation, teaching group dynamics and instructional conditions remain statistically inseparable. They noted that expert evaluations assessed students within one specific institutional cohort performing intermediate repertoire, and that the week 16 assessment reflected continuous platform access rather than complete tool withdrawal. Robust sensitivity checks confirmed that varying composite dimension weights between 0.20 and 0.40 preserved the statistical direction and magnitude of the intervention effects.

stories.Headline: Federal Reserve reports advanced computing debt tops $680 billion and flags circular financing risks
stories.Summary:
On November 13, 2026, the Federal Reserve Board published its November 2026 Financial Stability Report, which says asset valuation pressures remain elevated. The report says equity valuations are partly driven by market enthusiasm for what it calls "super intelligence" (SI). It details rapid growth in debt issued to finance advanced computing infrastructure. The report generally reflects information available as of October 28, 2026. The report is a financial-stability assessment and makes no statement about research funding, universities or grants.

The report states that asset valuation pressures "continued to be elevated" and that measures of equity valuations "have remained high." It adds that the ratio of equity prices to earnings for S&P 500 companies stayed well above its historical median. Section 1 says broad equity valuation metrics were partly driven by that enthusiasm, "though moderated by concerns over firms' capital expenditures and debt issuance plans." A boxed analysis, "Leverage in the Data Center Buildout," reports that debt issuance to finance advanced computing infrastructure has grown rapidly over the past year. The report says the debt is shifting from mostly corporate bonds to a mix of public and private debt, structured credit and project finance.

Advanced computing-related debt issuance rose to more than $680 billion by October 2026, about a fivefold increase from $130 billion in all of 2023. Such borrowing rose from less than 6 percent of nonfinancial investment-grade corporate debt issuance in 2023 to about 31 percent in 2026. Outstanding public debt related to advanced computing is estimated at more than $1.1 trillion as of October 2026. The report notes that private credit transactions make the full magnitude harder to measure. Not-yet-commenced leases have undiscounted values above $1 trillion, and take-or-pay contracts and residual value guarantees above $2 trillion.

The largest U.S. bank holding companies have close to $1 trillion of exposure to large technology firms, data center developers, advanced computing-related special purpose entities and private credit vehicles, and utility companies. The report says these exposures are evaluated in the annual supervisory stress test. The report describes a "circular financing" dynamic in which hyperscalers and GPU makers supplement debt financings with equity investments in smaller firms. It says the complex links among data center firms, public credit markets, private lenders and special purpose vehicles "create vulnerabilities that necessitate close monitoring." Box 5.1 summarizes a survey run by Federal Reserve Bank of New York staff, with responses from 23 contacts at broker-dealers, banks, investment funds and advisory firms in September and October.

The report notes the box does not represent the views of the Board or the New York Fed. AI was the top-cited risk. Respondents named three areas of concern: elevated equity valuations and the possibility of a market correction if earnings disappoint; cybersecurity risk, from sophisticated attackers or from damage caused by frontier AI models themselves; and complex forms of AI-related financing. Mentions of AI, higher long-term rates and cyberattacks rose the most relative to the spring survey. In Section 5, the report says private fixed investment tied to new computing technologies has been a significant driver of U.S. economic growth this year.

It says an unexpected downturn in corporate earnings could prompt lower asset valuations, tighter credit conditions and reduced capital expenditure. Research offices that depend on technology-sector gifts, sponsored agreements or endowment returns may find the report useful as background on how regulators characterize AI-sector exposure, alongside their own institutional risk processes. The report was released November 13, 2026, by the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. The article was published 14 Nov 2026 by the CASRAI Editorial Board. More to follow.

stories.Headline: OpenAI promotes its Codex tool at TwitchCon as attendees criticize the booth
stories.Summary:
OpenAI promoted its Codex coding tool through a hackathon at TwitchCon in San Diego on November 15, 2026. This annual convention brings together industry experts, Twitch personalities, and fans to discuss the future of streaming. Some attendees reacted negatively to the presence of the company that created ChatGPT on the expo floor. These critics described the activation as stupid, bland, boring, and tone deaf during the event. One user shared a community forum link on X to call for ending partnerships with AI companies.

The event took place in San Diego where OpenAI set up a booth to promote its Codex tool. Twitch previously introduced an option for streamers to opt out of content training for AI models owned by Amazon. This feature was criticized because users had to manually opt out rather than opting in to the process. Some streamers believe AI tools like clipping, auto-captioning, and speech-to-text could be helpful for accessibility and moderation. However, they remain concerned that these technologies might eventually be used to generate content and replace human creativity.

Twitch CEO Dan Clancy told NBC News that being automatically opted in does not mean data was already scraped. He stated the toggle is a preventive measure in case Amazon plans to train its AI on Twitch content. Clancy said he is not involved in what Amazon is doing but wanted creators to express their wishes. Chief Product Officer Mike Minton said offering the option drove a conversation where much of the nuance was lost. Minton declined to comment on past events because streamers have filed lawsuits regarding the controversy.

Attendee Chloe Van Ryn, 31, from Arizona, said she would not be comfortable with her content feeding AI models. She compared the scraping of streamer content to AI companies scanning and destroying books. A user named Rummeko stated that making content scraping widespread for all is a disrespectful way to operate. Rummeko suggested that creators who are desperate to cling to AI should find other people who use it. These streamers feel that the current opt-out system requires them to go several layers deep to turn it off.

Twitch stoked outrage a few months ago by introducing the opt-out toggle for its parent company, Amazon. AI was largely absent from the official programming of the San Diego convention despite the OpenAI booth. The technology remains a divisive issue for streamers who worry about their jobs and the future of creativity. Some users argue they never consented to have their content scraped by AI companies in the first place. The company claims most other services do not give users any option to opt out of AI training.

It remains unclear if Amazon has already used Twitch content to train its various AI models. Amazon did not immediately respond to a request for comment regarding these specific training practices. Mike Minton cited ongoing litigation as the reason he could not discuss what happened in the past. The articles do not state if Twitch will change the opt-out feature to an opt-in system. No further information is provided regarding the outcome of the lawsuits filed by the affected streamers.

stories.Headline: NAACP and Sanofi report warns AI could widen health gaps for Black communities
stories.Summary:
The NAACP and the pharmaceutical company Sanofi released a report during the AfroTech Conference 2026 in Houston, according to The Legacy Newspaper. The report is titled “AI Fluency is a Challenge on Both Sides of the Exam Room.” It is the third installment of the groups’ ACE Your Health StoryMap series, which looks at how AI, internet access, and healthcare inequities shape health in Black America. The findings draw on national datasets and input from nearly 23,000 community members across 47 states, the District of Columbia, and Puerto Rico.

The report warns that new technology does not erase old gaps on its own. It says one in three Americans lives in a healthcare desert, and in the Mississippi Delta all 154,000 Black residents live more than 25 miles from a hospital rated four or five stars. About 3.8 million Black Americans live in homes without a broadband subscription, which limits access to digital health tools. Nineteen percent of people who use AI for health information say they did so because they could not afford to see a provider, and Black adults are significantly more likely than White adults to use AI for mental health advice.

Dr. Chris T. Pernell, Director of the NAACP Center for Health Equity, said too many Black communities face healthcare deserts, provider shortages, clinic closures, inadequate internet access, and concerns about racial bias. She said that if these gaps remain unaddressed, AI could widen existing disparities instead of helping close them. She said equity and fairness must be designed into healthcare AI from the beginning, not added as patchwork fixes. Tanisha M. Sullivan, Head of External Engagement & Health Equity Strategy at Sanofi, said innovation must be matched by efforts to expand access, build trust, and address barriers. She said pharmaceutical companies should partner with community organizations, healthcare providers, and policymakers so innovations reach the people who need them most.

The report says nearly two-thirds of Black adults believe racial bias remains a major problem in healthcare, and one-third expect AI to make that bias worse. It lays out steps communities can take, including expanding broadband adoption, building AI fluency and digital skills, strengthening community-based health education, and advocating for equitable technology policies. It also invites community members to add their voices to the StoryMap. The full report and other ACE Your Health resources are available at naacp.org.

stories.Headline: Adaptive AI System Models Student Learning Pathways Using Educational Proxy Data
stories.Summary:
Educational researchers Feibao Bao and Xiuliang Zhang introduced an adaptive intelligence framework called the Hybrid Transformer-Graph Reinforcement Adaptive Competency Engine, or HT-GRACE, on November 14, 2026. The framework is designed to model college students' educational outcomes and simulate personalized learning strategies. The research team developed a computational model that integrates structural relational modeling, sequential temporal tracking, and policy optimization. The model evaluates student engagement and simulates supportive interventions in higher education contexts. The framework operates on benchmark data from the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset, known as OULAD.

OULAD comprises records from 32,593 online students and does not include direct assessments, empirical records, or validated competency labels for real-world innovation or entrepreneurship skills. The researchers treated these unobserved attributes as latent educational constructs inferred from observable behavioral signals, including engagement intensity, assessment performance, learning consistency, and online interaction frequency. The architecture maps structural relationships using a competency-aware heterogeneous graph with 32,635 nodes and 148,420 edges, connecting students, 22 competency concepts, and 20 activity types. The system applies an exponential decay formulation for recency-based weighting and an uncertainty-aware fusion layer that computes dynamic attention weights across data modalities. HT-GRACE achieved an overall classification accuracy of 94.8 percent, an F1-score of 94.86 percent, an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 94.95 percent, and a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.915.

The authors state that the resulting capability metrics represent model-defined educational proxies rather than direct, real-world measures of entrepreneurial ability. They emphasize that predicted scores and simulated policy actions cannot be interpreted as verified enhancements in human creativity, problem-solving, or entrepreneurship. They note that prospective recommendations generated by algorithmic policies have not undergone real-world trial deployment, where automated advising could introduce self-fulfilling feedback loops. They conclude that validation in operational university classrooms and prospective field trials remains necessary to ascertain whether simulated policy gains translate into meaningful educational improvements. The authors explain that OULAD contains no records of institutional intervention programs or subsequent outcomes, so outputs represent simulated policy recommendations rather than observed clinical or institutional interventions.

In comparative benchmarking against baseline models including Study-GNN and Transformer-based sequential predictors, the framework demonstrated consistent improvements in discriminative performance, with an error variance of 0.00007 and a normalized stability score of 0.91 in continuous regression evaluations. In reinforcement learning simulations, the agent attained a cumulative reward gain of 27.6 percent over baseline methods and demonstrated stable convergence across successive training iterations. Ablation experiments showed that removing the Graph Neural Network reduced classification accuracy to 90.7 percent, removing the Transformer temporal encoder dropped accuracy to 91.5 percent, and replacing the PPO module with a conventional policy mechanism decreased accuracy to 89.9 percent. Removing both the graph and transformer modules resulted in the lowest recorded accuracy of 87.6 percent. Learner outcomes were divided into three categories prior to training: low-outcome learners covering scores from 0.00 to 0.49, medium-outcome learners spanning 0.50 to 0.74, and high-outcome learners encompassing scores from 0.75 to 1.00, with medium-outcome learners registering an F1-score of 94.22.

The development of HT-GRACE was informed by architectural limitations identified across earlier intelligent education systems. Prior sequential models such as the Transformer-based Sequential Educational Prediction approach developed by Kusumawardani and colleagues modeled long-term behavioral dependencies but omitted structural relationships among students and competencies. Graph-focused frameworks like the Study-GNN architecture introduced by Li and collaborators and the relational network designed by Hakkal and co-authors modeled complex educational interactions yet lacked mechanisms for temporal tracking and reinforcement optimization. Adaptive systems proposed by Amin and collaborators or Yi and team incorporated reinforcement learning techniques such as Proximal Policy Optimization but either encountered reward sparsity constraints or omitted multi-head attention mechanisms required for extended behavioral trajectories. The authors describe a persistent gap in unified multi-modal modeling that their framework aims to address.

The experimental implementation was constructed in Python 3.10 and PyTorch 2.x, executed on hardware comprising an Intel Core i9 processor, 32 gigabytes of system memory, and an NVIDIA RTX 3090 graphics card with 24 gigabytes of video memory. The Open University dataset contains more than 10 million virtual learning interaction logs alongside tables for student demographics, assessment scores, and course registrations, with interaction attributes including student identifiers, module codes, interaction dates, and click sums. Records were partitioned into 70 percent for training, 15 percent for validation, and 15 percent for testing, utilizing the Adam optimizer across identical configurations. Supervised predictive comparisons benchmarked HT-GRACE against specialized baseline architectures including T-SEP, GNN-PP, the Graph-Enhanced LSTM model, and Study-GNN. The Consistency Index tracked the stability of student representations by averaging cosine similarities between adjacent hidden state vectors across successive time steps, while a Participation Diversity Score applied an entropy calculation across distinct activity categories.

Evaluation of computational overhead indicated that HT-GRACE maintained manageable training durations, low inference latencies, and reduced floating-point operations relative to comparative baselines under identical laboratory hardware conditions. Cross-domain transfer tests evaluating concept drift across differing course module presentations showed consistent adaptation recovery metrics, suggesting the unified embeddings remain resilient when exposed to shifted interaction distributions. The authors emphasize several core methodological boundaries and scope limitations governing the interpretation of these findings. Validation in operational university classrooms and prospective field trials remains necessary, and the articles do not report any such deployment or trial results. The articles also leave open whether simulated policy gains would translate into meaningful educational improvements in real settings.

stories.Headline: Ceribell launches AI delirium monitoring platform as shares rise 102.6 percent in a year
stories.Summary:
The medical technology company Ceribell launched an artificial intelligence platform for monitoring delirium around November 14, 2026. This new product has seen rapid adoption by hospitals and has contributed to significant revenue growth for the business. Consequently, the share price for the company has increased by 102.6 percent over the previous twelve months. The stock is currently trading near its recent highs following this powerful one year performance.

The current market value requires a price to sales ratio of 9.3x to support the recent stock surge. This figure is considerably higher than the medical equipment sector average of 2.6x and the peer group level of 5.6x. The company also plans to release a new hardware platform called Omni to further justify its revenue multiple. These metrics suggest the shares are overvalued when measured against the Fair Ratio benchmark for growth and risk.

Analysts from Simply Wall St provided a consensus narrative suggesting the stock is actually 12 percent undervalued. They stated that creating additional algorithms for stroke and delirium transforms the platform into a multi indication neuromonitoring system. This perspective relies on the growing installed base of the technology to drive future value. The analysts believe the current commercial momentum can lead to durable expansion of the top line.

The market is currently paying a premium because of optimism regarding the execution of future sales. There is little room for disappointment if the pricing power or hospital adoption fails to meet these high expectations. Investors are focusing on the revenue potential of the AI platform rather than on immediate profits. Future valuation will depend on whether the company can maintain its current trajectory of growth.

stories.Headline: AI CT analysis links myosteatosis to cardiometabolic risk in breast cancer
stories.Summary:
Researchers from Johns Hopkins University published a retrospective cohort study in Breast Cancer Research and Treatment showing that fully automated deep learning algorithms can quantify cardiometabolic biomarkers from routine abdominal CT scans in patients with high-risk invasive breast cancer. The study included 127 female patients diagnosed between 2016 and 2018. The work was reported on November 14, 2026, in an article by Nathaniel Bowman in Scienmag. The article appeared on bioengineer.org under the headline linking AI CT analysis of myosteatosis to cardiometabolic risk in breast cancer. The study's subject was deep learning analysis of CT scans for cardiometabolic biomarkers in breast cancer.

The study was a retrospective cohort of patients with Stage I to IV breast cancer who newly presented to the Johns Hopkins Health System and had an abdominal CT scan within six months of diagnosis. Of the 127 female patients, 64.6 percent were postmenopausal, 57.5 percent were White and 26.8 percent were Black. The team excluded patients with insufficient medical records, missing BMI data or incomplete CT image data. Myosteatosis was defined quantitatively as a mean muscle density of 18.9 Hounsfield units or lower for females, a threshold previously established in the literature. The article was published in Breast Cancer Research and Treatment, volume 220, issue 1, Article 38, with DOI 10.1007/s10549-026-08122-0.

The authors were Tsou, Yang, Wang, Qi, Blackford, Visvanathan, Summers and Sheng, and the authors noted several limitations. They said the observational design demonstrates important associations but does not independently indicate causation. They said the cohort was from a single institution and had few patients of Asian race or Hispanic ethnicity, which may limit generalizability to populations with different patterns of body adiposity. They said the sample size was small and did not provide sufficient power to study survival outcomes, leading them to analyze the Agatston plaque score dichotomously. They said the findings may only apply to patients with high-risk, invasive breast cancer who require CT scans as part of their routine care.

The results indicated that BMI was positively correlated with CT-derived adipose tissue area and muscle area and negatively correlated with liver intensity. Muscle intensity was significantly lower for patients in the overweight and obesity BMI groups than for those in the healthy weight group. The Agatston plaque score, measured as zero versus nonzero, did not significantly differ by BMI group. Postmenopausal women had significantly higher visceral fat area than premenopausal women, with a mean of 115.0 square centimeters versus 81.4 square centimeters. Of postmenopausal patients, 61.0 percent presented with aortic plaque compared to 15.6 percent of premenopausal patients, and 60.8 percent of patients with myosteatosis had a plaque score greater than zero compared to 34.2 percent of those without myosteatosis.

The research team aimed to address the limitations of body mass index in stratifying metabolic disease risk among cancer patients. The article states that BMI is the most accessible and commonly used surrogate for body adiposity, but previous scrutiny has highlighted its insensitivity to actual body fat distribution and its poor prediction of metabolic risk in certain demographics. Cardiometabolic diseases, including obesity and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, are significant factors influencing breast cancer recurrence and survival. Obesity is associated with an increased risk of breast cancer recurrence and overall mortality, while excess body weight elevates the risk of cardiovascular disease, the second leading cause of death among breast cancer survivors. The deep learning algorithms performed quantification and segmentation of muscle and adipose tissues, liver fat and abdominal aortic calcification.

The findings suggest that CT-derived myosteatosis is a promising metric for assessing cardiometabolic risk in breast cancer patients. The article states that breast cancer treatments may increase the risk of developing diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, ischemic heart disease and stroke, so monitoring these biomarkers is essential. The authors suggest that integrating these CT-derived biomarkers into routine clinical practice could help medical oncologists better monitor breast cancer survivors' cardiometabolic risk after diagnosis. The article states this approach aims to minimize cardiovascular morbidity and mortality and the progression of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease. The article leaves open how the single-institution, small-sample findings would generalize, and it states the observational design does not independently indicate causation.

Articles.Title: AI CT analysis links myosteatosis to cardiometabolic risk in breast cancer

stories.Headline: Google adds face blurring to Android XR glasses to stop secret filming
stories.Summary:
Google introduced privacy features for Android XR smart glasses on November 14, 2026, to prevent the secret filming of other people. Samsung developed these glasses in collaboration with Gentle Monster and Warby Parker to address long standing concerns about wearable camera technology. The system automatically blurs human faces, including the wearer's own reflection, before sending any visual data to Google data centers. Users must agree not to record in sensitive places or record others without permission before they can use the eyewear. These glasses also feature a privacy LED indicator that prevents the camera from working if the light is covered.

The Samsung Intelligent Eyewear starts at 395 dollars and will ship to South Korea and the United States on December 10, 2026. These glasses include a 12MP ultrawide camera, a microphone, built in speakers, and a battery that lasts for nine hours. All Android XR glasses will blur faces during Gemini queries, and this visual data will not be used for ad personalization. Gemini will not save images or videos in its history logs, and third party apps cannot use the camera for livestreaming. Play Store apps for these glasses are also prohibited from using the camera for any form of facial recognition.

Shahram Izadi, the Android XR Vice President and General Manager, shared these details in a post on the official Google blog. He stated that technology that can see the world has a responsibility to the people who are around the wearer. Izadi explained that Google listened to bystanders, wearers, and privacy experts during their years of research on smart glasses. He noted that bystanders expressed concerns about being filmed without their knowledge while wearers calculated their use out and about. The company designed these thoughtful features to provide peace of mind for both the users and the general public.

Some people may find the restrictions a bummer because they cannot use the glasses as an action camera for wildlife. The articles mention that bystanders may still be skeptical and will need to be told that their faces are blurred. Privacy experts and the general public are affected by the potential for these devices to be used for sinister things. A Harvard student previously tinkered with Meta Ray-Ban glasses to turn them into a full facial recognition device. There are also reports of government agencies asking Meta for special facial recognition models to be used by security agencies.

The original Google Glass failed partly because of privacy concerns regarding the secret filming and photographing of other people. Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses have also been involved in controversies, including claims that workers in Kenya saw intimate moments. Whistleblowers who exposed these Meta issues were fired, and some Ray-Bans were used for AI powered doxing of strangers. These previous failures informed the strict privacy framework Google is now implementing for the Android XR ecosystem and its partners. The new system aims to avoid the mistakes made by earlier wearable devices and their respective manufacturers.

Customers can currently pre-order the Samsung Intelligent Eyewear to receive the device when shipping begins in December of 2026. The articles leave open whether the blurring system is truly bulletproof or if some faces could slip through unblurred. It remains unclear if users will find ways to bypass the privacy wall to record people without their consent. The text does not state if other companies will adopt similar blurring standards for their own XR hardware. Future reports may reveal if government agencies attempt to bypass these filters for security or surveillance purposes.

Articles.Title: Google's AI glasses will have one surprising thing they're not allowed to see

stories.Headline: Edelman and LinkedIn report that 82% of B2B buyers value thought leadership more as AI spreads
stories.Summary:
Edelman and LinkedIn published the 2026 B2B Thought Leadership Impact Report in November 2026, a 35-page survey of 1,135 business executives in seven countries. The survey was fielded from September 4 to September 21, 2026, through online questionnaires and computer-assisted telephone interviews. It covered the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Germany, India, Australia and Singapore, with interviews in English except in Germany, where they were in German. The report is the eighth annual collaboration between the communications firm and the Microsoft-owned professional network. A commentary by Edelman's Annie Dunleavy introducing it is dated November 9.

The report defines thought leadership as content offering expertise, guidance or a unique point of view, made available free or in exchange for contact details. It excludes content primarily describing an organization's products or services and anything buyers pay for, such as client deliverables or subscription research. Managers made up 37% of respondents, directors 29%, vice presidents 7% and C-level executives 25%, with owners, founders and partners at 2%. Company size split 35% at 1 to 200 employees, 33% at 201 to 1,000 and 32% above 1,000. Most charts use a base of 1,063 B2B decision-makers, with final decision-makers at 317, C-suite executives at 310 and thought leadership suppliers at 495.

Edelman sells content strategy and business marketing services, and the commentary was written by its head of content strategy in the United States. LinkedIn sells advertising placements in its feed, including formats that promote posts by individual executives, and its B2B Institute promotes a framework it calls Buyability. Seven Edelman staff and three LinkedIn staff are credited as authors. The report names LinkedIn in one of its own questions as the example of a professional social media feed. The series has run since a combined 2017-2018 edition, with editions listed for 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2024 and 2025 and no 2023 report.

Ginny Cartwright Ziegler, chief marketing officer of Pearson, is quoted saying thought leadership is most powerful when it helps people see what's possible and gives them confidence to act. Victoria Whitney, vice president of corporate communications and external affairs at Ecolab, is quoted saying that in an AI-driven world information is everywhere and credible insight grounded in real expertise carries greater weight. Social Media Today, reporting on the study on November 11, said through Andrew Hutchinson that AI cannot provide real, hands-on experience and insights and cannot summarize information that does not already exist. The report cites a 6sense study, the 2025 B2B Buyer Experience Report, for the statistic that 95% of contracts are won by companies already on a buyer's Day One List.

The report says 48% of final decision-makers and 46% of C-suite executives spend four or more hours each week reading or viewing thought leadership. Some 89% of decision-makers agreed high-quality thought leadership makes a company feel like a more viable long-term partner, and 78% said it had changed their view of a company from a vendor to a potential strategic partner. Some 48% said a vendor's thought leadership influenced a lot or a great deal whether that vendor made the initial consideration list. Asked which attribute most increases trust, 56% chose content demonstrating a clear understanding of challenges, priorities and constraints, 14% chose content showing product strength and 11% chose market leadership. A November 4 post covered by PPC Land cited B2B Institute buyer data in which a recommendation from similar companies was chosen by 58% against 39% for being the market leader.

Some 76% of decision-makers said thought leadership shared within the group helped assess whether a vendor understood the organization's needs, and 52% said it helped decide which vendor to select. Final decision-makers were asked whether poor or absent thought leadership contributed to a vendor being removed from consideration, and 59% said yes, around 187 people on a base of 317 by PPC Land's calculation. During vendor evaluation, 84% of decision-makers used an AI assistant or AI-powered search tool to summarize thought leadership, 72% to learn about a market or solution category and 67% to compare vendors or approaches. When an AI tool cited a company's thought leadership, 78% then researched the company, 70% read or viewed the cited content and 52% used the information in an internal discussion or business case. Some 82% said thought leadership is becoming somewhat or much more valuable as AI becomes a more common way to get answers, ideas and advice about business challenges.

Asked about its most important roles, 57% said providing original research, data or perspectives not found elsewhere and 51% said adding context, nuance and human judgment AI answers may lack. Among the 495 suppliers, 84% said distributing through professional social feeds such as LinkedIn was incorporated a lot or a great deal, 74% said the same of traditional search engines and only 46% said they optimize so content can be surfaced in AI-generated answers. Semrush's March analysis of 89,000 URLs found LinkedIn ranked second among domains cited in AI answers, and in June LinkedIn published guidance that posts of roughly 200 to 300 words earn the most AI search citations. The May launch framework cited a 6sense finding that 94% of buying groups consult large language models during research, and Demandbase reported in August that ChatGPT referrals to B2B websites grew 303% in a year. The report does not publish results by country, does not say whether averages are weighted by market and gives no margin of error.

Articles.Title: 82% of B2B buyers value thought leadership more as AI spreads, Edelman finds

stories.Headline: Malaysian police investigate US claims that Malaysia is a transit hub for diverted Nvidia AI chips
stories.Summary:
The Royal Malaysia Police began an investigation in April 2025 regarding allegations from the United States. These claims suggest that Malaysia serves as a transit point for illicitly diverted advanced AI chips. Home Minister Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail confirmed the probe during a press conference in Sitiawan. The investigation focuses on whether proxy companies are being used for illicit procurement of Nvidia chips. These specific chips are essential for much of the artificial intelligence development happening across the world.

The probe is conducted under the Strategic Trade Act 2010 and involves several different regulatory agencies. These include Bank Negara Malaysia, the Inland Revenue Board, the Customs Department, and the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission. The Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry, known as Miti, serves as the lead agency for this case. Since July 2025, anyone transshipping or exporting high-performance US AI chips must obtain a permit from Miti. This requirement applies to those exporting, re-exporting, or transiting these specific chips through the country.

Home Minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail stated that the police began investigating immediately after the US allegations surfaced. He explained that gathering evidence on illicit procurement involves layered inquiries that are highly complex in nature. The minister noted that any findings from the police probe are relayed directly to the Miti agency. Because the US raised the complaint through Miti, that ministry is responsible for passing feedback to them. He confirmed that updates on the progress of the investigation have been conveyed to the lead agency.

Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim stated there was no indication that Nvidia-Megaspeed chips were exported from Malaysia. He added that Malaysia had received no formal requests regarding this matter from the US or Singapore. Miti clarified that it never cleared the Singapore-based Megaspeed International Pte Ltd or its affiliate, Speedmatrix Sdn Bhd. The Prime Minister affirmed that Malaysia would cooperate with all agencies involved in the ongoing chip investigation. These statements address the concerns of the US government regarding the diversion of advanced technology.

The articles state that no permit is currently needed to bring AI chips into the country of Malaysia. However, the US government alleges that Malaysia is being used as a transit hub for diverted chips. This situation involves the potential use of proxy companies to bypass trade restrictions on advanced AI hardware. Miti is currently working with the Customs Department to see if any chips had been re-exported. The investigation is a response to specific complaints raised by the United States through official channels.

The police have not yet stated whether they have found evidence that supports the original US allegations. Miti continues to monitor the movement of high-performance chips under the rules of the Strategic Trade Act. The articles leave open whether any specific proxy companies in Malaysia will be charged with illicit procurement. It remains unclear if the US or Singapore will issue formal requests for information in the future. The final results of the layered inquiries by the Royal Malaysia Police have not been released.

Articles.Title: A secret transit hub for Nvidia AI chips? Minister says Malaysian police on the case since April

stories.Headline: Bespoke Investment Group calls The Economist AI crash cover a possible contrarian signal for the AI trade
stories.Summary:
Bespoke Investment Group wrote on November 14, 2026, that The Economist had published a cover story in that week's issue titled "Why you should expect an AI crash," which the firm presented as the second part of a possible contrarian pair. The same magazine had published a cover story in the first week of September praising Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang as "The Sorcerer of Silicon," and Bespoke noted that this earlier cover did not mark the exact top for Nvidia shares. Bespoke's summary said contrarians watch major media outlets not because those outlets are ahead of the curve but usually because they are the opposite. The firm's quick insights said the AI crash warning could prove a contrarian sentiment indicator for the AI trade, though it remains to be seen whether it marks a sentiment low.

Bespoke's reasoning is that by the time something becomes major news and appears on a weekly magazine cover, it may already be reflected in prices, with the market looking ahead to the next development. The article listed a long set of tickers tied to the AI and robotics trade, including NVDA, WTAI, THNQ, LRNZ, AIQ, UBOT, ARTY, ROBT, ROBO, BOTZ, ARKQ, KOMP, ARKK, DTEC, IGPT, AIBU and ALAI. It described magazine covers as possible signals of turning points while saying the indicator is not a hard and fast rule. The piece carried a publication timestamp of November 14, 2026, at 12:30 AM ET and appeared on Seeking Alpha under the Bespoke Investment Group byline.

Bespoke Investment Group provides original content and intuitive thinking on the Street, according to the article's author description, and was founded by Paul Hickey and Justin Walters, formerly of Birinyi Associates and creators of the TickerSense blog. The description said Bespoke offers products that let institutions and modest investors gain the data and knowledge needed to make intelligent and profitable investment decisions. It said the firm runs the Think B.I.G. finance blog, provides timely investment ideas through its Bespoke Premium subscription service, and manages money for high net worth individuals. The article did not quote The Economist directly beyond the cover titles and did not give the contents of the crash story.

The context the article supplies is the contrarian habit of watching major media, with the September Nvidia cover as the first leg of what Bespoke called a potential contrarian two-fer and the AI crash cover as the second. Bespoke's quick insights asked how investors should interpret The Economist's AI crash cover and answered that the warning could prove a contrarian sentiment indicator for the AI trade. The article did not say what happens next beyond noting that it remains to be seen whether the cover marks a sentiment low. It gave no date for a coming crash and no figures beyond the tickers and the two cover dates.

stories.Headline: Ashish Manne presents Nucleus cancer AI platform at Berlin oncology congress
stories.Summary:
Ashish Manne, an associate professor at Ohio State University Comprehensive Cancer Center-James Cancer Hospital and Solove Research Institute, said on LinkedIn that he was traveling to Berlin, Germany, to present Nucleus, a clinician-facing AI-powered platform, at the ESMO AI and Digital Oncology Congress 2026. He said that a couple of years earlier, as AI began gaining momentum in healthcare, he and colleagues started thinking about how to translate its potential into meaningful improvements in everyday clinical practice. He noted that while AI holds tremendous promise, integrating it seamlessly into clinical workflows and demonstrating its practical value remain important challenges. That led the team to Nucleus, which he described as a ground-up, cancer-specific, institution-centered clinical intelligence platform designed to turn vast amounts of underutilized patient data into meaningful insights at the point of care.

Starting with pancreatic cancer, Nucleus helps clinicians identify comparable patients, understand their treatment journeys and outcomes, and visualize treatment-related toxicities, all within the routine clinical workflow, according to Manne. He said the goal is to make the collective clinical experience of an institution accessible when caring for the next patient. He said the team recently completed its first round of clinical pilot testing with support from Pannaga Malalur, Arjun Mittra and Shafia Rahman, and is now advancing toward a more comprehensive platform incorporating longitudinal treatment and toxicity intelligence. Manne said he is proud to lead the initiative through a collaboration between Ohio State, its comprehensive cancer center and Microsoft, alongside a multidisciplinary team.

The ESMO AI and Digital Oncology Congress 2026 is an international congress organized by the European Society for Medical Oncology, focusing on the application of artificial intelligence and digital technologies in oncology. According to the article, the congress brings attention to the growing role of AI and digital innovation in the field and provides a dedicated setting for exploring developments at the intersection of technology and cancer care. It highlights the importance of digital oncology as an evolving area within modern cancer research and clinical practice. Manne said he was looking forward to sharing the work and connecting with colleagues shaping the future of AI in oncology.

Articles.Title: Ashish Manne: New AI Platform Nucleus Aims to Transform Clinical Decision-Making in Oncology

stories.Headline: Alexa von Tobel says AI will make entrepreneurship the everyday job of the future
stories.Summary:
Alexa von Tobel, a serial founder who left Harvard Business School in 2008 to start the online financial planning firm LearnVest and later sold it to Northwestern Mutual in 2015, said on CNBC's Changemakers podcast that entrepreneurship will become the everyday job of the future. She told Julia Boorstin that she believes every person in America will be empowered to be entrepreneurial because of artificial intelligence. Von Tobel, who co-founded the venture capital firm Inspired Capital with former U.S. Commerce Secretary Penny Pritzker in 2019, said she reviews as many as 100 business pitches a week. She said anyone with any skill set can turn it into a business because of AI, and she described entrepreneurship as a commitment that will become low-stakes.

Von Tobel said Inspired Capital, which backs startups that could be worth $10 billion or more, has invested in ShopMy, a platform that lets creators earn commissions by sharing product recommendations and uses AI matching to connect brands with creators. She said platforms like ShopMy offer people more ways to build income around what they already know, with flexibility for those balancing work with family or caregiving. She also suggested entrepreneurship could serve as a fallback for people between jobs, letting them earn money while they retrain or look for their next role. She stressed that AI will enable businesses but the founder must always have the final say, adding that it is still her judgment making the final call.

On the data side, Liya Palagashvili, a labor economist and director of the Labor Policy Project at George Mason University's Mercatus Center, recently told CNBC that her preliminary research shows new business formation is rising among owners who do not expect to hire employees. In industries highly exposed to AI, business applications without early signs of hiring rose 26.8% from the first quarter of 2024 through the first quarter of 2026. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on David Senra's Founders podcast that we are about to see the greatest boom in people starting smaller businesses that we have ever seen. Von Tobel said her own fundraising for LearnVest taught her that some investors advising her had never built a company, a gap that shaped her idea for Inspired Capital.

Von Tobel said she meets with as many as 100 companies a week but may ultimately invest in fewer than eight firms a year, and she looks for founders with a distinct view of their industry and what it could become. She said those founders will have thought deeply about what the world should look like in five, 10 or 20 years. Her interest in financial literacy came from her own early life, after her father died when she was 14 and her mother, a nurse practitioner, had to navigate the family's finances alone. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the podcast episode and the research cited.

stories.Headline: FOLIO advises Goldman Sachs International on AI-driven allocation for SBI Okasan's new ROBOPRO fund
stories.Summary:
FOLIO, a subsidiary of FOLIO Holdings in the SBI group, announced on November 13, 2026, that a new publicly offered unit-type investment trust called "Goldman Sachs Corporate Bonds / ROBOPRO Strategy Fund 2026-12" will be set up by SBI Okasan Asset Management. FOLIO will provide investment advice on asset allocation ratios to Goldman Sachs International for the index linked to the fund. A securities registration statement was filed with the Kanto Local Finance Bureau on Friday, November 13, 2026, and subscription opens on Tuesday, December 1, 2026. The fund is nicknamed "Robotto Plus 5."

The fund invests in yen-denominated bonds issued by Luminis II Limited, backed by bonds issued or guaranteed by The Goldman Sachs Group, and aims for a redemption value about six years after launch that exceeds the principal. Its performance has two parts: a stable portion that invests heavily in the Goldman Sachs bonds to aim to preserve principal in yen terms, and an aggressive portion that aims for performance-linked returns tied to the ROBOPRO Strategy VT5 Index. That index uses asset allocations calculated by FOLIO with AI predictions, with risk control applied by Goldman Sachs International to keep annual risk at around 5 percent, and it covers seven assets: global stocks, bonds, REITs and gold, with investment ratios of up to about 150 percent. It follows the existing series of funds dated 2025-12, 2026-03, 2026-06 and 2026-10.

FOLIO says it has built a track record in AI-based asset management services since starting with its AI investing service ROBOPRO, and that AI use in publicly offered investment trusts is growing. It says it provides investment advice based on AI strategies, together with its group company AlpacaTech, for funds including the ROBOPRO Fund and the SBI Okasan NASDAQ AI Active Fund, both set up by SBI Okasan Asset Management. FOLIO says it will keep expanding and improving AI-based asset management and offer financial solutions through various approaches to help more people build assets. ROBOPRO is a registered trademark of FOLIO.

FOLIO is registered as a financial instruments business operator with the Kanto Local Finance Bureau under number 2983 and belongs to the Japan Securities Dealers Association and the Investment Management Association of Japan. Its securities account opening and management fees are free, but investing in its products may involve set fees and necessary expenses per product, and losses can occur, including below the invested principal, due to changes in share prices, exchange rates, interest rates and other indicators. FOLIO Holdings, led by President and CEO Shinichiro Kai and established on April 1, 2019, is listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange Prime Market and is part of the SBI Holdings group. FOLIO, led by President Masafumi Yotsumoto and established on December 10, 2015, is based in Chiyoda Ward, Tokyo.
